News.title: Cops hunt homeless knifeman who ‘tried to rape woman’ after body of Brit was found stuffed in suitcase
News.content:
GREEK cops are searching for a heavily-tattooed homeless man in connection with the murder of a Brit who was found stuffed in a suitcase.

The suspect, named Markos, is reportedly a volatile drug user and heavy drinker who allegedly tried to rape a woman at knifepoint last year.



He also lived in the derelict building in Kypseli, central Athens, where Elisabeth Ross, 38, was found murdered.

Markos has not been seen since the suitcase was discovered, with detectives combing the city for his whereabouts.



People in the area say it is well-known that Markos tried to rape a Bulgarian woman at knifepoint as she walked through an abandoned car park last year.

Hamid Reza, a homeless man who lives in a makeshift shelter yards from the building, said police told him that Markos is their number one suspect.

The Iranian, 67, told the Daily Mail: “They want to find and question him very quickly.

“They have been asking a lot of people and driving around the area looking for him.



“Everybody knows that Markos carries a knife, and local women are scared of him.

“He was always around this area, even living in the car park, but nobody has seen him since the body was discovered.”

Markos has been described as around 40 years old and heavily covered in tattoos.



He has reportedly lived in the building for months and has made an improvised “living room” there.

A Greek police source said: “We have a lead on a homeless man but can’t say any more.

“We want to question a particular individual, but we are also looking for a number of other people as part of this investigation.”

It has meanwhile been claimed that Elisabeth was a committed Christian who may have been in the area known for homelessness for compassionate reasons.

She had reportedly been visiting Greece for over seven years and worked with a number of NGOs that supported vulnerable people.



Elisabeth had arrived in Greece in late June and was staying with a Greek couple until July 15.

She told them she was going to meet some American friends in the Kypseli district.

But she may have deliberately misled friends because she did not want them to worry about her whereabouts.

Elisabeth’s body was found in a suitcase at the building on Evelpidon Street by another homeless man on July 18.

Her phone remained active until the day in Athens she was publicly identified on July 29.



Cops say a mystery user – believed to be the murder suspect – was texting friends and families to create the impression that she was alive.

They have not yet been able to locate the phone.

One text, sent to a Greek friend on July 15, read: “I need some time – I’m going to a Greek island.”

Other family members confirmed they had received similar texts in which she claimed she wanted to be alone and needed time to herself.

Cops are also trying to trace how Lisa’s body ended up in the building, believing the killer may have taken her there on foot.



The homeless man who made the grim discovery has insisted that the suitcase was not in the building the two days prior.

Officers have been combing the area for security cameras that might have captured the suitcase dump.

Local hotels and residences are also being examined, with police speculating that the body was likely taken to the building from close quarters.

And Greek authorities are fast forwarding crucial tests that could determine the cause of the Briton’s death, the Sun has learned.

Police spokesperson Konstantina Dimoglidou said: “We have made it a priority so we can have results in the coming days.



“Then we will know how she died. This can’t wait.”

Tests on blood, urine and vital organ tissues will be key to determining whether Elisabeth died as a result of foul play.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Police have also not ruled out alcohol or drugs playing a role.

But they revealed that whoever stuffed her in the suitcase had been “careful”, adding: “There were no fingerprints or traces of DNA on the suitcase. Whoever did it was careful.”

News.title: Shocking moment driver ‘cheats death’ as car flips and rolls twice in middle of M25 with wreckage strewn across motorway
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a driver and passenger appeared to cheat death after their car flipped and rolled twice across the M25.

Dramatic dashcam footage shows the black hatchback suddenly overturning before barrel rolling across the motorway and coming to rest on its side.



Debris was left strewn across the carriageway as stunned motorists slammed on the brakes.

The horror crash happened between junctions 12 and 13 near Staines, Surrey, on July 5.



Footage shows the hatchback moving into the middle lane of the five-lane motorway before clipping the vehicle in front at what appears to be low speed.

Moments later, the car suddenly flips over, its airbag goes off as it rolls twice across the tarmac before sliding to a halt on its side.



A man inside the car capturing the footage gasps: “S***.”

A woman then shouts: “F***.”



The man adds: “Oh my God.”

The woman replies: “What happened?” before dialling 999.

Traffic on the 70mph motorway quickly ground to a standstill.

Several motorists got out of their vehicles to help the occupants.

Two people were treated at the scene before being taken to hospital for further checks.



Motorist Lesley Shaw said: “What happened?

“It just suddenly flipped.”

Vik Singh added: “What the f***.”

The footage also sparked debate online after a silver BMW 1 Series was seen driving past the wreckage.

Martin Taylor said: “That’s a BMW driver for you, don’t give a t*** about anybody.”



Stephen Reeves added: “I thought it was illegal to leave the scene of an accident?”

Others defended the BMW driver’s actions.

Matt James said: “Could have been a woman with kids in the car.

“I wouldn’t stop in the fast lane with passengers.

“However, you’d pull up further down on the hard shoulder like.”



Jo Atherton added: “The BMW did the right thing.

“They were so close that they would’ve gone on fire if the overturned car did.

“They needed to get out of the way for emergency services.”

Matt Leith said: “Sitting still in a high speed lane isn’t safe, even in that situation.”

Cops said they were called to the M25 between junctions 12 and 13 at around 5.40pm on Sunday, July 5, following reports of a crash involving two vehicles.



Ambulance crews, firefighters and National Highways officers also attended the scene.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The two occupants of the overturned car were treated by paramedics before being taken to hospital for medical treatment.

The South East Coast Ambulance Service said both patients were assessed at the roadside before being transported to St Peter’s Hospital in Chertsey for further checks.

News.title: Sick daughter, 32, ‘stabbed dad to death then cut out heart & laid it on his stomach’ but told cops they ‘got on well’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BLOODY END Sick daughter, 32, ‘stabbed dad to death then cut out heart & laid it on his stomach’ but told cops they ‘got on well’

A TWISTED daughter allegedly stabbed her dad to death and then cut out his heart and placed it on his stomach.

Serena Dolnics, 32, was found covered in blood when police raided a home in northwestern Indiana on Sunday.



Officers reportedly found her 69-year-old father butchered, lying in a pool of blood on the floor.

Gregory Dolnics was next to blood-soaked furniture with slash wounds to his head, face, neck and hands.



Charging documents revealed his heart had been carved out and left lying on his stomach.

Police also found Serena with slice wounds on her hands that she blamed on gardening tools.

She reportedly told police the pair “get along really well, but have small tiffs and that they both get over it quickly”.

An autopsy later confirmed Gregory died from “multiple sharp force injuries” and his death was ruled a homicide.



Three knives were recovered inside the property with blood on them, according to WGN-TV.

Police initially reported to the home in Valparaiso – 80km southeast of Chicago – at around 8pm.

This was following calls from concerned members of Gregory’s family who were unable to reach him.

While one of the family members dialled 911, they started receiving calls and texts from a friend of Serena, who had made the harrowing discovery.

Serena has since been arrested and charged with murder.



She appeared in court on Thursday morning via video link wearing a suicide vest as she pleaded not guilty.

A judge ordered her to be held without bond, and she will appear in court on August 1 to determine the status of her legal representation.

Prior to the alleged incident, Serena had a long criminal history.

Her offenses include pleading guilty for substance abuse in 2024, driving while intoxicated in 2017 and public intoxication in 2016, NWI.com reported.

Dolnics’ heartbroken sister, Jennifer, launched a GoFundMe to help cover the costs of her father’s funeral.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Recently my father was murdered by my sister,” she wrote.

“This incident came and took a complete toll on me and my family. We have no preparation or anything to start.”

News.title: Teen fights for life after being stabbed in city centre as streets cordoned off & man arrested at major UK airport
News.content:
BLADE HORROR Teen fights for life after being stabbed in city centre as streets cordoned off & man arrested at major UK airport

A MAN has been arrested at an airport after a stabbing in the city centre.

Emergency services were called to the scene following reports of an incident at around 12.50pm today on Church Street in Manchester.

Cops arrested the suspect at Manchester Airport this evening.



Police found a 19-year-old victim with injuries “consistent with a stabbing”.



He was rushed to hospital with “life-threatening” injuries but is now in a stable condition, Greater Manchester Police reported.

Cops cordoned off a large stretch of the street in the Northern Quarter this afternoon, with blockades extending to other connecting streets.

The suspect, who is in his early 20s, was located three hours after the incident and arrested on suspicion of Section 18 assault.



He remains in custody as the enquiry continues.

Detective Chief Inspector Chris Woodburn said: “Following the incident on Church Street this afternoon, our officers have worked at an incredible pace to piece together what had happened, which has led to us arresting a suspect at the Airport.

“In any incident of this nature, it is understandable for those who live and work in the area, including members of the public who have come to visit Manchester to feel apprehensive.

“I would like to reassure everyone that there will be an increased police presence in the area as we head into the evening.”



He urged anyone with information that could assist the investigation to come forward.

More to follow… For the latest news on this story keep checking back at The Sun Online

News.title: Heatwave reveals lost 300-year-old garden at Britain’s ‘Greatest Palace’ that was once home to Winston Churchill
News.content:
PLOT THICKENS Heatwave reveals lost 300-year-old garden at Britain’s ‘Greatest Palace’ that was once home to Winston Churchill

A HEATWAVE has revealed a long lost 300-year-old garden at Britain’s “Greatest Palace” – that was once home to Winston Churchill.

The recent spell of hot and dry weather has uncovered a hidden outline of an 18th century parterre at Blenheim Palace, Oxfordshire.



The term parterre is taken from the French word meaning “on the ground”.

It refers to an ornamental garden arranged around flower beds, paths and symmetrical patterns.



The original parterre was created in 1705 by royal gardener Henry Wise and stretched across the full width of the palace, surrounded by a high stone wall.

Recent heatwave conditions revealed the outline of Blenheim’s lost garden, which was dismantled by landscape gardener Lancelot “Capability” Brown when he transformed the gardens in the 1760s.



The sudden appearance of the buried garden has offered staff and historians a unique opportunity to study a landscape that has not been visible for centuries.

Andy Mills, Head Gardener at Blenheim Palace, said the conditions had provided an extraordinary glimpse into the estate’s past.



“The excessively dry weather has given us a fascinating bird’s-eye view into Blenheim’s past, allowing us to trace the intricate design and scale of the original parterre,” Andy said.

“It’s a brilliant reminder of the formal gardens that came before and the layers of history that continue to shape the Palace’s landscape.”

Andy has a 10-year-plan to restore the gardens to their former glory.

He plans on reintroducing features and elements that have disappeared over the last three centuries.

The work will be the biggest shake up to the 90 acres of gardens in over 100 years.



The palace was built in the early 18th century as a reward to John Churchill, the 1st Duke of Marlborough, for his victory at the Battle of Blenheim.

The site remains the ancestral home of the Dukes of Marlborough.

The UNESCO World Heritage Site is also famous as the birthplace of Sir Winston Churchill, who was born there in 1874.



Elsewhere, in Wales the scorching heatwaves has revealed a long-lost tomb as ancient as the Pyramids.

Incredible shots taken from above reveal the outline of the 5000-year-old burial mound, once used by ancient Britons.

The mound would have served as a communal burial site and sacred gathering space during the neolithic age, the final phase of the Stone Age.

It is believed bodies were left outside of the barrow to decompose, before the cleaned bones were moved inside the stone chambers.

Aerial archaeologist Dr Toby Driver spotted the barrow in the parched landscape of Welshpool in mid-Wales.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Toby described the image as a “remarkable” cropmark of a “rectangular Neolithic long barrow” dating back several millenia.

According to the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales, its size can be determined by the tractor lines in the field.

News.title: Andy Burnham’s time away from No10 sparks concern inside Whitehall as Louise Haigh urges bold governing
News.content:
OUT OF OFFICE Andy Burnham’s time away from No10 sparks concern inside Whitehall as Louise Haigh urges bold governing

WHITEHALL mandarins are growing concerned by how little time Andy Burnham has spent in Downing Street since becoming PM.

The new Prime Minister has kicked off his premiership with a tour of Britain, using his first days in office to announce a string of flagship policies rather than bedding into No10.



His approach even prompted First Secretary of State Louise Haigh to joke at her Cabinet Office all-staff meeting earlier this week that No10 was “extremely distressed” by how often he was away from the building.

She stressed the PM was simply “so dedicated and committed” to getting out into the country.



But The Sun understands some Whitehall officials have expressed concern about how little time Mr Burnham has spent at the heart of Government during the crucial opening days of his premiership.

Addressing civil servants, Ms Haigh urged officials to “take your cue from the Prime Minister’s ambition”.



She said: “He is not the kind of politician that has to have a full plan before he starts diagnosing the problems in the country.”

Instead, she said the PM would set the direction of travel before tasking officials with working out how to deliver it.

Ms Haigh added: “Let’s start with the outcome and the vision and then let’s consider every possible way to achieve that, no matter how risky or politically unpalatable it seems.

“Put it in front of us and let’s thrash it out.”

News.title: Europe on edge after 60k migrants storm Spain enclave as France tightens borders & Italy suspends EU travel zone
News.content:
EUROPE is on the edge after more than 60,000 migrants stormed a Spanish enclave – sparking calls to suspend free movement from the country.

France has tightened its borders in response to the deepening crisis and Italy has suspended EU Schengen free-travel deal with the country.



The Schengen agreement is a treaty that allows passport-free travel across 29 European countries.

But after thousands of migrants “completely invaded” Ceuta – an enclave in northern Africa – concerned governments are rallying to remove Spain.



Finland backed calls for the Mediterranean country to be booted from the pact after France introduced stricter measures on its border.

Italy does not share a land border with Spain, but its move will mean people travelling by boat or plane between the two countries will need to show their passports.



Italy’s interior minister also said Paris has agreed to strengthen controls along the Franco-Italian land border to try to prevent any undocumented migrants from crossing.

Giorgia Meloni‘s government previously said it was considering “extraordinary measures” in response to the crisis in Ceuta.

It comes as terrified locals in the enclave are cowering in their homes, with some considering fleeing.



Shops have been looted, cars set on fire and the streets have been turned into an open toilet in “apocalyptic” scenes.

On top of the estimated 60,000 to have entered Ceuta in the last 24 hours, another 400 crossed into Melilla, another enclave around 200 miles away.

One Spanish business owner told RTVE: “It’s like an apocalypse. Waves of people everywhere.”



He said authorities had “no capacity” to control the chaos and that migrants are now bathing in public fountains and sleeping in the streets.

Around 25,000 people have already returned to Morocco after the deadly surge.

At least 57 migrants died in the perilous crossing, many drowning.



Others were crushed to death in a terrifying stampede near a beach border crossing.

Thousands of children are thought to be among the huge crowds.

One local said: “Businesses closed. Shops shut because if you open a business, it gets overrun.

“We’re scared. The streets are packed. There are no measures in place. It’s every man for himself. They’re not giving us any help.”

Shocking footage shows migrants appearing to break into homes in Ceuta and cars being set alight on the Melilla border.



Furious locals in Ceuta claim they have had to hide away and bolt up shops and businesses, with some considering leaving the city where the Spanish Army has been mobilised amid violent clashes.

Spain’s soft-touch Supreme Court has come under fire and blamed for the recent numbers being so high.

A ruling stated that migrants who arrive by sea should not be subject to immediate expulsion as they are not crossing a physical land border.

The decision has been exploited by people-smuggling gangs and brought with it a wave of undocumented migration.

In the majority of cases, migrants entered the Spanish territory by walking along the Tarajal breakwater, a stone barrier marking the maritime border where Europe meets Morocco, and by jumping into the sea.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ceuta and Melilla, Spanish autonomous cities in northern Morocco, have the European Union‘s only land borders with Africa.

Both experience surges in attempted crossings by migrants, but the scale of the latest rush appeared unprecedented.

News.title: Hunt for ‘Sharkzilla’ terrorising New York coast & leaving trail of horror as scientists fear beast is nuclear mutant
News.content:
THE hunt is on for a mysterious predator lurking off the coast of New York as scientists fear the beast is a nuclear mutant.

Marine experts were horrified when a humpback whale was found with 24-inch bite marks, and the carcass of a 400lb tuna was torn to shreds.



The unnerving scenes have now turned Montauk into a real-life hunting ground.

Local shark expert Craig O’Connell said the wave of brutal attacks could indicate the return of enormous predators long thought to have vanished from beneath the waves.



He also warned it raised the possibility that nuclear waste has been leaking into the ocean, affecting the wildlife.

Marine experts now face the daunting task of hunting what could be a mutant shark that is faster, stronger and deadlier than the rest of its species.

O’Connell launched an investigation in September 2025 following reports of marine animals being savaged off Long Island.

With a storm brewing, the team had just 30 hours to locate the creature, and collect a tissue sample for testing.



In the meantime, they dubbed the monster “Sharkzilla”.

Montauk was once a popular destination where fishermen could encounter all sorts of large animals, but years of intense fishing have devasted populations.

“In the past, this is the place you came to catch monster sharks,” O’Connell said.

“There are so many records right here off the shores of Montauk.

“All these monster sharks were completely fished out. They’re gone.



“But all the evidence we are seeing is telling me that all these big sharks might be back.

“I know those big sharks are out there, and we are going to find them.”

The team’s search efforts lead them to the Hudson Canyon, a gigantic underwater chasm that plunges to depths of 4,000ft.



Comparable in scale to the Grand Canyon, the pitch-black cavity provides the perfect hiding spot for some of the ocean’s largest predators.

Located approximately 160km off the coast of Montauk, it also has a dark history.

“In the late 1960s, they dumped 15,000 barrels of nuclear waste in the Hudson Canyon,” O’Connell said.

“Ten years later, they went out to check on these barrels, and they were all leaking.”

However, O’Connell stressed the controversial theory linking the nuclear waste to the unknown predator remains unproven.



“Radioactive leaks could be impacting wildlife, even top predators,” he said.

“If animals are subjected to nuclear waste, this could cause genetic mutations and abnormal growth.

“If this predator is genetically altered, it could be faster, stronger and deadlier than any predator on Earth. We are calling it Sharkzilla.”

After sending a camera into the depths, terrifying footage showed a huge mouth emerge from the darkness.

‘That is an absolutely massive great white shark,’ O’Connell said.



After further sightings, eventually a giant female mako charged toward to the boat.

Makos are the fastest sharks in the ocean and are capable of moving at speeds exceeding 64 kilometres per hour,

“This is Sharkzilla,” O’Connell declared.

Measuring nearly 12ft long, the female mako appeared powerful enough to have inflicted the enormous wounds found on animals off Long Island.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

After some initial struggles, O’Connell was able to attach a tracker tag and retrieve a tissue sample before the team headed home.



Tests ultimately found no evidence that the mako had radioactive mutations, destroying the team’s exciting theory.

News.title: Naples earthquake live: 4.7-mag Italy quake causes landslide and power outage
News.content:
Residents in Naples have been left terrified after a powerful earthquake caused damage to the Italian city - it registered at 4.7 magnitude

A powerful earthquake has struck southern Italy, causing damage in the city of Naples.

The 4.7 magnitude quake has left neighbourhoods without power, and residents are taking to the streets in fear. It occurred just before 8pm (local time).

According to data released by the INGV (National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology), the magnitude was 4.7. Power outages have been reported from Pizzofalcone to Fuorigrotta, and there has been a massive landslide in Pozzuoli.

News.title: Manchester mayoral election results LIVE: Labour and Reform go to second round of votes after major delays
News.content:
Results for Britain's biggest-ever by-election are expected at any moment, with Labour confident Bev Craig will be named Mayor of Greater Manchester at some point this evening

Manchester mayoral election results LIVE: Labour and Reform go to second round of votes after major delays

The Mayor of Greater Manchester race will progress to a second round of votes, it has been confirmed, as Labour's Bev Craig hopes to succeed Andy Burnham.

Following a long night of counting across Greater Manchester, Craig and Reform UK's Sian Astley will be going through to the second round. Tom Stannard, Manchester returning officer, told counters at Manchester's Co-op Live arena that a second preference count will take place.

He has told counters to "focus on accuracy over speed" after several hours of waiting in the room. Ms Craig is the favourite to succeed Andy Burnham, who vacated the post when he became MP for Makerfield last month. The new Prime Minister has since set up a No10 in the North in the heart of Manchester.

Reform UK were initially tipped to be a strong challenger for the coveted post, which is set to become more powerful as Mr Burnham devolves power from Westminster.

News.title: F-35B fighter jet crashes at Miramar Air Base as US Marines address 'mishap'
News.content:
F-35B fighter jet crashes at Miramar Air Base as US Marines address 'mishap'

The jet went down near the Miramar Air Base in San Diego, California, following what the US Marines called a 'Class A mishap' - the pilot has been rushed to a medical facility

View 2 Images The wreckage near Miramar Air Base in California (Image: Sky10)

An F-35B fighter jet has crashed near a California air base, with the pilot rushed to a medical facility following what the US Marines called a "Class A mishap".

‌



The jet went down Friday afternoon near the Miramar Air Base in San Diego.

‌



The US Marines described the incident as a "Class A mishap" - the most severe mishap category used to describe incidents where the damage totals more than $2million, a military aircraft is destroyed, or a service member has died.

‌



The pilot ejected, was recovered and then taken to a medical facility, the statement added.

"We can confirm a Class A mishap involving a Marine Corps F-35B in the vicinity of MCAS Miramar," a spokesperson said.

View 2 Images The US Marines said the pilot ejected (Image: Sky10)

‌



"The pilot ejected and has been recovered. More information will be made available shortly."

Aerial footage from a news helicopter showed smoke billowing from the wreckage in a dirt field, with multiple military and firefighting vehicles and people standing nearby.

Flame retardant material appeared to be placed on the ground, and at least one person was seen spraying the wreckage with a fire hose.

Article continues below

Candace Hadley, a spokesperson for San Diego Fire, said firefighters were on scene to respond to a vegetation fire that sparked near the crash site. She referred additional questions to Miramar.

The F-35B comes from a family of advanced stealth fighter jets flown by the Marine Corps, Navy and Air Force.

The "B" version is capable of vertical landings and has an engine designed for short take-offs.

News.title: Washington fire live: 'Explosions' at factory as 'close windows' warning issued
News.content:
Thick black smoke coming from the scene of the fire

Emergency services rushed to the incident at a factory in the Crowther Industrial Estate, Washington, in Tyne and Wear, with witnesses telling of 'several explosions'

Massive plumes of smoke can be seen coming from a raging fire at a factory after reports of "several explosions" in the North East.

Emergency services rushed to the incident in the Crowther Industrial Estate, Washington, in Tyne and Wear, with witnesses saying that there's no signs of the fire easing.

Northumbria Police says officers are on the scene to support the Tyne and Wear Fire and Rescue Service in responding to the fire in Washington, with a 'cordon currently in place'.

Pictures from the scene show five fire brigade appliances and an aerial ladder platform dispatched. Thick black smoke is billowing into the sky which can be seen for miles.

News.title: Drone images show Suffolk wildfire devastation as helicopters scrambled
News.content:
A wildfire ravaging Dunwich Heath in Suffolk is still 'unstable' according to the local council with the number of firefighters at the scene increasing

A wildfire that has destroyed an area the size of 200 football pitches in Suffolk remains "unstable".

The blaze at Dunwich Heath has devastated wildlife habitats, which could now take up to 25 years to recover, after it went up in flames at about 5pm on Wednesday.

Hundreds of people were evacuated from caravan sites, and they have now been given a short window to collect their belongings.

National Trust director-general Hilary McGrady described the “heartbreaking” loss of important habitat - which was home to rare species such as nightjars, skylarks and the rare Dartford warbler - due to the blaze.

The land was also home to adders, lizards and slow worms, as well as butterflies including the rare silver-studded blue.

The lowland heath habitat is one of the UK’s rarest, and an estimated 92% of it has been lost in England over the last 120 years, the charity said.

News.title: Family of missing US tourist issues heartbreaking update amid search in Grenada
News.content:
Family of missing US tourist issues heartbreaking update amid search in Grenada

Elizabeth Waddell, 44, was last seen leaving her beachside Airbnb on Grenada to go for a swim - the alarm was raised when her friend found her towel abandoned beside the water

View 4 Images Cailen, the husband of missing Elizabeth Waddel, has issued an update (Image: Facebook)

The family of a tourist who went missing from a Caribbean island are flying home after days of searching for her.

‌



Elizabeth Waddell, from the US, was last seen on July 22 leaving her beachside Airbnb on the tropical island of Grenada to go for a swim.

‌



The 44-year-old was seen going for her solo swim at Grand Anse Beach around midday, but after entering the water and swimming beneath the jetty she vanished.

‌



There were reports of a possible sighting at around 5:30pm, just before the alarm was raised by her friend, Heather, who was vacationing with her on the island. Elizabeth’s husband Cailen said this week that the family had “done what we can here” and would now return to the US.

View 4 Images Some of the last known images of Elizabeth Waddell leaving her apartment (Image: WRAL News)

“To everyone invested in Liz’s story: The family will travel home today, Friday, July 31. We have done what we can here, and the investigation will continue,” his post read.

‌



Her family members have said they were not ready to take part in interviews, but asked that people keep on sharing information about the case.

“Without you, so many people would not know her story,” Cailen said, thanking members of the press for publicising his wife’s disappearance.

He also thanked the people of Grenada for the genuine concern and support shown by everyone they had encountered there.

‌



View 4 Images The family have been desperately searching on Caribbean island

“To the Grenadian people: Thank you so, so much. Every Grenadian we have encountered has warmly welcomed us and expressed so much genuine concern for Liz,” he said.

There were also thanks for the hundreds of donors who contributed to a GoFundMe to help cover the cost of the family’s search efforts.

‌



In a deeply moving tribute to his missing wife, Cailen said: “On a more personal note, I am simply not ready to write about all the things Liz means to me. We met in 2003 at American Dance Festival in Durham and have been together ever since.

“I realised this year that Liz and I have been together longer in life than we have been apart. We balance each other, and that makes for a great partnership."

He added: “For now, both of our Instagram accounts, as well as Liz’s business and personal YouTube channels, are the best examples of who she is.”

‌



Alongside the touching message, Cailen shared a picture of his wife on top of a fake crocodile on a day out at an aquarium, which he said captured her “sense of fun”.

View 4 Images Elizabeth's family will continue to fight for answers

“I was looking back through photos last night, and this picture popped up in my memories from exactly 22 years ago today,” he said. Elizabeth has been described by loved ones as an experienced traveler, an avid swimmer and adventurer who loved exploring new places.

‌



Police in Grenada are continuing to investigate her disappearance.

“After careful and thoughtful consultation with family, local authorities, the U.S. Embassy, and others here in Grenada, I join authorities in believing there was no foul play,” her husband said in a statement.

A friend told reporters how Heather went to look for her friend after she didn't return from her swim, only to find her towel by the pier. Her phone and other belongings were left at the Airbnb they had booked together for the three-week trip.

Article continues below

A missing person’s report was filed when she failed to appear, and her family and friends flew out to search for her. The Grenada Coast Guard, divers and canine units have been searching the island’s southern coastline for several days, authorities said. Meanwhile, the FBI and the US Embassy have been alerted.

The investigation into her disappearance continues.

News.title: Donald Trump gives curt answer to question about Gianni Infantino's FIFA World Cup selloff
News.content:
Donald Trump gives curt answer to question about Gianni Infantino's FIFA World Cup selloff

Donald Trump was asked whether he'd spoken to Gianni Infantino about his plan to sell stakes in the FIFA World Cup to a firm linked to his family

View Image Trump and Infantino have grown very close (Image: Bradley Collyer/PA Wire)

Donald Trump has denied speaking to Gianni Infantino about his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to a firm linked to his family.

‌



The US President was hit with the question after a televised Cabinet meeting at Camp David. Infantino's secret proposal, revealed on Tuesday, would spin off its commercial operations in a new $20 billion subsidiary 20% owned by private investors, whose core investor would be a New York investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

‌



"No, I never spoke to him about it," Trump insisted.

‌



Trump has developed a close friendship with Infantino - and has spent a great deal of time with him in recent weeks, while the World Cup was taking place in North America. Infantino has been courting Trump since early in his second Presidency.

Within weeks of returning to the Oval Office, a replica of the World Cup was put on display - a gift from Infantino. Trump was later allowed to display a replica of the World Club Cup trophy in the Oval.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



And most prominently, knowing Trump coveted a Nobel Peace Prize, something he is unlikely to be in contention for, Infantino invented the "FIFA Peace Prize" earlier this year, and awarded it to Trump. Trump and Infantino spent most of the day together during the World Cup Final in New Jersey, less than two weeks ago.

Days later, it was reported that Trump wants Infantino to be named the next UN Secretary General, something that is even less likely to happen than Trump's peace prize ambitions. Last year, Infantino opened a new FIFA office inside Trump tower, deepening ties between the football body and the US President.

Senior FIFA adviser Carlos Cordeiro, who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned Friday to protest its private equity plan.

‌



“I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup,” Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker, said in a statement resigning as adviser to FIFA President Gianni Infantino that urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.

Cordeiro often joined Infantino on working visits to meet Trump at the White House in recent years.

“Let me be clear. I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally,” the former U.S. Soccer Federation president said, calling the $20 billion commercial subsidiary “a bad deal for football.”

Article continues below

“Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking, I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away” he said. “That is why this proposal should be rejected.”

News.title: Woman saw start of Suffolk wildfires and tried to stamp it out - but 'it went up like a torch'
News.content:
Woman saw start of Suffolk wildfires and tried to stamp it out - but 'it went up like a torch'

The Mirror captured the images on Dunwich Heath, near Sizewell nuclear power station, after firefighters took us inside the cordoned-off site in Suffolk

View 7 Images Emergency services near the scene of the wildfire at Dunwich Heath, near Leiston (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

Burnt out, blackened and still smouldering, this is part of the heartbreaking aftermath of the Suffolk wildfire.

‌



The Mirror captured the startling images on Dunwich Heath, near Sizewell nuclear power station, after firefighters took us inside the cordoned-off site, estimated to span 150 hectares - the size of 220 football pitches. Other poignant images showed firefighters covered in soot, rescue workers surrounded by the barren landscape and a camp site abandoned by residents and holidaymakers since the blaze began two days ago.

‌



Local resident Charlotte Du Cann today told how she witnessed the fire begin and tried to stamp it out with a friend before calling 999 at around 5pm on Wednesday. Speaking about the aftermath, Ms Du Cann told us: "It's just devastating and absolutely heartbreaking. It's like a bomb site".

‌



View 7 Images Two fire service workers being driven away from the site covered in soot (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily mirror)

The writer and editor, 70, said she and a friend were alerted to the fire after hearing the crackle of the blaze before smelling smoke near a kissing gate in woodland. She said: "I heard it first... this crackle. I thought 'that sounds like fire'. I looked down and my friend said 'I can smell smoke'.

"We went down and saw this circle on fire, maybe 20ft across. We tried to stamp it out, but it didn't work. We didn't have enough force. We were trying to stamp it out for a few minutes, but then it just caught the heather... umph... up it went, it hit the Scots pine and just got out of hand." Ms Du Cann added: "It went up like a torch - the noise of it was horrible. It escalated fast - within minutes. It was furious."

‌



Asked if she was scared, she said: "You can't be scared if you've got to act, you've got to get in and do it. But I was pretty stunned afterwards."

Ms Du Cann, who lives in the nearby village of Eastbridge, did not see any evidence of what caused the ignition. She said: "People are saying it's human induced, but we don't know. There was nobody else there, we didn't see anyone, didn't see a cigarette butt, camping equipment or a BBQ - nothing. It wasn't by the path, it was away, not somewhere somebody would casually smoke a cigarette."

View 7 Images Smoke rises at the scene of the wildfire (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

‌



More than 100 firefighters, including some from as far afield as London, Sussex and West Yorkshire, are tonight still fighting the blaze in other parts of the sprawling rural area, which is a flagship UK nature reserve. They are also using water backpacks, 4x4 vehicles and quad bikes in order to get water to hard to reach areas while also being helped by a helicopter dropping up to 1,000 litre buckets of water over the area, which includes RSPB Minsmere.

Officials today said the winds are currently pushing the fire away from Sizewell nuclear plant and added the bird sanctuary, which includes marshes and other waterways, is acting as a natural fire break between the fire and the plant.

Around 200 families, including residents and holiday makers staying in caravans and lodges near the heath, were evacuated around two miles to a pop-up rescue centre at Westleton Village Hall late on Wednesday night after police banged on their doors telling them they were in danger.

‌



Those who had remained in the area were finally allowed to collect essential belongings from their properties this afternoon after being escorted in and out by police officers in what officials described as "a very small window of opportunity" lasting just 15 minutes.

View 7 Images A general view of tents that were evacuated near the scene (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

Among them were holidaymakers Dave Johnson, 67, a retired IT technician, and his wife Jen, 55, an artist, own two lodges at Cliff House holiday park. The couple drove in convoy, escorted by the police, to pick up their essentials from their lodge.

‌



Dave said: “It looked better than I expected, although there’s still fires breaking out. We didn’t go as far as where most of the destruction is so you get the false impression it’s probably better than it is. From what we could see, [Cliff House] it’s alright at the moment, but there’s talk of the fires still.”

David Knapp, 59, and his wife Alison, 59, from Herne Bay, were also allowed to retrieve their motorhome. David said: “When you’re driving down, there’s no sign of fire. There’s no smoke, nothing. Its totally clear. You pull in the campsite and its absolutely deserted, all you see is empty tents. There’s no people."

He added: “The motorhome stinks of fire. The window was slightly open and the vent was open so it stinks of smoke. I was going to change my clothes, put a new top on, but what's the point.”

‌



View 7 Images A burnt and discarded parking sign at an evacuated and deserted camp site (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

The National Trust, who have been caring for Dunwich Heath since 1968, today launched a public appeal in a bid to gain donations to help restore the iconic site to its former glory. Hilary McGrady, the Trust’s Director-General, said: “We are looking at total devastation of a beloved and important landscape.

"We’ve lost precious habitats, wildlife, trees, and a place where people have made memories over generations. It’s heartbreaking. But together we can and will restore Dunwich, and crucially, make it more resilient and better adapted for the climate we’re facing now, and the climate we’ll be facing in future. We’re working hard to tackle climate change and prepare for more of it, but there’s more hard work to be done. We can’t do it alone."

‌



Countryside manager for Suffolk Matt Wilson added: "The impact on this site in particular is looking to be fairly catastrophic. We're looking at total devastation across the National Trust site."

Adam Rowlands, Suffolk area manager for the RSPB, said it is too early to know the full scale of the impact on wildlife. But he admitted: "Shockingly, one of our site team at first light spoke about the acrid smell and said it's not just smoke, you have a sense that animals have perished in the flames so it's not a pleasant sight.

View 7 Images A bench remains amid the barren landscape (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

‌



"We'll wait to see in time really. With a lot of this you can only really assess the impact once you see a full season, but I think we can be pretty assured we're going to see some shocking results." Mr Rowlands added the recovery will "take years, decades, in come cases."

Suffolk fire service deputy chief fire officer Henry Griffin said: "It remains a significant and dynamic incident. We've been working with the Met Office, looking at the wind directions to monitor and mitigate in the hotspots to prevent flare-ups and re-ignition."

He added: "There has been some heat damage to some buildings - scorched cladding, melted gutters, things like that. But based on the information I have at this point in time, there has been no total loss to any buildings, which is a remarkable feat."

‌



Shortly before 5pm on Friday, a spokesperson said: "While the incident remains significant and resource intensive - and is still classified as a Major Incident for Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service and Suffolk Resilience Forum partners - conditions are currently improving and planning for the recovery phase has begun.

View 7 Images Cottages were saved despite all around them being burnt to the ground (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily mirror)

"Firefighters and partner agencies will continue to monitor the weather and situation closely over the coming days. Thank you to everyone affected for your patience and co-operation."

Article continues below

Meanwhile, England is on track for its driest July on record, the Environment Agency announced on Friday. It said reservoir storage stands at 72%, down from 75% a week ago and nearly 10 percentage points below the long-term average for the time of year.

It added three reservoirs were now classed as having "exceptionally low" levels, including Blagdon in Somerset (56% full), Hanningfield in Essex (65%) and Wimbleball in Somerset (54%).

A further seven reservoirs are "notably low": Ardingly in West Sussex (66% full); Blithfield in Staffordshire (63%); Clatworthy in Somerset (56%); Clywedog in Powys, which provides water for central and north-west England (69%); the Dove group of reservoirs in Derbyshire (77%); Grafham in Cambridgeshire (78%); and the Lower Thames group of reservoirs in Berkshire and west London (74%).

News.title: Watch: Moroccan police clash with migrants near border with Spain's Ceuta
News.content:
Tens of thousands of migrants have entered Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, with many swimming and using inflatables to travel from Morocco.

Others ran through a gate in the border fence.

The territory's leader, Juan JesÃºs Vivas, said the number of arrivals has been overwhelming resources and urged the Spanish government to intervene.

Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez described the situation as an "attack" and said all illegal migrants would be returned to Morocco "as soon as possible".

Ceuta, on Morocco's northern coast, has long been a focal point for migrants attempting to reach Europe.

More than 25,000 have returned to Morocco voluntarily so far, officials said.

More on this story.

News.title: 'If that means I lose my job, so be it': Top Fifa official questions Infantino's World Cup plan
News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino's position came under further scrutiny on Friday as the governing body's chief operating officer strongly criticised his plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors.

In a statement released to the Associated Press, Kevin Lamour described the controversial plans as "the project of one person" and said "the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions".

He added Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project. BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

The lengthy statement did not mention Infantino by name.

It came on the same day a third confederation spoke out against the plans, a senior adviser to Infantino resigned, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the Swiss was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

US President Donald Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.

The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.

Lamour said in his statement: "Our mission - the mission of the hundreds of passionate, dedicated, and exemplary Fifa employees - is to serve football.

"A president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them. Today, we are experiencing the opposite."

Lamour acknowledged he had a duty of loyalty to his employer but also to "certain values" and supporting his colleagues.

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

News.title: No sentence long enough for jailed funeral director Robert Bush, say families
News.content:
Karen Dry, who organised monthly vigils for the victims' families when the investigation began, said: "No sentence was ever going to be enough."

She said families were hoping Bush would be sentenced to more than 30 years, but what was "really messing with people's heads" was the prospect of him only serving half of his sentence.

When asked does it feel fair? She replied: "No, it really doesn't.

"For some people, I totally get that today is the end of it for them.

"But I'm my mam and dad's daughter, and we are a bit more determined than just letting these things lie."

She said without regulation of the industry, "in five or 10 years' time there will be another funeral director with another 300 families in a courtroom somewhere".

"We've got to put a stop to it and it's got to stop now."

News.title: How Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In broke the UK's singles chart record
News.content:
This reworking of Rein Me In, from Fender's third studio album, the Mercury Prize-winning People Watching, features an extra verse about the breakdown of a relationship from a female perspective, from Dean.

"[It's] very personal and reminded us of home, but when Olivia put her touch on it, it became a much more universal track," he told Radio 1, adding "that's what made it so huge and so beautiful".

He said he wanted to "personally thank" Dean, who helped him achieve his first ever number one single, adding: "It wouldn't have happened without Olivia obviously, but now I feel like it belongs to the fans, they've made it what it is".

When asked how he'd be celebrating the achievement, Fender joked "I think I'm just gonna have a really big sandwich".

It hasn't been a straightforward ascent to the top for Rein Me In - originally released as a solo Fender track and repurposed as a duet in June 2025, it took eight months to reach number one in February this year.

Dean said when the track came out, external that the original version of Rein Me In was her "favourite song on Sam's album" and it was "a pleasure to write a new verse from a female perspective".

A lot of the song's success as a duet comes from its authenticity, with the lyrics exploring the fallout from the end of a relationship and the difficulties faced by both parties as they try to move on from each other.

Whilst Fender's verses feel full of anger and regret at not being able to open up and be the partner he wanted to be, they are complimented by the softer and more reflective tone of Dean's, in which she encourages him to try again to make it work.

It has been described by Blunt Magazine's Jake Fitzpatrick, external as "stormy, tender and anthemic" and a "love letter to the kind of songwriting that knows when to burn slow".

The song has also received praise amongst many critics and bloggers, including Cult Following's Ewan Gleadow, external, who says that Dean's addition helps it to find "a new depth", noting "charm is a big part of it too, with all those reflections on where you come from and where you're headed".

News.title: Two more small boat pilots jailed for Channel crossings
News.content:
Two men who piloted overcrowded small boats have been jailed for endangering others while crossing the Channel.

Omar Heidari, a 34-year-old Afghan national who steered a dinghy carrying 95 people to the UK in June, has been jailed for two years.

Manas Yuk, an 18-year-old Sudanese national, was sentenced to 18 months in youth detention after piloting a boat carrying 81 people - including a number of children - just days prior.

The men were sentenced at Canterbury Crown Court on Friday having earlier pleaded guilty to endangerment.

It means 10 people have now been sentenced under a law targeting those who risk the safety of others by piloting small boats since it came into force in January.

The Home Office said Heidari had endangered the largest number of lives of anyone so far sentenced for the offence.

The boat was overcrowded during the crossing on 23 June, with some passengers hanging their legs over the sides of the vessel, it said. A number of the passengers were not wearing life jackets.

He was jailed for endangering others as well as arriving in the UK without valid entry clearance.

News.title: AI firms must answer for rogue bots, says boss of hacked company
News.content:
The boss of one of the companies recently hacked by out-of-control artificial intelligence (AI) says bot makers must be accountable for cyber attacks carried out by their creations.

Clement Delangue's company Hugging Face was breached by a rogue OpenAI bot that broke out of a test environment and autonomously attacked his firm earlier this month.

Hugging Face had to rebuild around a third of its IT network after the unprecedented incident.

He told CNN his company - which is a small start-up - will not be taking legal action against OpenAI, but added that these types of hacks are illegal and should remain so.

"Everyone has to remember that a cyber-attack is a crime and it is illegal," he said.

Delangue said he hoped legal frameworks would ensure the companies that make mistakes leading to the hacks are "accountable."

He added that he didn't want cyber attacks on other companies to become "normalised".

His remarks come after Anthrophic, the maker of the chat bot Claude, also admitted that its bot had attacked three companies in similar circumstances in recent months.

Anthropic revealed on Friday that it only realised its bot had escaped the containment system and hacked the organisations after doing a review prompted by the recent OpenAI incident.

In both cases neither of the artificial intelligence giants knew that their models had roamed the internet attacking companies until long after the attacks had been carried out.

The AI models were being tested on their hacking skills and carried out the attacks by breaking out of seemingly secure "sandboxes" to search the internet for ways to complete the tasks set by researchers.

The unprecedented incidents have sparked fierce debates in the cyber-security and legal world about who, if anybody, should be held liable for attacks by out-of-control AI agents.

"Agentic security failures unfold at machine speed, but determining who is materially liable still moves at a lawsuit's pace," said Dor Sarig, co-founder and Chief Builder at Pillar Security.

Sarig was concerned that accountability is already becoming "ambiguous".

"Today the industry is extending grace, but the first time an autonomous agent causes a breach involving real data, a real plaintiff, and real financial losses, liability won't be an academic debate anymore," he said.

"That's when the legal framework, and not just the technical safeguards, will be stress-tested."

News.title: Parents sue school over 'inhumane' calming rooms after BBC report
News.content:
Parents are suing a special school after a BBC investigation uncovered CCTV footage showing autistic children being locked inside calming rooms and abused.

Ten families are claiming that their children â all of whom had learning disabilities or several mental disorders - were amongst those harmed by their treatment in the rooms.

A police investigation into the abuse, recorded inside the rooms at Whitefield special school in north London, ended two years ago without any charges.

The school is now run by a new trust which says the failings have led to "important learning".

Many special schools use seclusion spaces such as calming rooms outside of classrooms to address sensory needs or challenging behaviour.

But the leaked footage obtained by the BBC showed children being shoved into padded rooms, thrown to the floor, restrained by the neck - or left alone, sitting in vomit.

One 12-year-old boy appeared in over 55 hours of CCTV footage filmed inside the rooms.

At the time, the Children's Commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, said the use of the rooms was "horrifying".

Leigh Day is now bringing a civil legal claim on behalf of 10 families against the trust which ran the school and the London borough of Waltham Forest.

The law firm says the use of the rooms was "barbaric", according to its clients. The claim alleges that children were falsely imprisoned and their human rights were breached.

"What was done to these children was profoundly harmful, and its impact continues to be felt by families every day", says Alison Millar, who is leading the case.

The CCTV obtained by the BBC had been recorded between 2014 and 2017 but only emerged in 2021.

Last month, a long-delayed review commissioned by Waltham Forest found that restraint and seclusion became "normalised" and a culture developed that allowed "pejorative views of non-compliant children".

It added that parents were clear that the practices were "unimaginable" and "inhumane".

The BBC has also found evidence of mistreatment in seclusion rooms at other schools across the UK.

CCTV from a different school showed a boy being "brutally" and "unlawfully" restrained, while elsewhere an autistic child was kept inside a cage.

News.title: Burnham faces criticism over plans for mayors to get share of income tax
News.content:
The government is facing criticism over its plan to allow regional mayors to keep a share of income tax and business rates in England.

Andy Burnham says that the proposals, expected to be phased in from next April, will give metro mayors powers to invest the money in their communities for public services.

The prime minister said on Friday that this amounted to "the biggest shift of power out of Whitehall and Westminster" to regions across the UK.

But Lord Houchen, the Conservative mayor of Tees Valley, argues he should be able to offer taxpayers a rebate instead, while opposition parties say the plans could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out.

"The prime minister has said he wants to alleviate the cost of living [crisis] and give people room to breathe - what better way to do that than allow them to keep more of their own money?" the Tory mayor told BBC Radio 4's World at One.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh told the BBC that there was not currently a mechanism in place for mayors to offer a rebate.

But Lord Houchen said it was "not beyond the wit of man" to create a system, adding it would not be "overly complicated" and would not be particularly controversial.

"I think the prime minister and what this government is doing on fiscal devolution is a move in the right direction, but for it to be real devolution we've got to have local decision-making and choose what's best for the people we represent."

Burnham later directly rejected the idea of mayors giving their taxpayers rebates, telling reporters the plans were not about making local leaders into "mini-chancellors of the exchequer, undermining or rewriting policy on tax and personal finance".

As it stands, mayors of English strategic authorities receive most of their funding by central government grants.

Mayors are expected to start retaining some revenue from business rates from April 2027 and receive a portion of income tax from April 2028.

The rates of income tax will not change as a result of the reform.

Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, has made devolution a centrepiece of his agenda in the early weeks of his premiership.

He said this policy would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country".

Chancellor John Healey will set out more of the detail when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October.

News.title: Disgraced funeral boss who failed to bury bodies jailed for 20 years
News.content:
This story contains details some might find distressing.

The court heard Bush defrauded nearly 200 families out of Â£562,117 and had acted out of "financial greed".

Hilliard warned that unless a body was one of those recovered by police in 2024 and properly identified, no-one who had used Legacy's cremations services "at any time can be absolutely certain they received the ashes of their loved one".

"He must have a heartless side to him - which allowed him to treat the living and the dead in the way he did, and he was very confident he would get away with what he was doing."

The judge added: "I don't think I have ever known offences affecting so many people and so deeply."

The court was told relatives of 46 people who were cremated between 2017 and 2024 were given the wrong ashes and the loved ones of another 11 never received any.

"How betrayed they now feel," said the judge.

"Husbands and wives, partners, parents, children, grandchildren, now discovering that they are left with nothing, or in some cases we heard, an empty plastic bag or a teaspoonful of ash which the police managed to recover for them."

News.title: Southport killer charged with prison attacks and possessing weapon
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has been charged with three attacks while in prison and possessing a weapon.

Police say the offences took place at HMP Belmarsh over six months from May to October 2025.

The 19-year-old murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a 52-year sentence in January 2025. Earlier this month he was moved to a secure psychiatric hospital.

Rudakubana is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court remotely on 11 September.

He has been charged with the following four offences:

Assault on an emergency worker on 6 May 2025

Attempted grievous bodily harm on 8 May 2025

Unauthorised possession of an offensive weapon in prison on 26 June 2025

Assault on an emergency worker on 28 October 2025

In May 2025, it was reported boiling water had been thrown on a prison officer at Belmarsh. They were taken to hospital and discharged on the same day.

When Rudakubana was jailed, the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to him being under-18 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

On 23 July, the MoJ confirmed Rudakubana was transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, a high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Under the Mental Health Act, the MoJ is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.

The decision to transfer him was criticised by a lawyer representing the families of victims.

News.title: Puberty blockers trial can start recruiting children after judge rejects legal challenge
News.content:
A high-profile clinical trial of drugs that can delay puberty in children questioning their gender can go ahead after the High Court rejected a legal challenge by campaigners.

The Pathways trial, run by researchers at King's College London (KCL), will start recruiting more than 220 children aged between 11 and 16 years old from 1 August.

The study was commissioned to assess the benefits or risks of puberty blockers, after a landmark review into gender services found the evidence for treating young people with the drugs was "remarkably weak".

Campaigners who brought the legal action had argued the safeguards in place were inadequate and raised concerns about the long-term physical and psychological effects on young people.

The judge, Mr Justice Chamberlain, refused the application for a judicial review saying that none of the claims made by the campaigners had a realistic chance of success.

He said that each patient involved in the trial will have been assessed over "many months" by specialist doctors who will have "formed the opinion that a child has a reasonable prospect of receiving a clinical benefit from the treatment".

A spokeswoman for KCL welcomed the court's decision, saying the "safety and welfare of young people will remain our highest priority in carrying out this research".

Campaigners, including parents of gender-questioning children, said they were disappointed by the decision saying the "world is watching" a case which has "global implications and high stakes".

News.title: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.

Burnham will also allow English strategic authorities to keep some cash from business rates collected in their areas, and gain greater control over services such as housing, transport, skills.

The government has not yet decided the exact portion of taxes mayors will get, with more details to be announced when Chancellor John Healey delivers his first budget in the autumn.

Opposition parties said the plans lacked detail and could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out on funding.

But Burnham said the move would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country".

"Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community," the prime minister added.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh told BBC Radio 4's Today programme areas without mayors would also benefit from investment because devolution powers would be held by new strategic authorities across England.

Strategic authorities bring together local councils to control regional issues such as transport and economic development, with decisions taken collectively by council leaders rather than a single elected mayor.

But Labour backbencher Perran Moon said the government's plans were "discriminatory" and could create a "two-tier system".

The MP for Camborne and Redruth in Cornwall said the area would never have a mayor or become a combined authority and so risked not having access to devolved powers that other areas would have.

"What we're asking government to do is to provide us with the same powers, the same funding that mayoral combined authorities have without the requirement of becoming a combined authority or having a mayor."

The government has also announced that mayors will be given a fast-track route to building new tramways, roads and light rail in their areas.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the threshold at which local leaders need to seek approval for projects will rise to Â£500m, up from Â£200m.

News.title: England and Wales on course for driest July on record
News.content:
England and Wales are on course for their driest July since records began 190 years ago.

The Met Office reports that England has seen just 5.6mm of rainfall up to 30 July â just 8% of its long-term meteorological average for the month and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.

For Wales it is 7.9mm of rainfall, also 8% of its long-term average for the month and almost a third of the previous record of 22.6mm, again set in 1911.

The UK as a whole is currently on track for its third driest July, and driest nationally since 1868.

News.title: Budget to be held in October, Healey announces
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has announced the date of his first Budget will be Wednesday, 28 October.

In aâ¯video message,â¯ he said: "This will be a Budget that moves money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain.

"It will be built on fiscal discipline. It will meet our fiscal rules. It'll give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future. Now, let's get on with the job."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his government will stick to Labour's fiscal rules on spending and borrowing as well as the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance contributions.

Burnham also said he will honour the fiscal rules imposed by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

An influential think tank said earlier this week that the prime minister only has a small margin of error to do this, and that Healey may have to cut spending or raise taxes to meet Burnham's policy priorities such as such as extra defence spending and better social care.

Healey was Defence Secretary under Keir Starmer, but resigned after a row over defence spending commitments - saying he was "certain" that Britain shouldl lift its spending to 3% by 2030.

But questioned about funding on Thursday, Burnham's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting repeatedly refused to commit to that target.

"Before we set out specific spending commitments, we will also set out how we pay for them at the same time," he said.

News.title: Sainsbury's agrees to sell Argos for £120m
News.content:
Sainsbury's has agreed to sell Argos for Â£120m after a long process of trying to offload it as the supermarket chain aims to focus on its main food business.

Sainsbury's said it would be "business as usual" for Argos customers, staff, and suppliers. Shoppers will see no change as Argos will still operate in Sainsbury's shops, sell Habitat products, and offer Nectar points.

The buyer, Swift Partners, is a company that has been created to buy the brand and includes former Co-operative Group boss Richard Pennycook.

There are 667 Argos shops across the UK, with 201 operating as standalone stores and 466 operating within Sainsbury's. It also has more than 450 collection points.

Founded in 1973, Argos opened shops where customers browsed its catalogues and placed their orders, with products being delivered to tills from warehouses connected to the stores.

The Argos catalogue, once described by comedian Bill Bailey as the "laminated book of dreams", used to be a physical book.

Argos no longer prints this hefty tome, with its full range now available online instead. In store, customers can browse the product collection on tablet computers.

Sainsbury's has been trying to sell Argos - which has been seen as an underperforming brand - for some time.

Sainsbury's bought Argos â together with Habitat and all the other retail brands owned by Home Retail Group â in 2016 for Â£1.4bn. It then sold Argos financial services, which runs the Argos card, for around Â£720m in 2024.

In September last year, its talks to sell the rest of Argos to Chinese online retailer JD.com fell through.

Sainsbury's chief executive Simon Roberts said that all of Argos's nearly 14,000 staff would be transferred over to Swift Partners as part of the deal.

He also confirmed that Argos would continue to operate in Sainsbury's shops; Nectar will continue to be used across both Argos and Sainsbury's; and Sainsbury's will continue to sell Habitat products

Swift Partners' Pennycook said he believed "strongly in Argos's future and see real opportunities to invest and build on its progress".

The deal is expected to be completed in February next year.

Pennycook said there was the potential to open new standalone Argos shops â and did not rule out the possibility of the return of its print catalogue.

News.title: Passenger on British Airways mayday flight describes fear and shout of 'I don't want to die'
News.content:
A passenger on a British Airways flight that issued a distress call on approach to Heathrow Airport earlier this month has described the rising fear in the cabin and a lack of information from the crew.

Edward Killiwick had been travelling back from a friend's birthday party with his partner Julie, on the flight from Dusseldorf in Germany on 6 July.

He said passengers were told that the landing had been aborted, and then he felt a "very violent manoeuvre" and "did think we could crash". He and his partner had to comfort a woman who "completely lost it and started screaming, 'I don't want to die'".

The flight landed safely, but the incident is being investigated with assistance from BA.

The UK's Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said it was "investigating a serious incident", and France's accident investigation authority, the BEA, said on Wednesday that the plane, an Airbus A320, had issued a distress call.

Edward said: "The violent manoeuvre almost felt like it was avoiding another aircraft. You could feel the engines going at full power.

"It was a bit odd going around in a holding pattern with no information. I thought if they're not talking, then they're not in a good place."

He said they were in a holding pattern for about 15 minutes.

The BEA said that as the plane approached Heathrow, there was a data system failure which triggered a stall warning.

The crew then flew the aircraft in a different mode called "alternate law", which removes some automated flight protection systems. Another stall warning then occurred at 3,000 feet â which experts say was likely to have been just miles away from the airport.

The urgency call the crew had already made was upgraded to mayday, indicating imminent danger.

A British Airways spokesperson said the airline was assisting the AAIB with its investigation and was not legally able to comment further at this stage.

Edward said: "I was definitely scared. After the violent manoeuvre I thought, there is definitely something very badly wrong here. I did think we could crash.

"I did think it was a possibility, and I think everyone else did."

Recent reports have highlighted AI-generated “doctors” spreading dubious health advice to millions of social media users. Fabricated wellness trends can travel just as quickly. A supposed “pink jelly” weight-loss treatment, for example, reportedly fooled at least one celebrity.

These examples gain credibility in different ways. Influencers can appear familiar and sincere, while AI-generated doctors can look like qualified professionals. Neither familiarity nor the appearance of expertise tells us whether a medical claim is accurate.

Turning to friends and family for health advice is understandable. They may know our circumstances in ways that a healthcare professional cannot during a brief appointment. They can provide emotional support and practical help, and their advice is usually well meant. But somebody can care about us, speak honestly and still be wrong.

open image in gallery But somebody can care about us, speak honestly and still be wrong ( Getty Images )

Truth and trust

My own research and wider research on digital health misinformation shows that trust can play an important part in deciding which claims people accept. Trust in clinicians and scientific institutions is generally associated with lower susceptibility to false health claims.

Misinformation can nevertheless spread through trusted social networks when people share it because they want to help or warn others.

Social media influencers can reproduce some of the signals of friendship without having a personal relationship with their followers. They address followers directly, share details about their lives and communicate in an informal style.

Over time, followers may develop what researchers call a parasocial relationship: a one-sided sense of familiarity with a media figure. A recent meta-analysis found that parasocial relationships can influence health attitudes and behaviour, although their effects vary across different contexts.

AI-generated doctors use a different route to credibility. Accounts designed to resemble real clinicians can borrow the appearance and language of medical authority without providing any reliable way to check who created the content, what qualifications lie behind it or whether the advice is supported by evidence.

Personal stories are especially persuasive. Someone describes being ill, discovering a treatment and recovering. The account is easy to follow and often more memorable than a discussion of probabilities.

Even a completely truthful anecdote cannot show that a treatment caused the recovery or that it will be safe and effective for other people. Symptoms may have improved naturally.

The person may have used several treatments at once, received an uncertain diagnosis or left out relevant details. Experiments have found that anecdotes can influence medical decisions even when people are also given stronger statistical evidence.

Fear, hope and accuracy

Emotion can add to the effect. Fear or hope may draw attention to a claim and make it feel urgent. Emotional tone does not show whether the information is accurate. Research suggests, however, that heightened emotional responses can increase susceptibility to digital health misinformation.

Identity can also shape judgment. Advice from another parent or fellow patient may appear more credible because the speaker seems to understand our experience. Rejecting the advice may then feel like rejecting a community to which we belong. A systematic review found that existing beliefs, knowledge, trust and reasoning styles can all affect how people evaluate health claims.

People may also have sound reasons for distrusting healthcare institutions. Dismissive treatment, discrimination, rushed appointments and poor explanations can damage trust. Research on trust in health organisations suggests that mistrust may be a rational response to institutional failure or unequal treatment. Telling patients to trust experts will not repair relationships that healthcare systems have damaged.

About the author Anna Stone is a Senior Lecturer in Psychology, University of East London. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

So how can we assess a health claim without dismissing personal experience?

1. Examine the claim separately from the person making it

A source may be sincere, charismatic or visually convincing without having the expertise to judge whether a treatment works. Check their relevant qualifications and whether their identity can be independently verified.

2. Look for supporting evidence and independent agreement

Do the NHS, an appropriate professional body or a reputable medical charity offer similar guidance? A single study rarely settles a medical question, so substantial claims should be supported by a wider body of research.

3. Check for commercial interests

Look for products, affiliate links, paid partnerships or private treatment programmes. Financial involvement creates a potential conflict of interest that readers should know about.

4. Be cautious about sweeping promises

Claims that a treatment produces rapid results, works for almost everyone or has no meaningful risks are unlikely to reflect the uncertainty and individual variation involved in medicine.

5. Know the warning signs

Treat secrecy claims and advice to abandon prescribed care as serious warning signs The greater the potential harm, the more important it is to check the advice with an appropriately qualified professional, such as a pharmacist or GP.

Individuals cannot carry the whole burden of detecting misinformation. Social media platforms influence which claims are amplified, while health services influence whether people feel heard and respected. Researchers are increasingly calling for a systems approach to health misinformation that combines clearer public information, responsible platform design, effective regulation and trustworthy clinical communication.

Friends and relatives can provide valuable support and personal testimony can reveal experiences that medical research may miss. Judging whether a treatment is safe and effective, however, requires evidence that extends beyond any one person’s story.
