World.title: Africa: AHEFT Prize Launched to Recognise African Universities Leading Higher Education Transformation
World.content:
interview

Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — As Africa grapples with shrinking international development funding and rising pressure to create jobs for its rapidly growing youth population, the Mastercard Foundation is making one of the continent's biggest long-term investments in higher education, committing US$500 million over the next decade to transform African universities.

In an interview with AllAfrica's Melody Chironda, Dr. John Nkengasong, Executive Director for Higher Education, Collaboratives and Strategic Initiatives at the Mastercard Foundation, said the Foundation views universities as critical engines for developing the talent, innovation, and leadership needed to drive Africa's economic transformation. He argued that strategic investment in higher education has helped countries around the world build knowledge-based economies. He said African institutions have the potential to play the same role by preparing young people for dignified work while advancing research, entrepreneurship, and inclusive development.

Nkengasong, a Cameroonian-American virologist, was the inaugural Director of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and served as the U.S. Global AIDS Coordinator in the Biden administration and the World Health Organization Special Envoy for Africa during the COVID-19 pandemic,

$500 million over a decade is a significant bet on higher education specifically, at a moment when many donors are pulling back from Africa. Why did the Foundation choose universities as the lever, rather than, say, direct scholarships or workforce programs?

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Human capital investment, through higher education, is at the centre of every story of national economic transformation around the world. Through strategic investments in higher education for human capital development, many countries around the world have successfully transformed from resource-scarce nations into advanced, knowledge-based economies with sustained GDP growth. With strategic investments in higher education, Africa can generate the necessary talent that can propel the continent towards economic growth and sustained livelihoods for its young people.

The Mastercard Foundation is committed to a world where every young person has the opportunity to learn and prosper. Our Young Africa Works strategy aims to enable 30 million young people to access dignified and fulfilling work by 2030. Through the Africa Higher Education for Transformation (AHEFT) Prize, the Foundation is strengthening Africa's higher education system as a catalyst for talent development, expanded opportunities for young people, and inclusive socio-economic growth. Building on two decades of experience supporting African institutions to reimagine higher education, the AHEFT Prize converts proven success into sustained momentum through a decade-long commitment to advancing homegrown excellence and driving system-wide transformation across the continent.

The Prize talks about 'systemic, institution-wide transformation' rather than individual achievement. How do you actually measure that a university has transformed, as opposed to simply having a strong department or a few good graduates?

The AHEFT Prize is not intended to rank institutions, departments, or graduates. Instead, it aims to establish a benchmark for transformational impact in African higher education. All applications were assessed against a common set of criteria, including transformational impact, alignment with Africa's development priorities, community engagement, inclusion and access, student experience, and collaboration. Through their applications, African institutions are defining what transformation looks like by sharing their own stories of innovation, impact, and measurable change.

The Prize focused on institution-wide transformation rather than isolated excellence. It assessed whether change is embedded across the university's core functions, including teaching and learning, research, entrepreneurship, and transitions to employment and whether that change delivers measurable outcomes for students, communities, and society.

The inaugural winners exemplified this wide-ranging transformation in different ways. From creating effective pathways from learning to earning, to advancing applied research and innovation, strengthening health systems, influencing national development priorities, and expanding regional and continental impact. Together, they demonstrate that transformational universities do more than excel in a single department; they become engines of opportunity, innovation, and socio-economic progress.

What insights did this inaugural cycle provide, and how will those lessons inform the Prize as it expands to universities across the continent?

The inaugural cycle reinforced the critical role of African higher education institutions as drivers of human capital development and socio-economic progress, showcasing diverse models of transformational impact across the continent. It also validated the importance of assessing universities holistically and in context, examining how leadership, systems, partnerships, teaching, research, and student outcomes work together to create lasting change. These insights will help strengthen future cycles of the Prize as we identify, recognize, and elevate a broader range of institutions delivering institution-wide transformation and measurable impact for young people and society.

Every winning institution has a genuinely different story, from refugee employment in Uganda to health workforce training in Rwanda. Is there a common thread the jury was really looking for, or is 'transformation' being defined differently in each context?

Every application was assessed against the same standardized criteria: transformational impact, relevance to Africa's development priorities, community engagement and service, inclusion and access, student experience, and collaboration and partnerships. We see this diversity as a strength.

The winning institutions demonstrated the breadth of transformational impact being driven by African higher education institutions. Across diverse contexts, they are strengthening pathways from education to employment and entrepreneurship, advancing applied research and innovation to address societal challenges, transforming health systems through workforce development and clinical excellence, and embedding industry-relevant, experiential learning. Beyond their campuses, these institutions are influencing policy, contributing to national and regional development, fostering strategic partnerships, and building resilient, sustainable models that position higher education as a catalyst for human capital development, innovation, and inclusive socio-economic growth across Africa.

How does the Foundation think about supporting these institutions to keep the momentum going after the initial $3 million grant?

Beyond the financial award, the AHEFT Prize will provide programmatic support to help winning institutions scale their transformation initiatives. We will also bring winners together to share learning, foster collaboration, and amplify their work to create ripple effects across institutions and ecosystems. The inaugural Higher Education for Transformation Convening, scheduled for September 22 in Accra, marks the beginning of this journey.

Leveraging the Foundation's network of more than 200 African higher education institutions, the goal is to create a platform through which institutions can access the support, partnerships, and connections needed to sustain and scale their transformative work.

You've committed to at least 150 institutions over ten years, but Africa has thousands of higher education institutions. How do you think about the trade-off between depth of impact at a few flagship universities versus breadth across the continent's weaker systems?

The Prize is designed to achieve both depth and scale. First, it strengthens high-performing institutions so their impact in teaching and learning, research, entrepreneurship, and transitions to employment can reach more young people. Second, it seeks to catalyze broader system-wide change by demonstrating what transformative higher education can look like and encouraging governments, funders, and institutions to invest in and adopt similar approaches. This is an ambitious goal that the Foundation cannot achieve alone. We recognize that we are one of many stakeholders working toward the same objective.

Beyond the Prize itself, the Foundation advances systemic transformation through Higher Education Collaboratives- multi-stakeholder partnerships across sectors with significant potential for job creation and social impact, including health, agriculture, climate resilience, digital transformation, and education. For example, the Africa Higher Education Health Collaborative brings together universities across the continent to strengthen health workforce development and health entrepreneurship, extending impact far beyond individual institutions.

Close 

Africa's graduate unemployment and brain drain numbers remain stark. Where does this Prize actually move the needle on young people finding dignified work at home, versus simply making strong universities stronger?

Supporting universities and improving employment outcomes for young people are linked and aligned to our Young Africa Works strategy, which aims to enable 30 million young people to access dignified and fulfilling work by 2030. Through the AHEFT Prize, the Foundation is strengthening Africa's higher education system as critical human capital and talent infrastructure, enabling institutions to deliver quality, inclusive, and industry-relevant education that prepares young people for dignified and meaningful work. This is why transitions to employment is one of the Prize's four core thematic areas, alongside teaching and learning, research, and entrepreneurship.

The AHEFT Prize launches as some traditional donors are stepping back from the continent. Do you see the AHEFT Prize as the Foundation stepping into a gap left by others, and does that change how much responsibility philanthropic capital should carry for Africa's education systems?

For more than 20 years, the Mastercard Foundation has partnered with African institutions and witnessed their ability to redefine what higher education can deliver. Rather than responding to changes in the funding landscape, the AHEFT Prize builds on this experience, transforming proven success into momentum through a long-term commitment to recognize, elevate, and scale African-led excellence. By strengthening universities and the broader higher education ecosystem, the Prize aims to advance talent development, innovation, and leadership, enabling institutions across the continent to become powerful engines of opportunity and socio-economic transformation for millions of young people.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Purges Senior Security Officials Across Multiple Agencies
World.content:
President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has dismissed or suspended senior officials at Roberts International Airport, the Liberia National Police, the National Security Agency, the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency and the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection over the country's two record cocaine seizures, and ordered that those implicated be turned over for prosecution.

The action, announced Thursday by the Executive Mansion, is the widest personnel purge of the investigation so far and reaches into every institution that touched the shipments.

Among those dismissed is Mark Egon Kuiah, deputy director for operations at Roberts International Airport. His removal came a day after the president's son, Joseph Nyuma Boakai Jr., devoted part of a public statement to a friendship with a man he named as Mark Kuiah, describing him as a friend of many years who he had never had reason to believe was anything but law-abiding, and adding that friendship is not immunity from the law.

Also dismissed were Johnny Bolar Dean, the police commissioner for criminal investigation, intelligence and Interpol, and Patrick Doe, deputy director for administration at the National Security Agency. Dean had already been removed from his post last week after admitting he took US$10,000 to provide comfort to two suspects held in the airport case.



The president recalled and suspended without pay Patrick Komasu, an NSA agent seconded to the LDEA, and placed him under investigation.

Boakai ordered the dismissal of all government and law enforcement employees implicated in the cases. Those named include the airport's security director, Mohammed O. Gbowrah, and LDEA deputy commander Moses Jallah, both stationed at Roberts International Airport.

Two police officers were dismissed over the use of official vehicles to move narcotics. The Executive Mansion named them as Anthony T. Blaye and Wadell W. Kwarbo, and said they moved a consignment from Vincent Town on the Bomi Highway to the vicinity of Mega Mart in Thinker Village, Paynesville.

That account sits alongside, and does not obviously match, the one Inspector General Gregory Coleman gave reporters hours earlier, in which the two men were said to have escorted narcotics from a landing site to a holding ground with police vehicles running ahead of and behind the load. Coleman did not name the route.

Four others were ordered dismissed and turned over to the Ministry of Justice for prosecution: NSA agents Jammel V. Jallah, Christian L. Nyantee and Albenigo Janior, and Caycee Nelson, procurement director at the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection.

The Executive Mansion said the removals are meant to hold public servants to account. "These actions demonstrate his Administration's resolve to ensure that no public official or government employee who engages in criminal conduct remains in public service," the release said.

Close 

Boakai said the law would be enforced without fear or favor, directed security institutions to press the investigations further, and said everyone connected to the cases must go before the courts with due process observed.

The announcement followed the public destruction earlier Thursday of the cocaine recovered in both cases. The government put the Duazon haul at US$317 million and the June 8 airport seizure at US$19 million, a combined US$336 million, and said the two hauls together came to 4,169 plates.

World.title: Africa: Cotton to Cloth - The Story Africa Has Always Needed to Tell
World.content:
editorial

Africa grows more than half of the world's finest long-staple cotton. It earns less than three percent of what that cotton is eventually worth. This is not a trade problem. It is a narrative problem — and allAfrica is setting out to fix it.

There is a number that explains much of what is wrong with how the world finances Africa. It is not a trade figure or a debt ratio. It is an annual cost — up to $4.2 billion — the amount by which negative media stereotypes inflate African sovereign borrowing costs every single year. The story the world reads about Africa costs Africa, concretely, in higher interest rates and slower capital flows.

allAfrica has spent close to 3 decades building the infrastructure to change that story. Eight million articles in archive. A network of 140+ media partners spanning every corner of the continent. Direct distribution reaching tens of millions of decision-makers globally through Bloomberg, Dow Jones/Factiva, Thomson Reuters, Moody's Analytics/NewsEdge, LexisNexis, Syndigate & Tagaday (Europe). We are, in the most literal sense, the channel through which Africa's story reaches the people who price African risk.

Cotton to Cloth is the moment we unlock the full power of the infrastructure we have built over the years.



"The gap between raw commodity and finished product is not a production gap. It is a perception gap — and journalism, data, and storytelling can close it." — Amadou Mahtar Ba · Co-Founder, allAfrica Global Media

The initiative

Beginning June 2026 and running through December, allAfrica launches its most sustained and investment-grade editorial programme to date — a dedicated hub on all its platforms covering every dimension of Africa's cotton-to-cloth transformation, built on the conviction that Africa's cotton story — told well, distributed broadly, and anchored in data — can measurably shift how the world's capital allocators think about the continent.

The story begins in the field. West African cotton is among the finest on earth — long-staple, clean, commanding a premium on international markets. It leaves the continent as raw fibre. It returns as finished garments at twenty, thirty, sometimes fifty times the price. The countries that grow the raw material that clothes the world are rarely named as manufacturers. That is the gap this initiative addresses, one story at a time.

What you will find on this hub



This page is the entry point for all allAfrica content on this initiative. Over the coming months, it will grow into the most comprehensive English and French editorial resource on African cotton industrialisation available anywhere online — spanning original journalism, investor intelligence, documentary storytelling, policy analysis, and voices from across the continent and its diaspora.

Original long-form journalism. A sustained monthly publication series going deep on the economics, the geography, the people, and the policy architecture of Africa's cotton transformation — written to the standard that institutional investors, policymakers, and informed readers require. Evidence-based, rigorous, told from the inside.

Investor-grade data and intelligence. A major annual data publication mapping Africa's cotton processing investment landscape, a live deal tracker updated monthly, and sector intelligence briefs — all structured for capital markets audiences and distributed through allAfrica's global institutional wire network.

Policy voices and thought leadership. Commissioned essays, opinion pieces, and in-depth interviews bringing African ministers, industrialists, economists, and sector leaders directly to the audiences that shape policy and move capital — wire-distributed to the financial press and reaching Bloomberg, Factiva, LexisNexis, and beyond.

Documentary and multimedia storytelling. Original documentary features, a podcast series, and data-driven visual content placing human faces and real places at the centre of the industrial story — from the floor of a processing zone to the hands of a cooperative farmer, the cotton-to-cloth story in full depth and colour.

Close 

Youth and diaspora voices. A continent-wide storytelling contest inviting contributors from across Africa and the African diaspora to tell the cotton-to-cloth story in their own words. The next generation of African economic narrators, brought in from the first day.

Live events and convenings. A virtual roundtable, a physical exhibition at the allAfrica Media Leaders Summit, and allAfrica's presence at major African institutional forums throughout the year — taking this story from screen to room.

Follow the story



Everything on this hub is free. Every article, data release, documentary, and podcast will be published in both English and French — because the cotton-to-cloth story is as much a Francophone African story as it is an Anglophone one, and allAfrica serves the full continent.

Subscribe and receive each new publication directly in your inbox from launch day.

World.title: Uganda: HIV Injection Is Not a Vaccine, Experts Warn
World.content:
Kampala — Experts have urged those who already received their first injection of the twice-yearly HIV preventing drug Lenacapavir to consider using combination prevention options, warning that the game changer injection is not a vaccine.

The initial recipients of the drug that has since had a lot of demand countrywide are set to receive their second dose in October and Dr Vincent Bagambe, the Policy Planning and Strategic Manager at the Uganda AIDS Commission says for those who access it, they should be keen on receiving their next dose on the prescribed dates if they are to maintain optimal drug levels in their blood.

Bagambe says that with the injection now part of the prevention tools in the country, they hope to cut the 37,000 new infections recorded yearly to less than 10,000 by 2030, which will all depend on how compliant people be to maintain the required drug levels in their blood to guarantee protection.

At the launch of the prevention option in April, Uganda had received 19,200 doses supplied across 103 health facilities across the country. The main clients targeted for the drug include people at highest risk of infection such as sex workers, couples in discordant relationships, fisherfolk and pregnant women engaging in risky behavior among others. But reports by the Ministry of Health show that the drug was accessed by those not listed as high risk as demand surpassed available supplies.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Asked about supplies for those who will soon need the second dose, Dr Herbert Kadama who coordinates Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) at the Ministry of Health said sixty - percent of the facilities that received the first batch have now received second batches.

Kadama explains that the facilities received the second batches earlier than scheduled because the doses were running out in two to three weeks and yet at the beginning, they had thought they would be supplying every two months.

Meanwhile, the country expects a top-up consignment of another 19,200 doses donation.

In an earlier interview with URN, Dr Peter Mudiope who heads HIV Prevention in the ministry this consignment was initially expected to arrive in the country in June only to be informed by the manufacturer Gilead Sciences that this couldn't happen due to shortages of a tablet that complements the injection, also called the loading dose.

Mudiope says that as calls for more doses continue and the valid need for people to comply on the prevention treatment, government cannot do much to avail the game changer drug for now. He says the current price of Lenacapivir is still too high to be afforded by the government. At 28,000 dollars per dose, the official says Uganda can for now only count on more donations expected from Global Fund and the American government to guarantee availability.

Close 

With supplies not yet guaranteed, Mudiope says the public should continue relying on other prevention options such as condoms, Pre and Post Exposure Prophylaxis tablets and being faithful as they are equally scientifically tested and confirmed to prevent HIV infection.

However, a study conducted by Makerere University School of Public Health in which they assessed access to HIV prevention services found use of key prevention options low.

According to results of this study which were released on Wednesday, researchers found only 24 percent of female sex workers and injection drug users, who are also a high at-risk group used PEP in the last three months. Seventy-six percent reported to have not used the prevention option despite knowledge of where to access it.

In terms prevalence, while national prevalence currently stands at 4.9 percent, among sex workers and injection drug users, HIV prevalence is high at 30 percent and 17 percent respectively.

Ideally, Kadama says such groups are the ones targeted as a top priority for Lenacapavir.

World.title: East Africa: U.S. Senators Urge Rubio to Address Impact of Ebola Outbreak on Women
World.content:
press release

WASHINGTON — Yesterday, U.S. Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging the State Department to take swift action to protect women and infants from the deadly impact of the Ebola outbreak in eastern Africa. The Senators called on the Trump Administration to promptly use congressionally appropriated funds for voluntary family planning programming to distribute already purchased family planning commodities and back the UN Population Fund’s (UNFPA) health clinics operating in the region.

In the letter, the Senators emphasized the catastrophic toll of Ebola on pregnant women and warned that conflict and displacement in Ituri and North Kivu—in addition to increases in gender-based and sexual violence and transactional and survival sex—are exacerbating the outbreak.

“Ebola during pregnancy is catastrophic, with a nearly 100 percent fetal loss rate and catastrophic maternal mortality risk due to severe hemorrhaging. By providing women with the option to voluntarily prevent unplanned pregnancies and to protect themselves from transmission of the virus and have access to clinics, the United States can prevent further deaths of women and the cruel and certain death of any fetus exposed to the virus,” wrote the Senators.

“The inclusion of family planning in the U.S. response to the Ebola virus, including condoms and hormonal contraceptive methods, post-rape care and lifesaving anti-hemorrhage maternal health medicines is paramount. Congress, on a bipartisan basis, supports voluntary family planning programs because such programs support families and reduce maternal and infant death rates. In East Africa right now, access to family planning is essential to protecting women and babies and to reducing viral transmission,” continued the Senators.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

“The rapid spread of the virus, with more than 2,000 confirmed cases and 796 confirmed deaths as of this week in the DRC, leaves no time for delay in providing all possible interventions to save lives and prevent the transmission of the virus. The cost of United States response is approaching $1 billion. Investment now in voluntary family planning is fiscally rational in addition to being morally urgent,” concluded the Senators.

Full text of the letter is available HERE and provided below.

Dear Secretary Rubio,

We write to urge the State Department to take swift action to address the devastating impact of the Ebola outbreak in eastern Africa on women and infants by utilizing funding provided by Congress for voluntary family planning programming, to distribute already purchased family planning commodities and supporting the UN Population Fund’s (UNFPA) health clinics in the region.

Ebola during pregnancy is catastrophic, with a nearly 100 percent fetal loss rate and catastrophic material mortality risk due to severe hemorrhaging. By providing women with the option to voluntarily prevent unplanned pregnancies and to protect themselves from transmission of the virus and have access to clinics, the United States can prevent further deaths of women and the cruel and certain death of any fetus exposed to the virus.

During the Ebola outbreak in West Africa from 2014-2016, maternal mortality rose an estimated 75%. The staggering increase in maternal mortality was a result of the Ebola virus, as well as pregnant women forgoing antenatal and attended delivery care because of fear of contracting the virus at health clinics.

Currently, conflict and displacement are exacerbating the Ebola outbreak with spikes in gender-based and sexual violence in Ituri and North Kivu, as well as an increase in transactional and survival sex. Access to voluntary family planning counseling and supplies is critical to protect the lives of women and babies and to control the spread of the virus.

The inclusion of family planning in the U.S. response to the Ebola virus, including condoms and hormonal contraceptive methods, post-rape care and lifesaving anti-hemorrhage maternal health medicines is paramount. Congress, on a bipartisan basis, supports voluntary family planning programs because such programs support families and reduce maternal and infant death rates. In East Africa right now, access to family planning is essential to protecting women and babies and to reducing viral transmission. We urge you to utilize the $608 million in international family planning funding included in the Fiscal Year 2026 Appropriations bill and to distribute the remaining $1.7 million in already purchased family planning commodities in storage in Geel, Belgium which we understand will otherwise be destroyed.

Close 

We also ask that you issue a humanitarian exemption to support UNFPA's sexual and reproductive health programming in affected areas. UNFPA is already operational across 29 health zones in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and in Uganda; emergency contributions would be deployed immediately through an existing, proven delivery system with no ramp-up delay. Providing sexual and reproductive health support to women is not a parallel track alongside the Ebola response: it is the Ebola response for the 642,000 women of reproductive age - including an estimated 37,820 pregnant women - in the affected areas.

The rapid spread of the virus, with more than 2,000 confirmed cases and 796 confirmed deaths as of this week in the DRC, leaves no time for delay in providing all possible interventions to save lives and prevent the transmission of the virus. The cost of United States response is approaching $1 billion. Investment now in voluntary family planning is fiscally rational in addition to being morally urgent.

World.title: Nigeria: South African Singer Tyla Cancels Lagos Performance Amid Xenophobia Backlash
World.content:
South African singer Tyla has removed Lagos from the schedule of her upcoming APop world tour following online backlash from some Nigerians over renewed reports of xenophobic attacks against Nigerians in South Africa.

The Grammy-winning artiste unveiled the dates for her world tour on Monday, with the initial itinerary including a Lagos concert scheduled for December 22, alongside stops across Europe, North America and South Africa.

However, the announcement sparked heated reactions on Nigerian social media, where several users questioned the decision to host the singer amid reports of fresh xenophobic violence targeting Nigerians in South Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The controversy revived long-standing tensions between both countries, with some social media users calling for a boycott of the Lagos concert.

Others argued that entertainment should not be linked to diplomatic disputes and maintained that musicians should not be held responsible for political or societal conflicts.

A number of public figures also weighed in on the debate.

Media personality Do2dtun questioned the promoters behind the planned Lagos show, while activist and former presidential candidate Omoyele Sowore urged Nigerians to channel their frustrations toward political leaders rather than the artiste.

Neither Tyla nor her management publicly addressed the criticism.

However, checks by VANGUARD showed that Lagos has been removed from the list of tour venues on the official ticketing platform.

The previously announced December 22 show in Nigeria no longer appears among the available dates.

The updated schedule now lists only the remaining international stops, including performances across Europe, North America and two South African shows in Cape Town on January 4 and Johannesburg on January 9.

Tyla has not announced whether the Lagos concert was cancelled permanently or if it could be rescheduled at a later date.

World.title: Ghana: Govt Backs Five-Year Presidential Term
World.content:
The government has accepted the recommendation of the Constitutional Review Committee (CRC) to extend the term of office of the President from four to five years, with the tenure of Parliament adjusted accordingly.

The Attorney-General and Minister for Justice, Dr Dominic Akurutinga Ayine, said the move was aimed at providing administrations with more time to plan, implement and assess policies.

"Under the current four-year cycle, the early months of every administration are consumed by transition, and the final year is lost to elections. A five-year term provides a more realistic timeframe for policy formulation, implementation and assessment," he explained.

Dr Ayine made this known at the Presidency in Accra yesterday when he presented the government's position paper on the recommendations of the CRC.



Related Articles

He said, subject to approval through a referendum, the government also supported a fixed single, non-renewable 10-year term for the Chief Justice, up to the mandatory retirement age of 70 years.

He added that the government had proposed capping the number of Supreme Court justices at 19, comprising the Chief Justice and 18 other justices.

"The Committee recommended a cap of 15 justices; government proposes 19 justices; Chief Justice plus 18 Justices of the Supreme Court. This promotes efficiency, manages public expenditure, while remaining sufficiently robust to discharge the Court's constitutional mandate," he said.

Dr Ayine, who is also the Member of Parliament for Bolgatanga East, said Ghanaians were expected to vote in a referendum next year on the proposed amendments to the 1992 Constitution.

The referendum, he explained, would be held alongside the District Assembly elections to allow citizens to endorse or reject the government's position on the recommendations of the Prof. Henry Kwesi Prempeh-led committee.

The CRC report, titled "Transforming from Electoral Democracy to a Developmental Democracy," was presented to President John Dramani Mahama in February 2026, after which three Cabinet retreats were held before government arrived at its position.

Among the other recommendations considered were presidential election dates, election petitions, presidential taxation, the minimum age for presidential candidates, the size of government and Parliament.

On the minimum age for the Presidency, Dr Ayine said although the committee recommended 30 years, the government's position was that it should be raised to 35 years.

"Thirty-five is consistent with modern democratic constitutions towards greater inclusivity of youth, whilst ensuring candidates have maturity and experience," he said.

He said government had also accepted the proposal for presidential elections to be held in the first week of November, arguing that a fixed date would provide certainty in the electoral calendar and allow sufficient time between elections and the January 7 inauguration.

Dr Ayine said government supported a constitutional requirement for presidential election petitions to be filed within 14 days after the declaration of results and determined by the Supreme Court within 30 days.

He added that the Electoral Commission would be required to provide relevant electoral data to the court and all parties involved in the hearing.

On presidential taxation, the Attorney-General said government had accepted in principle that the President should pay taxes on salary, allowances and applicable direct taxes on bills and services. However, taxes on presidential retirement gratuity and pension would remain exempt.

Close 

On the size of government, Dr Ayine said while the CRC recommended a maximum of 57 ministers, government proposed an upper limit of 60.

He added that ministers could either be appointed from Parliament or outside it.

Regarding Parliament, he said the legislature would be capped at 300 members, with an additional 24 seats created through proportional representation for women, persons with disabilities and the youth.

Dr Ayine further disclosed that dual citizens by birth would no longer be barred from contesting parliamentary elections solely because of their dual citizenship.

"Multiple citizenship will no longer disqualify a person from holding specified offices, except that of President and Vice President," he stated.

He also announced that District Chief Executives would be elected, with the President nominating five persons including two women from whom three candidates would be shortlisted for election.

World.title: Tanzania: President Unveils Roadmap to New Constitution
World.content:
Dar es Salaam — PRESIDENT Samia Suluhu Hassan announced yesterday that the government will establish a reconciliation commission to facilitate the next phase of the constitutional review process, reaffirming her administration commitment to political dialogue and national unity.

The Head of State made the remarks at State House in Dar es Salaam during a meeting with leaders of the country's 18 registered political parties, where discussions centred on political reconciliation, constitutional reforms, economic development, employment, investment and the preservation of peace.

President Samia said the proposed reconciliation commission would help accelerate consensus building ahead of constitutional reforms while ensuring that all processes are conducted in accordance with the country's laws, regulations and established procedures.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"We already want to form a reconciliation commission to expedite the process of the Constitution or constitutional amendments," President Samia said.

She stressed that safeguarding Tanzania's peace, unity and national resources is a shared responsibility that extends beyond the government to political parties and all citizens.

"The responsibility of protecting Tanzania belongs to all of us. Democracy is about participating in elections, accepting the outcome and allowing the winner to form the government. But protecting our country and the blessings God has given us is the duty of every Tanzanian," she said.

The President called on political parties to continue working together with the government in preserving national peace and stability, noting that democracy thrives where there is shared responsibility and collective commitment to the country's prosperity.

"Democracy is about shared prosperity and shared responsibility before success. The government may be formed by the winning party, but the benefits of development belong to all Tanzanians," she said.

President Samia also reaffirmed the government's commitment to sustaining political reconciliation efforts, saying consultations with political parties would continue regularly as part of efforts to strengthen democracy and inclusive governance.

She announced that the government would continue convening meetings with leaders of political parties at least three times a year to discuss issues of national importance.

The meeting was the second of its kind convened by President Samia since the 2025 General Election.

The first meeting was held on March 31 this year, bringing together presidential candidates and their running mates who contested the election.

Referring to reconciliation efforts in Zanzibar, the President briefed party leaders on the progress made in preparations for the next phase of political reconciliation, which will pave the way for constitutional review.

Close 

She assured participants that every stage of the process would be guided by the law and undertaken in the broader national interest.

On the economy, President Samia said Tanzania maintained strong economic performance, with the economy growing by six per cent last year and projected to expand by 6.3 per cent this year.

She said the government remains focused on completing ongoing strategic development projects while continuing investments in key infrastructure, including railways, roads, ports and other major facilities.

The President noted that improvements at the Dar es Salaam Port have significantly enhanced its capacity to serve domestic and regional trade, adding that expansion works are also continuing at ports along the Indian Ocean as well as Lakes Victoria, Tanganyika and Nyasa.

Political party leaders also presented their views on governance, economic growth, social development and citizens' welfare.

The government pledged to continue receiving and considering their recommendations through established dialogue platforms and formal decision-making mechanisms.

World.title: Paulina Gretzky celebrates rumored LIV deal in a watermelon dress, Monica McNutt embarrasses ESPN & Paige!
World.content:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

Final Friday of July ... Final DAY of July.

Has this been the longest month ever? I feel like we get two months every year that seemingly last forever.

January and July.

The rest fly by. But those? They just drag. I don't mind July dragging a bit because we respect summer around here (until Labor Day Monday), but January is always such a grind.

Luckily, that's not a today problem. There are no problems today. We're on the brink of August, which is the true calm before the storm.

Let's ride this out together and end the month strong.

Welcome to a Friday Nightcaps — the one where Paulina Gretzky celebrates the rumored LIV deal on a yacht in a watermelon dress. As one does, of course.

What else? I've got Tony Romo getting put on leave (any guesses on when he'll be back?!), insufferable ESPN analyst Monica McNutt somehow becoming even more insufferable, and would you ever go back to a job that fired you just for the love of the game?

Karl Ravech did it last night, and I couldn't believe my eyes. What a move.

Pro's pro.

Grab you whatever you need to get you through the rest of this day — dealer's choice! — and settle in for a Friday 'Cap!

Monica McNutt and ESPN continue to give the people what they want

Let's spin the wheel and start with ... OutKick fan-favorite, Monica McNutt! You didn't think we'd go a whole day without talking about the WNBA, did you?

To be fair, we're not really going to talk about it today. Don't worry. Don't leave! I promise, this has nothing to do with that shameful league.

Instead, it has to do with McNutt, ESPN's WNBA analyst, who is pretty much hated by everyone. Somehow, she still has a job after all the layoffs earlier this month (more on them in a bit), which means we'll get plenty of racial Caitlin Clark takes over the next month or two.

Thank goodness.

Anyway, McNutt joined a version of SportsCenter that nobody watches last night, and decided to give her hot take(s) from a nail salon, which was, frankly, the most pathetic thing I've seen from that network in a while.

Imagine this coming on your screen and not changing the channel:

Now, to an ESPNer who actually deserves some screen time

Lordy. What a time to be alive. What a world we live in at the moment. This isn't the first time we've heard from McNutt this week, by the way.

Don't forget, just a few days ago, she stuffed Caitlin Clark in a locker and insisted she was to blame for the negative headlines surrounding the WNBA because she lacks "accountability" and "self-awareness."

Seriously:

Goodness gracious. And Ryan Clark had the audacity to blame racism on his firing when Monica McNutt is still employed and allowed to spout off takes like that.

Yeah, OK, Rhino! Whatever you say.

Anyway, who else is looking forward to another drama-free weekend out of the WNBA!? Sophie Cunningham plays tonight in lefty Portland. Surely nothing will happen.

OK, moving on ...

... From one ESPN staffer to another (former?) ESPN staffer:

Paulina, Romo & Paige, oh my!

Whoaaaaaaaa Nellie! Imagine my surprise last night when I flipped to the Nats-Braves game, and heard Karl Ravech on the call.

Yes, the same Karl Ravech that was part of those layoffs a few weeks ago. He's back! He just showed back up to work like nothing happened.

No explanation. No comment. No nothin'. Just put his hard-hat on and acted like he never left. Amazing.

Some context:

Sources tell OutKick that, in addition to last night’s assignment, Ravech will do a few remaining assignments in the coming weeks, including another MLB game and his usual Little League World Series work. What we don't know is why. I would assume this is Ravech's choice. Duh. He was laid off, along with Ryan Clark, Cam Newton, and others. The only way he'd essentially finish out his duties would be if he decided to come back. My biggest takeaway? Pay attention to how Ravech responded to his firing, compared to Ryan Clark, who ran to his podcast, sobbed like a child, and then shouted "RACISM."

Should tell you everything you need to know.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

OK, let's rapid-fire this Friday class into a big Friday night. First up? Amazingly, LIV Gold reportedly has an interested investor who is willing to step in and essentially save the league. Nothing is official, but that's the word on the street right now.

Paulina Gretzky — wife of Dustin Johnson — seems to be celebrating the news appropriately:

World.title: NY school district pauses AI robot teaching assistant rollout amid controversies about manufacturer
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A school district in rural New York has paused a program to bring in a robot assistant teacher as it reviews privacy concerns.

The Salamanca City Central School District's board initially approved the nearly $60,000 purchase of an AI-driven robot from Realbotix, which would not only be in the classroom, but could communicate with students through their laptops.

The robot, named Sally, is designed to resemble a human, with silicone skin and long brown hair. It will remain seated but will be capable of a range of facial expressions and upper-body movements. The robot would not be a replacement for teachers or staff or operate unsupervised, but be a tutor of sorts that remembers previous interactions with a student and tailors its responses to each student's learning history.

However, the program has met with two major controversies.

WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL

According to the Associated Press, Realbotix’s sister company, Intima LLC, "holds an ownership stake in RealDoll, a longtime maker of sex dolls, including a line of AI-powered models billed as the ‘world’s most advanced sex robot.’"

Realbotix, however, has asserted that these companies have completely different products with "no crossover."

"Realbotix Corp. is a holding company with two separately operated businesses: Realbotix LLC, which focuses on AI-powered humanoid robotics for commercial service sector applications, and Intima LLC, which focuses on direct-to-consumer products. Realbotix LLC and Intima LLC have different product offerings with no crossover."

The Salamanca City Central School District’s given reason for pausing the program, however, is students’ data concerns regarding any information they share with the robot.

The Associated Press reported that in a now-deleted statement from the district’s Facebook page, the robot teacher assistant pilot program is paused as the district works through "enhanced student data privacy agreements" with the state education officials and does community outreach.

"The robot also has been programmed to steer clear of inappropriate topics such as sex, violence and gambling, and it won’t be able to search the public internet or draw answers from unvetted generative AI services," the Associated Press reported. "Instead, all information on ‘Sally’ will be stored locally, with the life-sized robot consuming roughly the same amount of energy as a laptop, according to the district."

Mark Beehler, Salamanca's superintendent, has addressed concerns about a robot replacing humans in the classroom.

"There is no possible way a robot can replace a human in a school," he said Tuesday. "Even if it were possible, it would in no way be in the best interest of students. Teaching is a human-to-human process."

HUMANOID ROBOT VIDEOS SHOW MACHINES LASHING OUT

He noted, however, that in their rural area, many students do not have easy access to the developing technologies of the future that could help unlock career pathways for them.

"In most cases, our students need to travel 1-2 hours to have opportunities to see emergent technology," he said. "One of the intents of the robot is to help level the playing field and motivate students to continue studying robotics, AI, and STEAM related-career pathways."

When reached by Fox News Digital, the company provided a statement from a Realbotix spokesperson: "Realbotix respects Salamanca City Central School District’s decision to temporarily pause the proposed pilot while the district engages with its community and Realbotix works with the district and the New York State Education Department to put an appropriate data privacy agreement in place. The physical robot has not been deployed."

It provided further clarification on how the robot would protect students’ privacy.

"Realbotix understands the questions being raised by parents and believes they deserve clear, verifiable answers. The proposed physical unit would operate locally through the school and would not be connected to the public internet. It does not record audio or video and does not use facial recognition," the spokesperson said. "Student authentication would be handled entirely through the district’s existing systems, and any student-linked information would remain encrypted and under the district’s control. Realbotix would not receive, access or store personally identifiable student information or student interactions."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The statement added further that the robot indeed will not be a replacement for teachers , but to "serve as a supervised classroom resource for older high school students participating in the district’s STEAM curriculum. Like a calculator, laboratory apparatus or other instructional tool, it can help students engage with educational material and gain hands-on exposure to AI and robotics, but it does not perform the work of a teacher. Characterizations suggesting that the technology would replace teachers or assume their responsibilities are false."

The company also distanced the robot from any adult associations, arguing that media reports have been outright false.

"Some media reports have also falsely connected the Salamanca project to an adult product or adult-products business. The Salamanca robot is a newly manufactured, purpose-built educational unit; no existing consumer product or hardware is being modified or repurposed for the school. Realbotix LLC focuses exclusively on non-adult commercial applications, including healthcare and education. No adult-products business has any involvement in the Salamanca project or in any product or initiative developed by Realbotix LLC."

Fox News Digital's Rachel del Guidice contributed to this report.

World.title: Foreign robot ban targets China over security fears
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A humanoid robot can carry equipment through a factory or help researchers test new artificial intelligence. However, its cameras can watch everything nearby. Its internet connection can also send valuable information beyond the building. The Trump administration now sees that combination as a potential national security problem.

On July 28, the Federal Communications Commission added foreign-produced advanced robots and connected power inverters to its Covered List. The action blocks many new models from receiving the FCC authorization required before companies can import or sell them in the United States.

Although the final language applies broadly to foreign-produced equipment, China reportedly sits at the center of the crackdown. Officials want to prevent surveillance and cyberattacks while reducing America's reliance on Chinese technology. They also hope companies will move more manufacturing to the United States.

HUMANOID ROBOT VIDEOS SHOW MACHINES LASHING OUT

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com .

Why the foreign robot ban is happening now

Humanoid robots are no longer limited to flashy demonstrations that rack up views online. Companies are preparing them for factories and warehouses. Researchers are also testing them inside laboratories. Four-legged robots can inspect dangerous areas or patrol large properties. Meanwhile, robot developers are building new safety systems as these machines begin working closer to people.

That sounds useful, but these machines also see and hear a lot. Many come equipped with cameras and microphones. Other sensors help them map rooms, recognize objects and respond to people. The robot may connect to cloud services for AI processing. A company might also use that connection to install software updates or provide remote support. That connection is where the FCC sees a potential problem.

If a hacker gets inside the system, the robot could collect sensitive information or send data somewhere it should not go. An attacker might also interfere with its movements. In some cases, that person could gain remote control. We have already seen how those risks can surface in ordinary connected machines. A recent security report involving Yarbo robot mowers raised concerns about remote access, live camera feeds and saved Wi-Fi information.

Now think about a more powerful robot working inside a factory or research lab. Federal national security agencies say some foreign-made robots could create unacceptable cybersecurity and supply chain risks. They worry that hostile governments could use the technology to monitor Americans. The machines could also gather intelligence from sensitive locations. A stolen password is bad enough. A hacked robot can move through a building while recording what it sees. It may also operate close to valuable equipment.

How the FCC foreign robot ban works

The FCC did not tell Americans to surrender robots they already own. The government also did not automatically order retailers to remove every foreign robot from store shelves. Instead, the agency added foreign-produced advanced robotic devices to its Covered List.

Equipment on that list generally cannot receive a new FCC authorization. Most connected electronic products need that approval before companies can import, market or sell them in the United States. As a result, the restrictions mainly affect new models that have not received authorization. Previously approved products can remain available, although the FCC reportedly retains the authority to revoke earlier approvals.

Companies may also seek conditional approval. Federal national security agencies can review a device and decide whether it presents an acceptable level of risk. Officials expect many non-Chinese suppliers to reportedly receive exemptions. That suggests the broader foreign-made restriction will hit Chinese manufacturers the hardest.

This move did not come out of nowhere. Lawmakers had already introduced a bipartisan proposal that would block federal agencies from using certain robots tied to foreign adversaries. The latest FCC action reaches much further because it can prevent new products from entering the broader American market.

Why power inverters are included in the crackdown

Power inverters rarely attract the same attention as walking robots. Still, they play an important role in America's energy system. An inverter converts direct current electricity into alternating current electricity. Solar panels and batteries generate or store direct current. Homes, power grids and data centers generally need alternating current.

Many inverters today connect to the internet. Operators use those connections to check performance and install updates. Some systems also allow remote adjustments. However, remote access creates another potential doorway for attackers.

Federal officials worry that foreign companies or hackers could interfere with connected inverters. A coordinated attack might disrupt equipment or expose information about how energy moves through a facility.

A major interruption could affect internet cloud services and the businesses that rely on them. An inverter may look like a metal box mounted beside a solar array. Still, when thousands of connected units feed electricity into important systems, their security becomes much harder to ignore.

OHIO ROBOT COP RETIRES AFTER ZERO ARRESTS

Why China sits at the center of the robot fight

Chinese companies have become major players in advanced robotics. They have gained attention by offering capable machines at prices that U.S. developers may struggle to match. The ban could reportedly hit Unitree especially hard. Counterpoint Research estimates that the Chinese company holds just under one-fifth of the global humanoid robot market.

Unitree has also worked with Nvidia to use its Blackwell AI chips in a robot platform. Nvidia has said data from those robots will remain in the United States. The company also said many Unitree customers in America are universities and research institutions. China strongly criticized the FCC action. Its embassy in Washington accused the United States of unfairly targeting Chinese businesses. It also warned that Beijing could respond if the restrictions harm Chinese interests. Meanwhile, China's Foreign Ministry called the policy protectionist. A spokesperson argued that the restrictions could hurt American companies and consumers. We reached out to Unitree for comment, but did not hear back before our deadline.

Could the robot ban slow American innovation?

The foreign robot ban may give U.S. manufacturers more room to grow. American companies will face less competition from low-cost Chinese machines in the domestic market. However, the policy could create short-term problems for researchers and startups. Some American teams use affordable Chinese robots to test software or train AI systems. Losing access to newer models could raise costs and limit the hardware available for experiments.

The restrictions could also complicate partnerships between U.S. chipmakers and Chinese robotics companies. That may slow certain projects even as Washington tries to strengthen domestic production. The bigger question involves timing. Building a competitive American robotics supply chain will take investment and skilled workers. Manufacturers must also secure motors, sensors and other components. Until that happens, tighter restrictions could leave a gap between the robots American developers want and the machines they can afford.

How to protect yourself when buying a connected robot

You may never bring a humanoid robot into your home, but smaller connected robots are already everywhere. Robot vacuums, lawn mowers and security devices can collect video, map your property and connect to remote servers. Before you buy one, take a few minutes to check how the company protects that access.

1) Look for an FCC ID

Connected devices sold in the United States should include an FCC identification number. You can usually find it on the product, packaging or manufacturer's website. Be cautious if the company provides no clear regulatory information.

2) Check where your data goes

Find out whether the robot stores camera footage and room maps locally or uploads them to the cloud. The privacy policy should explain where the company stores that information and who can access it.

3) Review remote access settings

Turn off remote viewing or cloud controls when you do not need them. A feature that lets you control a robot from anywhere could also become an entry point for someone else.

TOP TRUMP AGENCY PURGES OVER 20 SUSPECTED CHINA-LINKED PRODUCTS FROM FEDERAL MARKETPLACE

4) Install every security update

Robot software needs updates just like your phone or computer. Enable automatic updates when available and avoid products from companies with a poor support record.

5) Use a separate Wi-Fi network

Place connected robots and other smart devices on a guest network when your router supports it. That can help keep a compromised device away from your computers and sensitive files.

6) Secure the account controlling the device

Use a strong, unique password for the account that controls your robot. A password manager can create and securely store it for you. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) if the manufacturer offers it.

7) Ask questions before installing a connected inverter

If you are installing a connected solar or battery inverter, ask the installer who can access it remotely. You should also find out how the company handles software updates and what happens if its online service shuts down.

Kurt's key takeaways

I understand why Washington is paying close attention to this. A network-connected machine with cameras and powerful motors warrants a thorough security review. That concern grows when the robot enters a factory, research center or part of America's energy infrastructure. At the same time, banning new foreign models creates a real tradeoff. Chinese companies currently build many advanced robots at prices American researchers can afford. Restricting that hardware may protect sensitive systems, but it could also slow some U.S. innovation while domestic manufacturers catch up. The success of this policy will depend on what comes next. America needs secure products, strong testing and enough domestic production to give buyers a genuine choice.

Would you accept fewer robot choices and potentially higher prices if the government said the restrictions could prevent foreign surveillance? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

World.title: Shark Week advisory as warming seas push blacktips farther north along East Coast

As Shark Week puts the spotlight on ocean predators, researchers say blacktip sharks are spending more time farther north along the East Coast, expanding their summer range into areas where beachgoers historically encountered them less often.

Researchers at Florida Atlantic University say warming ocean temperatures are reshaping the sharks' annual migration, allowing them to travel farther north before returning south for the winter, according to FOX 35 Orlando.

For more than a decade, researchers have tracked blacktip sharks along the East Coast using aerial surveys and satellite tags. Their data shows the sharks travel north each spring, with many reaching as far as Long Island, New York, by late summer, the outlet reported.

SHARK SIGHTINGS SPIKE NEAR AMERICA'S BEACHES AS JULY 4 CROWDS HEAD TO SHORE FOR WEEKEND

As waters continue to warm, researchers expect the sharks to push even farther north while spending less time in South Florida during the winter.

"They are just like us. They like our air-conditioned temperature," Dr. Stephen Kajiura, a Florida Atlantic University professor who has studied blacktip sharks for about 15 years, told FOX 35 Orlando.

"Our room temperature is 72 or so. [That's] the perfect temperature for these blacktip sharks," Kajiura said.

Researchers are already seeing evidence of that shift, with blacktip sharks occurring farther north, including off Long Island, where beachgoers historically encountered the species less frequently, Kajiura noted.

CLICK HERE TO 

As blacktip sharks swim close to shore, they are among the species beachgoers are most likely to see.

"These are the ones that are in close proximity to the surfers and the swimmers," Kajiura said. "That's the species that's most likely to have encounters with people."

The migration research comes as a new Florida Atlantic University study suggests beach nourishment projects may also influence where blacktip sharks gather during their annual winter migration.

The study, published in the Journal of Coastal Research, found the sharks consistently stay within about 50 meters of the shoreline.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Murky water created by beach nourishment projects could make it harder for the sharks to hunt, potentially changing their behavior and increasing the chances of accidental encounters with people, researchers said.

"What’s striking is how closely the distribution of blacktip sharks overlaps with areas impacted by turbidity events," Kajiura said in a Florida Atlantic University news release.

Researchers said beach nourishment remains an important way to protect coastlines from erosion, but the findings highlight the need to better understand how those projects affect marine life.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Despite the changing migration patterns, Kajiura stressed that shark encounters remain rare and said people shouldn't let the research keep them out of the water.

"The chances of you having a negative encounter with a shark are so minuscule," Kajiura said. "Don't let that diminish your ability to take advantage of the beautiful beaches we have here in Florida."

World.title: Trump defends ‘anti-weaponization’ fund, further complicating Blanche nomination
World.content:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Friday defended his administration’s controversial proposal for a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” for Jan. 6 defendants and others who he says were unfairly targeted by the government.

Trump’s continued flirtation with the weaponization fund undermines assurances from his acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and others in the administration that the idea, which faces strong opposition from some key Republicans, is dead.

The issue delayed for several weeks and nearly derailed a $70 billion bill to fund Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Border Patrol through the end of Trump’s term.

And it has thrown Blanche’s nomination to be the nation’s chief law enforcement official into limbo, with two Republicans — Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — blocking it over concerns about the settlement between Trump and the IRS that created the weaponization fund.

But Trump’s comments Friday are only worsening tensions with the two senators.

Asked Friday at a Cabinet meeting whether the fund is dead, Trump replied: “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t. To be honest with you, I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused. This has nothing to do with Todd.”

Blanche is now unlikely to be confirmed before the Senate departs next week for its five-week summer recess. The chamber is not slated to return until after Labor Day.

In a post on Truth Social earlier in the day, Trump specifically lashed out at Cornyn, suggesting that the longtime senator was standing in the way of the Blanche nomination because the president had backed a primary challenger, Ken Paxton, who defeated Cornyn in May.

“John Cornyn never had a problem with the so called ‘Fund,’ which will not benefit me, but rather the great American Patriots who were hunted down like dogs and whose lives were unfairly and illegally destroyed by the Crooked Joe Biden Administration, until after I decided to Endorse and Support his Republican Primary opponent in Texas, who easily won the Nomination for the United States Senate,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that Cornyn had been among the Republicans who had decried the FBI’s 2022 raid on Mar-a-Lago.

“I will always feel that these victims of government abuse should be paid back for what they were forced to endure, their lives have been ruined!” he wrote.

“Todd Blanche, a good man, should be immediately approved as U.S. Attorney General,” Trump added.

Cornyn has not directly responded to Trump’s post. But on Friday, he retweeted two individuals who questioned Trump’s comments on X. One was GOP strategist Steven Duffield, who wrote: “This does not sound like citizen Trump has agreed to end the Fund.”

Responding to Trump’s post, Tillis on Friday wrote on social media, “The President made it clear today that the so-called Anti Weaponization Fund is still alive, which is exactly why we are attempting to formally end it.”

Blanche, Tillis said, “has been forthright, thoughtful and patient.”

The senator added that Blanche’s confirmation has “hit a snag only because an incompetent personal advisor to the President refuses to amend the bogus settlement.”

“Anyone who attacked law enforcement should still be in prison, not getting a check from the federal government,” Tillis said.

During his Senate confirmation hearing this month, Blanche testified that the Trump administration was abandoning plans for the weaponization fund and that it was “dead.”

But the administration has yet to put anything in writing stating it will not try to launch the fund in the future — something that has raised alarm bells with some skeptics like Cornyn.

“What it suggests to me is they are looking for an out to do something different than what Todd Blanche testified to at his hearing,” Cornyn told reporters Thursday, “and that’s a problem.”

Both Cornyn and Tillis serve on the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee. And a single GOP defection means that Blanche’s nomination cannot get out of committee and be sent to the full Senate.

Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, was forced to punt a Thursday vote to advance Blanche’s nomination until outstanding issues could be resolved. Grassley said he was committed to finding a resolution on Blanche.

“I’m not going to consider any other options because there’s no reason to consider other options at this point,” the chairman told reporters Thursday.

Both Tillis and Cornyn huddled with Blanche Thursday afternoon for about 45 minutes, according to a source familiar with the meeting. The three worked in a positive, collaborative manner in an attempt to resolve the IRS settlement issues, the source added.

There’s another issue with the IRS settlement that could cause problems for Blanche: It includes an agreement that the IRS will not prosecute Trump, his family members or his businesses over any tax claims through May of this year. Both Tillis and Cornyn have said that deal should be narrowed.

Blanche’s challenges may not be confined to just Cornyn and Tillis, who is not seeking re-election this fall. “We’re just on the front line because we’re in the Judiciary,” Cornyn said.

Indeed, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., whom Trump also worked to successfully defeat in a GOP primary this year, also expressed concerns about Blanche’s nomination, telling reporters, “I am very concerned about the weaponization of the Justice Department.”

“Shouldn’t every American be afraid of the weaponization of the Justice Department? If there’s not adequate answers for that, then probably there needs to be somebody else,” Cassidy said of Blanche.
