World.title: How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018830/How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.content:
This is the first article in a two-part series exploring how Chinese culinary terms came to be included in the Oxford English Dictionary (OED).

For more than two decades, I have studied how Chinese words enter the English language, particularly through food. So when the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) released its second batch of updates this past June, one updated entry felt especially meaningful to me: “Cantonese.” For the first time, the dictionary formally recognized the word as a culinary term, defining it as food prepared in the style of Guangzhou and the surrounding region in southern China, as well as the restaurants that serve such cuisine.

The entry is accompanied not just by a simple definition, but by a timeline of citations tracing the term’s culinary history. The earliest example dates back to April 6, 1892, when New Jersey’s Trenton Times referred to “Fashionable Cantonese dishes.” This phrase shows that the term was already being used in relation to food more than a century ago, long before the era of modern globalization.

Western interest in Cantonese cuisine also stretches back to the late 19th century. The OED cites an 1894 report from The Washington Post describing a dim sum dumpling as “shaped exactly like a fishing creel.” By 1908, The New York Herald was explaining the dish to its readers by comparing it to a “second cousin to steamed sponge cake.” These early descriptions reveal how unfamiliar foods were introduced to Western audiences through comparisons with things they already understood.

Over the following decades, Cantonese cuisine continued to leave its mark. A 1950 publication by the Hong Kong Young Women’s Christian Association highlighted “Cantonese specialties” such as turnip pudding, while a 1997 culinary memoir recalled dining at a large “Cantonese restaurant” where dim sum was served from rolling trolleys. More recently, a 2015 article in The Guardian recommended Wong Chi Kee in Hong Kong for its “traditional Cantonese congee.”

These citations connect to a broader ecosystem of existing terms. The Cantonese practice of yum cha, literally “drinking tea,” the social meal of dim sum and tea traditionally enjoyed in the morning, was added to the dictionary in 2016, while dim sum has appeared in the dictionary since 1989.

Today, my research shows that the dictionary contains a vocabulary of 25 Cantonese culinary terms. Beyond the widely recognized dim sum and yum cha, the list includes char siu, wonton, chop suey, hoisin sauce, egg foo yung, and moo goo gai pan. These are no longer treated as foreign concepts requiring lengthy explanations; they have become established English words.

Yet this lexicographical milestone is not simply a retrospective look at history; it also reflects a living culture. Just months earlier, in March 2026, three new additions expanded the OED’s Cantonese culinary vocabulary: dan tat (egg tart), pineapple bun, and yin yeung (a Hong Kong drink combining milk tea and coffee). Their inclusion highlights that Cantonese cuisine is not a static relic of the past. It continues to evolve, innovate, and influence the English language. This ongoing linguistic exchange shows that the relationship between East and West remains an active and continuing process.

The contrast with other regional Chinese cuisines highlights that global influence is not simply a product of modern international presence. Shanghai, for instance, is one of China’s most globally connected cities, yet its local Benbang cuisine has left far fewer traces in the English language. Cantonese cuisine’s deep roots in English developed instead through generations of migration, trade, and everyday use.

Etymologically, “Cantonese” derives from “Canton,” the former English name for Guangzhou, which was first recorded by Portuguese traders in the 16th century. Over time, the term evolved from a geographic reference into a marker of a distinct cultural and culinary identity. This reflects a broader historical reality: Cantonese cuisine established an overseas presence earlier than many other regional Chinese cuisines, spreading through centuries of maritime trade and migration.

Historically, because the vast majority of early Chinese immigrants to many Western countries came from Guangdong, Cantonese restaurants dominated many Chinatowns. Iconic establishments such as New York’s Port Arthur Restaurant, which opened in 1897 and introduced upscale Cantonese dishes to Western diners, and San Francisco’s Shanghai Low, a Cantonese restaurant that adopted a Shanghai-inspired name to appeal to Western customers, did more than serve food. They became gathering places for immigrant communities and helped establish Cantonese cuisine’s prominence in Western societies.

As a linguist, I often argue that translation is not merely a tool for communication between languages; it is also a means of cultural understanding. The inclusion of these terms shows that English speakers are capable of adopting culinary vocabulary from other languages on its own terms.

For readers interested in exploring this vocabulary, here are eight popular Cantonese culinary terms currently included in the OED, with condensed definitions for clarity.

Many of the early Cantonese restaurants that introduced these dishes to Western audiences have since disappeared. Yet the vocabulary they helped popularize has endured, and a new generation of Cantonese restaurants continues to thrive in Chinatowns and communities around the world. The OED’s recognition of Cantonese cuisine reflects this longer history of cultural exchange: carried across borders by generations of immigrants, Cantonese food has become a lasting part of the global culinary vocabulary.

(Header and in-text images: Visuals from VCG, edited by Ding Yining/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018828/China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.title: China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018828/China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.content:
Chinese state-owned bookstore chain Xinhua Bookstore is partnering with food delivery giant Meituan to roll out a nationwide same-day book delivery service, promising to deliver books in under an hour.

The agreement, signed on Friday at the 34th National Book Expo in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, will connect the more than 10,000 Xinhua stores across China to Meituan’s instant retail network, Instashopping. Customers ordering through the network will be able to receive books in as quickly as 30 minutes.

The initiative marks the expansion of multiple pilot initiatives in the last two years comprising several regional Xinhua branches, including in Zhejiang, Shanghai, and the southern city of Shenzhen.

Founded in 1937, Xinhua is China’s largest and oldest bookstore chain.

Instant retail combines online ordering with inventories from nearby physical stores and a network of couriers to deliver products rapidly, typically in under one hour. China’s instant retail market is expected to surpass 1 trillion yuan ($150 billion) in 2026 and double to 2 trillion yuan by 2030, according to a report by the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.

The push into instant retail comes amid intensifying competition between China’s e-commerce platforms and weakening demand for printed books. The country’s book retail market totaled roughly 110 billion yuan in 2025, down 2% from 2024, according to a report by Chinese analytics firm OpenBook.

Jiang Chuanyang, chairman of Xinhua’s Zhejiang branch, said at the event that China’s book market is evolving to comprise e-commerce, local instant retail, and physical bookstores. More than 100 stores in the province were active on Instashopping throughout 2025, generating combined sales of several million yuan, according to domestic media.

But the picture is more mixed for independent bookstores.

Su Shanna, brand manager of Yinxu, a chain of five bookstores in the eastern coastal city of Xiamen, told Sixth Tone that instant delivery orders account for roughly 15% of the company’s monthly revenue. The store joined Instashopping in May 2025, and also accepts on-demand orders through its WeChat mini program, fulfilling local deliveries through courier services such as SF Express and JD Logistics.

“It’s more of a bonus than a lifeline,” Su said, noting that demand for instant book delivery remains limited to a handful of scenarios. These include parents ordering extracurricular reading materials or textbooks for their children, tourists ordering books to their hotels, and patients looking for something to read during hospitalization.

Instant retail fills the gap where consumers need a book immediately and traditional e-commerce can’t meet the demand, according to Jiang Han, a senior researcher at Beijing-based think tank Pangoal.

But books are a low-profit business. Because instant retail platforms take a cut of bookstore sales, instant delivery is unlikely to become a major profit driver, he said.

The service’s real value isn’t in generating significant new revenue, but in generating new revenue sources, Jiang added. “Its significance should be on how it helps bookstores reconstruct their connection to readers.”

Jiang said that bookstores are increasingly trying to become “cultural service hubs” by diversifying their revenue sources, selling tourism-related products, and integrating with the local community. Instant retail is part of this trend.

In the case of Yinxu, members pay an annual fee of 188 yuan, which gives them discounts on books, book delivery services, and tickets to local performances, as well as access to various community activities.

“The key to success depends on whether bookstores can offer irreplaceable cultural experiences and emotional value,” Jiang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from iNueng/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018827/China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.title: China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018827/China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.content:
One graduate trained to restore ancient artifacts now generates AI video clips for short dramas. Another, schooled in landscape design, builds virtual scenery instead of physical sets.

Both are part of a hiring surge across China’s film industry, as AI creates demand for hybrid creative roles and cuts production timelines from months to days. Recruitment for AI video editors jumped 179% year over year in June, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

At one cultural communications company in Zhengzhou, capital of China’s central Henan province, monthly production of AI-generated short dramas has risen from a handful to nearly 100, according to CCTV. The expansion has created demand for AI video editors and “card pullers,” who write prompts, generate footage, and select clips that fit a production’s characters and plot.

The shift is drawing workers from fields including design, animation, digital media, and information technology, according to recruitment platform Zhaopin. AI film roles typically pay between 8,000 and 20,000 yuan ($1,100 to $2,800) a month, depending on experience.

“This indicates that AI is not simply a substitution, but a technological enabler that is driving the transformation of traditional professions and roles,” Li Qiang, a vice president at Zhaopin, told CCTV.

AI is also changing how short dramas are made. Some productions that once required crews of dozens can now be completed by a few people, or even one creator handling scripts, storyboards, visuals, and effects. CCTV reported that AI has compressed some production cycles from months to days, with certain episodes completed in hours and effects and previsualization work becoming three to 10 times faster.

Director He Ziqiang, an early adopter of AI filmmaking tools, has added AI storyboard artists, image generators, card pullers, and editors to his team, many without formal film training.

“Anyone can make their own film, as long as they have ideas,” He told CCTV. “This will greatly enrich artistic creation and vitality, enabling more talented ordinary people to express themselves through AI.”

The hiring surge comes as China’s short-drama industry’s annual output value approached 90 billion yuan in 2025, nearly double the previous year, while some AI-generated productions have reported net profit margins above 50%.

Li Yuan, who is not related to Li Qiang, founder of a Henan-based AI film company, told domestic media his firm had cut the cost of producing a drama from 300,000 yuan to 50,000 yuan while increasing output.

“We thought large models would take longer to nail video fluency, but they got it done in the first quarter of this year,” Li told state media.

But he also cautioned that AI short dramas remain at an early stage, with both the technology and audience tastes still evolving. “Only when the market stabilizes can creators and platforms offer better products,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Staff at a short-drama production company use AI tools during post-production in Jiaxing, Zhejiang province, July 21, 2026. VCG)

World.title: Grade 9 boy stabbed dead by fellow student in Las Piñas school
World.content:
The Schools Division Office of Las Piñas City says it is 'working closely with local authorities, barangay officials, and the Philippine National Police' as they investigate the incident

MANILA, Philippines – A Grade 9 student died after being stabbed by a fellow ninth-grader inside school premises in Las Piñas City on Friday, July 31.

In an initial report, the Southern Police District said two male students of Las Piñas National High School, 13 and 14 years old, had an altercation during recess in front of a classroom on the school’s fourth floor.

The 14-year-old “drew a bladed weapon” and stabbed the 13-year-old “at the left portion [of the] chest,” said the police.

The victim was rushed to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead, while the student who stabbed him was taken into police custody.

Minors 15 years old or below are exempt from criminal liability and must instead undergo an intervention program, according to Republic Act No. 9344 or the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act.

The Las Piñas National High School administration confirmed the incident, saying that it happened despite strict security guidelines.

It said it would provide psychological first aid and other interventions to students, teachers, and staff.

“Nananawagan din kami sa mas matibay na ugnayan ng tahanan, paaralan, at komunidad tungo sa paghubog ng mga mag-aaral na may disiplina, paggalang sa kapuwa, at pananagutan,” added the school.

(We call for stronger coordination between homes, schools, and communities in molding students with discipline, respect for others, and accountability.)

Meanwhile, the Schools Division Office (SDO) of Las Piñas City said it is “working closely with local authorities, barangay officials, and the Philippine National Police as they conduct a thorough and impartial investigation into the matter.”

“Appropriate actions and administrative reviews are also being undertaken regarding the security measures and protocols at the school,” said the SDO.

The incident came over a month after the fatal school shooting in Tacloban City last June 22, which left three students dead and 20 others injured.

The shooting prompted the Department of Education to review school safety protocols and security measures. The DepEd ordered stricter enforcement of bag checks, among others.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara previously said they will seek higher funding for security guards and metal detectors. – Rappler.com

World.title: Visayas, Mindanao, parts of Southern Luzon rainy due to trough of LPA
World.content:
LPA. Satellite image of the low pressure area as of July 31, 2026, 8 pm.

The low pressure area is 865 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon as of 8 pm on Friday, July 31

MANILA, Philippines – The low pressure area (LPA) that formed outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility last Wednesday, July 29, entered PAR on Friday, July 31.

As of 8 pm on Friday, the LPA was located 865 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said the LPA has a low chance of developing into a tropical depression within 24 hours.

While the LPA is still far from land, its trough or extension has been causing scattered rain and thunderstorms in the Visayas, Mindanao, Bicol, Quezon, Laguna, and Marinduque.

PAGASA advised the affected areas to remain on alert for flash floods and landslides.

The rest of Luzon, not affected by the trough of the LPA, is seeing generally fair weather, with just localized thunderstorms.

The other LPA that PAGASA was monitoring in the final week of July already dissipated over the West Philippine Sea on Thursday, July 30. It formed last Tuesday, July 28, then crossed Southern Luzon on Wednesday.

The Philippines is currently experiencing a monsoon break, with no rain from the southwest monsoon or habagat. Monsoon breaks, which can last for days or even weeks, are normal during the rainy season.

But the southwest monsoon may return next week, as it is expected to be enhanced by the tropical cyclone with the international name Dolphin, which is currently a super typhoon around 4,000 kilometers away from the Philippines.

Based on initial forecasts, Dolphin itself appears unlikely to make landfall in the country, but the monsoon rain could trigger floods and landslides.

The Philippines saw four tropical cyclones in July: Tropical Depression Henry, Super Typhoon Inday (Bavi), Tropical Storm Josie (Haishen), and Typhoon Kiyapo (Noul).

PAGASA said two to four tropical cyclones could develop within or enter PAR in August. – Rappler.com

World.title: Talacogon LGU: Baterbonia family requests privacy for Rene’s siblings
World.content:
MOTHER'S GRIEF. Rovelyn Baterbonia weeps by her son Rene Clert's casket during his burial in Talacogon, Agusan del Sur, on June 24, 2026.

Since Ateneo basketball player Rene Baterbonia’s death in June, his six siblings, five of whom are minors, have drawn unexpected attention from fans and content creators

MANILA, Philippines – The local government unit (LGU) of Talacogon, Agusan del Sur, informed the public that the family of late Ateneo basketball player Rene Baterbonia has requested privacy for his siblings.

Baterbonia’s six siblings, five of whom are minors, have drawn unexpected attention from fans and content creators since the Talacogon star athlete’s death in June.

Fourteen-year-old Rhenz, the third oldest of the Baterbonia siblings, has particularly attracted public interest in Mindanao as he plays basketball like his older brother Rene.

“The family respectfully requests that the welfare and privacy of Rene Clert’s siblings, who are currently in school and are minors, be respected,” Talacogon’s Municipal Information Office wrote in Filipino on its Facebook page on Thursday, July 30.

“Please refrain from going to their school, as well as taking photos or videos of them for vlogs or any form of online publication, as doing so has caused the children fear and distress.”

The Baterbonia family, according to the LGU, also asks the public to avoid creating social media content that alludes to any form of fundraising.

This comes after the LGU became aware of reports that financial assistance intended for the Baterbonias did not reach the family.

“The family is making a strong appeal to everyone, especially those who create vlogs or any form of social media content, to refrain from sharing statements or content that may give the impression of requesting or soliciting financial assistance,” said the LGU.

Vlogging activities at the Barangay Labnig Memorial Cemetery, where Baterbonia was laid to rest, have also been strictly limited.

Even nearly two months after Baterbonia’s death, fans continue to visit his grave and pay their respects by leaving flowers.

“It’s being requested that visits to Labnig Cemetery remain solely for visitation purposes,” the LGU said.

The LGU also urged the public to refrain from spreading unverified reports regarding legal matters surrounding the deaths of Baterbonia and teammate Divine Adili during Ateneo’s team-building activity in Dipaculao, Aurora.

“To maintain order and prevent the spread of misinformation, all official updates regarding the case will be released only through the family’s authorized representatives,” the LGU said.

Baterbonia’s mother, Rovelyn, said on Friday, July 31, that those who wish to purchase products from their Baterbonia Collections may contact the LGU to prevent fraudulent activity.

“There are so many scammers nowadays. It’s already difficult to find money, only for it to end up in the hands of bad people or scammers. Please also be careful with the people you ask to deliver help to our family, as you might also get scammed. That’s why I am urging everyone to message the Talacogon LGU instead,” Rovelyn wrote in Filipino on Facebook.

“Thank you to everyone who sent us their messages of condolences and love and those who gave us material assistance.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Two founders weigh in on learning, building, and adapting, to grow an MSME in e-commerce
World.content:
Through Shopee, the founders of Tech Smart Philippines and Samara Baby & Kids share how continuous learning helps them grow their businesses



Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Shopee and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

Building a successful business takes more than one good idea. As industries evolve and customer needs change, business owners must continuously rethink how they grow.

For Christopher Bautista of Tech Smart Philippines and Jennalyn Indigado of Samara Baby & Kids, growing an MSME on Shopee has meant continuously learning, adapting, and responding to customers’ changing needs.

Their stories show how Shopee supports MSMEs beyond providing a place to sell. Through seller education, platform tools, campaign opportunities, and account management, Shopee supports entrepreneurs as they grow.

Reinventing after uncertainty

For Jennalyn Indigado, that journey began with learning an entirely new industry.

Before founding Samara Baby & Kids, her family ran a hog-raising business for five decades as their primary source of income. When African Swine Fever (ASF) disrupted the industry in 2019, they were forced to start over.

Looking for a new source of income, Jennalyn turned to Shopee. Initially, she just wanted to find tie-sides for her baby daughter, Samara, the namesake of the brand. She realized she could provide them to other parents, too.

“Coming from agriculture, we had very little knowledge about garments, e-commerce, or digital marketing. That was all new to us,” she said.

What helped her business grow was embracing the learning opportunities available through Shopee’s seller programs. The platform introduced her to the fundamentals of running an e-commerce business, from sales and marketing to inventory management, customer insights, and even financial management.

“We made it through that journey because Shopee made it possible,” Jennalyn said. “It was like they created a blueprint that I could simply follow, step by step.”

Jennalyn also credited Shopee’s account managers for guiding her as the business scaled, from encouraging participation in campaigns and new opportunities to conducting regular business reviews that looked at shop performance and day-to-day operations.

“You will never feel alone because the platform is up-to-date with the tools you need,” she added.

Eight years into Shopee, the brand expanded from a handful of listings to hundreds of products while steadily building a loyal customer base driven by its mission: to create jobs and provide quality, affordable products for Filipino families, especially moms.

Today, with Shopee’s support, what began as an alternative source of income grew into a business with 700 products, 1.7 million followers, and around 400 employees.

Building around a problem worth solving

Christopher Bautista’s journey highlights another side of long-term business growth: continuously understanding what customers need.

When Christopher listed his very first product, a power bank on an online marketplace, he wasn’t following a detailed business plan.

“I started with what I like personally: technology, gaming, and electronics,” he shared.

As a gadget enthusiast, Christopher often searched for electronic accessories that were difficult to find in the Philippines. Recognizing that many consumers faced the same challenge, he built Tech Smart Philippines around making these products more accessible.

Over the past eight years on Shopee, Tech Smart Philippines has grown by continuously listening to customers and adapting as e-commerce evolved.

Christopher credits Shopee University for helping him better understand pricing and new platform features, while initiatives such as Free Shipping, Mega Vouchers, and Shopee Ads helped the business reach more customers.

“It’s one of the valuable resources they provide,” he said. “The Seller Education Hub is easy to understand, even without formal training. For example, they provide pricing computations, which I use as a guide to price our products fairly for our customers.”

For him, earning customer trust is a value every aspiring MSME should prioritize from the start.

“Focus on building your brand while delivering excellent customer service,” he added. “Because when you have a good reputation, customers will come back to you even if you’re priced slightly higher than others.”

Today, Tech Smart maintains a 4.9 customer rating and a 100% chat response rate on Shopee, reflecting its focus on building customer trust over time.

While Christopher serves technology enthusiasts and Jennalyn supports parents and young families, their journeys point to the same lesson: growing an MSME in e-commerce is rarely the result of one successful product or one good business idea.

Long-term growth comes from continuous learning, responding to customers, and adapting as markets evolve. For aspiring MSMEs, both founders encourage starting with a genuine understanding of the problem they want to solve while remaining open to learning along the way.

Shopee brings together experienced sellers like Christopher and Jennalyn to share practical lessons with the wider MSME community. Their journeys show that lasting growth in e-commerce is built not only by selling more but also by continuously learning, listening to customers, and improving how the business is run. – Rappler.com

World.title: In letter to Palace, new DOH chief Pujalte accused of gambling at casinos
World.content:
OATH. Dr. Jose Pujalte Jr. takes his oath at Malacañang as the new secretary of the Department of Health on July 14, 2026.

The Department of Health denies the allegations, adding that Secretary Brix Pujalte was only at a hotel recently for a meeting with provincial government officials

MANILA, Philippines – Newly appointed Department of Health (DOH) Secretary Jose “Brix” Pujalte Jr. is the subject of a complaint letter addressed to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for allegedly frequenting casinos.

In a letter submitted to Malacañang on Friday, July 31, anonymous “concerned citizens” claimed Pujalte has repeatedly been seen gambling at Okada Manila and Solaire Resort & Casino.

The complainants also alleged that he uses the aliases “Louis Santos” and “Louis Santoss” to hide his identity.

“Nakakabahala nang malaman namin na siya ang itinalaga na acting secretary ng DOH dahil ang isang mataas na opisyal ng gobyerno — na dapat ay modelo ng moralidad at integridad — ay nagtatapon lang ng oras at pera sa pasugalan,” the complainants wrote.

(It is alarming to learn that he has been appointed secretary of the DOH, because a high-ranking government official — who ought to be a model of morality and integrity — is simply wasting time and money on gambling.)

They accused Pujalte of violating Presidential Decree No. 1869, Section 14(a), which says that government officials are prohibited from playing in casinos, and Republic Act No. 6713, or the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees.

The complainants are seeking the preventive suspension and dismissal of the health secretary.

DOH response

The DOH denied the allegations, adding that Pujalte was only at a hotel recently for a meeting with provincial government officials. The hotel was not named.

“Noong Hulyo 20, naimbitahan siya para dumalo sa isang opisyal na pagpupulong kasama ang mga opisyal ng Masbate at Sorsogon sa isang hotel. Tanging ang pagbibigay ng tulong sa mga pampublikong ospital sa rehiyon ang pinag-usapan sa naturang pagtitipon,” the health department’s statement read.

(On July 20, he was invited to attend a formal meeting with officials from Masbate and Sorsogon at a hotel. The discussion at the gathering focused solely on assisting public hospitals in the region.)

Marcos appointed Pujalte as health secretary on July 13 after his predecessor Teodoro Herbosa resigned, citing medical reasons. – Rappler.com

World.title: With Azerbaijan, Central Asia Seeks Greater Geopolitical Weight
World.content:
ASTANA – The leaders of Central Asia and Azerbaijan gathered in Cholpon-Ata on July 31 for an informal summit aimed at translating years of improving political ties into practical regional integration, as Azerbaijan expands the grouping’s reach across the Caspian and Kazakhstan pushes for an action plan for a landmark cooperation treaty.

The consultative format brings together Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan to discuss trade, energy, transport corridors, tourism, humanitarian cooperation and regional security. Since its launch in 2018, the five Central Asian states have met annually in an informal format without outside powers, demonstrating their growing readiness and political willingness to address shared challenges on their own terms.

“Over the past eight years, the format has clearly evolved. In 2018, the main priority was to rebuild trust among the countries of the region and restore regular high-level dialogue. That was particularly important after a prolonged period in which many regional issues were addressed primarily through bilateral channels,” said Bauyrzhan Auken, lead expert of the Department of Asian Studies at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, in a comment to The Astana Times.

The meeting in Tashkent in 2025 marked a turning point, as it formally admitted Azerbaijan as a full participant and opened the way for a more ambitious phase of regional cooperation.

At the meeting, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for a concrete action plan to implement a regional friendship treaty, formally known as the Treaty of Friendship, Good Neighborliness and Cooperation for the Development of Central Asia in the 21st century.

The document was signed in 2022 by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan following the fourth consultative meeting. Tajikistan joined the treaty in August 2025, followed by Turkmenistan in June 2026.

Describing the document as historic, Tokayev stressed it “marks a new stage in strategic partnership” and “establishes a political framework for regional cooperation.”

“I believe the next step should be the practical implementation of the document’s provisions. In this regard, I propose developing and subsequently adopting an action plan with clear benchmarks for our long-term cooperation, aimed at further strengthening friendship and good-neighborly relations, as well as expanding trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian cooperation,” Tokayev said.

“It can be said with confidence that, thanks to growing mutual trust and the consistent development of regional cooperation, Central Asia is now experiencing the most successful period in its modern history,” he added.

The consultative format may be entering a more demanding phase, focused less on declarations and more on delivery.

“Today, the consultative meetings are no longer limited to an exchange of views among leaders. A working system has gradually developed around them, with summit rules, road maps, a Council of National Coordinators and closer cooperation among relevant ministries,” Auken said.

“The main question now is how to give the regional treaty practical substance,” he added.

According to him, Tokayev’s proposal to develop a separate action plan directly addresses that challenge. The aim is to define specific priorities, deadlines and responsible agencies. The consultative meetings can therefore now be viewed as a mechanism for setting a common agenda in trade, transport, energy, and investment, among other areas.

Growing trade

This push for closer regional cooperation is increasingly supported by trade. According to Yernar Serik, a foreign trade analyst and founder of the Trade Report Telegram channel, Kazakhstan’s trade with its Central Asian neighbors rose 28.9% year on year to a record $4.2 billion in January-May 2026, with exports reaching $3.2 billion.

Uzbekistan alone accounted for more than half of its regional trade. Bilateral trade rose 37.2% to $2.3 billion in January-May.

The region has also become a particularly important market for Kazakh manufacturers, absorbing 40% of the country’s finished-goods exports, excluding re-exports.

Why coordination matters now

“Coordination among the Central Asian countries has become a necessity,” Auken said, noting that disruptions to transport routes and supply chains, energy and price volatility and conflicts beyond the region can quickly produce consequences across Central Asia.

“At the same time, Central Asian countries face shared challenges involving water resources, climate change, food and energy security, and the need to adapt their economies to global technological shifts. Addressing these issues solely at the national level is becoming increasingly difficult. The countries, therefore, need to align their interests, exchange information and jointly plan their next steps,” he explained.

Transport and logistics are also taking on a greater importance in discussions.

“Geopolitical instability has increased the need to diversify routes between Asia and Europe. Developing alternative corridors allows the countries of the region to strengthen the resilience of supply chains and reduce their dependence on individual routes,” he said.

Informal format

According to Auken, the format’s flexibility is its strength. It does not require governments to transfer authority to a supranational body, build a large permanent bureaucracy or surrender elements of national sovereignty.

“It allows leaders to discuss sensitive issues openly, coordinate their positions and advance joint initiatives without excessive bureaucracy,” the expert said.

Auken cautioned that closer coordination does not mean the countries were seeking to build a closed regional bloc or distance themselves from outside partners. Instead, the objective was to align their positions more effectively and defend shared regional interests amid intensifying competition among major powers.

“At the same time, the format’s flexibility does not relieve the countries of the need to implement the agreements they reach. Decisions made at the leaders’ level must be followed through by executive agencies,” he said.

Azerbaijan expands the format across the Caspian

Azerbaijan’s inclusion as a full participant marks a significant expansion of the consultative format beyond Central Asia’s five states. Its participation strengthens the trans-Caspian dimension and creates new opportunities for cooperation in transport, energy, trade and investment. With Azerbaijan serving as a key link to the South Caucasus, Türkiye and European markets, the enlarged format could help advance a more integrated regional transport and logistics network, including the Middle Corridor.

According to Tokayev, Azerbaijan’s inclusion marked a new stage in the format’s evolution.

“Through our joint efforts, we are creating conditions for deeper political dialogue, expanded cooperation in investment, energy and industry, and the development of an integrated transport and logistics system,” he said.

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev reinforced that broader vision, saying Azerbaijan’s accession had elevated the consultative format to a “qualitatively new, macro-regional level.” His remarks pointed to an emerging geopolitical concept that links Central Asia with the South Caucasus and Afghanistan through transport, trade and development ties.

According to Auken, Azerbaijan’s participation does not transform the grouping into a broader political bloc and does not alter the Central Asian character of the format.

“Rather, it gives the grouping greater substance and strengthens its practical dimension. It enables the countries to advance projects whose significance extends across the wider trans-Caspian region,” he said, noting that it creates additional opportunities for Central Asian countries to pursue joint projects in transport, energy and digital infrastructure.

“This is most visible in transport,” he said, stressing that Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are key actors in the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, which links China and Europe through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus.

“For the countries of the region, developing the corridor offers a way to diversify routes, reduce dependence on individual transit channels and strengthen their position in Eurasian logistics,” Auken said.

He also highlighted opportunities in energy, industry, investment and digital infrastructure.

“One example is the planned fiber-optic cable across the Caspian Sea between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, which is expected to improve regional digital connectivity and create an additional data-transmission route,” said the expert.

Stronger voice of Central Asia

Addressing the meeting, Tokayev said Central Asia’s role in global affairs is steadily growing and that the region’s voice is becoming increasingly prominent on the international stage.

“Kazakhstan remains committed to the agreements reached and will continue advancing constructive initiatives aimed at strengthening friendship, good-neighborly relations and strategic partnership among our countries. I am confident that, through our joint efforts, we will achieve even greater progress,” Tokayev said.

The expanded format does not amount to a closed regional bloc. Instead, it reflects an effort by Central Asian states to coordinate more effectively, reduce their vulnerability to external shocks and approach larger powers with a clearer sense of shared interests.

World.title: How Trans-Caspian Cable Fits Kazakhstan’s Evolving Connectivity Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA — For decades, Kazakhstan’s connectivity strategy was measured in highways, railways and pipelines. Today, that vision is expanding. As global competition increasingly depends on the movement of data alongside the movement of goods, the country is investing in a new layer of strategic infrastructure — one designed not to carry cargo, but information.

Among the clearest examples of this shift is the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable project. The first-ever underwater telecommunications link across the Caspian Sea will connect Aktau and Sumqayit, creating a new digital corridor between Central Asia, the South Caucasus and Europe.

The project reflects a broader vision articulated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who has increasingly framed Kazakhstan’s connectivity agenda as extending beyond physical transport routes to include cross-border digital infrastructure. In his September 2024 State of the Nation Address, he called for the project to be completed, describing it as essential for “creating a digital infrastructure linked with international corridors and cross-border data flows.”

Several months later, speaking at an informal meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Organization of Turkic States in Budapest, Tokayev expanded that vision beyond Kazakhstan.

“This project will significantly improve digital communication between our countries and will be a strategic step towards strengthening regional integration. Such initiatives open up opportunities to create a new digital corridor across the Eurasian continent,” he said.

The regional context continues to evolve. As the cable enters its final construction phase, regional leaders are once again gathering, this time in Cholpon-Ata for an informal Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, underscoring how cooperation between the countries increasingly extends across transport, energy and digital connectivity.

Nearly two years after Tokayev first identified the project as a strategic priority, it is entering its most tangible phase. Kazakhstan is now carrying out the final stages of the project, with commercial commissioning expected by the end of 2026. The latest phase has shifted from engineering preparation to offshore construction.

According to the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development’s release from July 31, regulatory, customs and organizational procedures have been completed, including the approval of equipment required for the offshore works, allowing construction to proceed without administrative delays.

Preparatory work in 2025 included desktop and offshore engineering surveys, selection of the optimal route avoiding anchorage zones and military training areas, environmental approvals from the Mangystau Region authorities, and the production and factory testing in China of a specially armored submarine cable equipped with ROPA optical amplifiers.

With the planning phase complete, attention has shifted from engineering design to execution at sea. The cable, previously delivered from China to the port of Kuryk together with three cable baskets weighing a combined 600 tons, was transported to Baku aboard a specialized logistics vessel. It has now been transferred into the cable tank of the cable-laying vessel, which has departed Baku and is laying the line toward Aktau.

The operation is being carried out by a cable-laying vessel with a displacement exceeding 20,000 tons and equipped with dynamic positioning technology to ensure precise installation on the seabed. Around 70 crew members are involved, including technical supervisors and representatives of Kazakhtelecom. The project is being implemented by CaspiLink B.V., the joint venture established by Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom.

A dedicated jointing room has also been installed onboard to allow engineers to repair or reconnect the cable if required during installation. Both the Kazakh and Azerbaijani cable ends have already undergone testing. Subject to favorable weather conditions, installation of the submarine cable is expected to be completed within the next 15 to 20 days, while the overall commissioning process remains on schedule for completion by the end of 2026.

The significance of the project, however, extends well beyond the technical operation. As economies become more deeply integrated through both physical and digital infrastructure, international corridors are no longer defined solely by the goods they carry. They are increasingly shaped by the data they enable to move across borders. While the cable spans just 380 kilometers across the Caspian seabed, the vision behind it reaches much further. The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable reflects Kazakhstan’s ambition to remain an important link in the movement of both goods and data across Eurasia.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Air Taxis, Energy Security and Middle Corridor
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from international media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights the country’s plans to launch Central Asia’s first air taxi service, developments in energy security, transport connectivity and regional diplomacy.



Speaking alongside Putin, Kazakh President calls for freeze of Ukraine war

Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said on Saturday ​that a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine might be reached ‌if the sides froze the conflict and resumed negotiations, reported Reuters on July 25.

Speaking alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin at a Russia-Kazakhstan forum in the Siberian ​city of Omsk, Tokayev praised Putin’s “utmost diplomatic flexibility.”

“If I may offer my humble opinion, since I have been asked, perhaps it is time to freeze this conflict and return to the Istanbul formula 2.0,” he said.

Moscow ​and Kyiv participated in talks in Istanbul soon after Russia’s full-scale invasion in early 2022 and again in 2025, though the discussions failed ​to produce a breakthrough.

Tokayev proposes launching digital transport corridor between Kazakhstan and Russia

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed launching a pilot digital transport corridor between Kazakhstan and Russia to further develop logistics and boost bilateral trade, reported Trend on July 25.

According to the press service of the President of Kazakhstan, Tokayev made the proposal while addressing the 22nd Kazakhstan-Russia Interregional Cooperation Forum in Omsk.

The president said Kazakhstan and Russia have unique opportunities to shape Eurasia’s transport and logistics architecture.

“Kazakhstan and Russia, which share the world’s longest continuous land border, are destined to play a leading role in developing the transport and logistics architecture of the Eurasian continent,” Tokayev said.

US, Kazakhstan discuss energy security, Caspian oil exports

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Kazakh Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev held high-level talks Wednesday on regional energy security and the stability of global oil supply chains, reported ED News on July 29.

“The two officials discussed the importance of energy security, including the reliable and uninterrupted export of Kazakhstan-origin oil via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), for regional stability and prosperity,” said State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott.

Rubio expressed gratitude for Kazakhstan’s support of US President Donald Trump’s peace initiatives and signaled interest in deeper economic ties, he added.

The Kazakh Foreign Ministry confirmed the conversation covered the “Enhanced Strategic Partnership” and preparations for Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s upcoming trip to the US for the G20 Summit in December.

Middle Corridor opens new route for Kazakh exports

Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ) has organized the first-ever multimodal shipment of mineral fertilizers from the city of Ekibastuz to the United Kingdom, AzerNEWS reported on July 28.

The shipment is being carried via the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, using both rail and maritime transport. The cargo will travel through Kazakhstan, across the Caspian Sea, and onward through Azerbaijan and Georgia before being transported by sea from the ports of Poti and Batumi to the Port of Felixstowe in the United Kingdom.

The new route will enable Kazakhstan’s fertilizer producers to increase exports to the UK market. The use of the Middle Corridor will also help diversify logistics routes and ensure more reliable cargo deliveries.

Kazakhstan set to become first Central Asian country to launch air taxi service

Kazakhstan is preparing to become the first country in Central Asia to introduce electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) air taxis into its transport system, reported Reuters Connect on July 24.

“The Prosperity eVTOL aircraft, developed by Chinese manufacturer AutoFlight, was unveiled during a demonstration flight at the Kazanat Hippodrome in Astana. The event was organized by Kazakhstan’s Alatau Advanced Air Group (AAAG) in cooperation with AutoFlight.

The aircraft can carry one pilot and five passengers, reach speeds of up to 200 kilometers (124 miles) per hour, and travel about 200 kilometers (124 miles) on a single charge.

The air taxi service is expected to launch in Alatau, a new city being built from the ground up under Kazakhstan’s digital city concept,” reads the article.

World.title: Kazakhstan Joins Top Five Gold Buyers Amid Reserve Strategy Shift
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan ranked among the world’s five largest central bank gold buyers in the second quarter of 2026, purchasing 15 tons of the precious metal as monetary authorities worldwide accelerated efforts to strengthen reserves amid persistent geopolitical uncertainty and shifting global financial conditions.

According to the latest World Gold Council (WGC) report, the National Bank of Kazakhstan (NBK) was the fourth-largest purchaser globally during the quarter, behind only Poland (51 tons), China (33 tons) and Uzbekistan (16 tons). Jordan and the Czech Republic each added six tons, while Ghana, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and the Kyrgyz Republic made smaller purchases.

Kazakhstan’s acquisition came during a record quarter for central bank demand. Global official sector purchases reached 289 tons between April and June, the strongest second-quarter result on record and a sharp rebound from just 57 tons in the first quarter. The WGC attributes the recovery to a combination of geopolitical tensions, lower gold prices compared with first-quarter peaks, and central banks’ continued efforts to diversify reserve assets.

The trend appears far from temporary. According to a recent World Gold Council survey, 89% of central banks expect global official gold reserves to increase over the next year, while a record 45% plan to expand their own holdings.

For Kazakhstan, the latest purchases continue a long-term strategy rather than representing a short-term reaction to market volatility.

According to Amir Aktanov, an analyst at Halyk Finance’s Analytical Center, central banks have remained net buyers of gold for 15 consecutive years, purchasing more than 1,000 tons annually over the past three years. He also described sustained official demand as one of the key drivers behind the metal’s recent rally.

Kazakhstan has been one of the most consistent participants in that trend. Between 2011 and 2021, the National Bank steadily expanded its gold reserves, purchasing more than 335 tons over the decade. Although the regulator shifted its reserve management strategy in recent years, it also announced in February 2025 that it had suspended gold sales from its foreign exchange reserves, citing the complex geopolitical situation worldwide.

The renewed purchases in the second quarter suggest that reserve diversification remains a priority as policymakers seek assets perceived as resilient during periods of economic and geopolitical uncertainty. The broader gold market reflects the same dynamics.

Total global gold demand, including over-the-counter trading, remained stable year-on-year at 1,269 tons during the second quarter, while demand for the first half of 2026 increased 2% to 2,522 tons. In value terms, however, global demand reached a record $380 billion, highlighting the impact of elevated prices.

Kazakhstan’s position among the world’s largest buyers underscores both the strategic importance of gold in its reserve policy and the broader shift among central banks toward assets viewed as relatively insulated from geopolitical and financial shocks.

With official institutions expected to remain major buyers through the coming year, central bank demand is likely to continue providing structural support for gold prices, even as market attention shifts between inflation, interest rates and global political risks.

World.title: Almaty Airport’s Next Takeoff: Can Kazakhstan Build Central Asia’s Leading Aviation Hub?
World.content:
ALMATY – As Central Asian countries accelerate airport expansion to capture growing passenger and cargo flows between Europe and Asia, Kazakhstan is entering a new phase of competition. While Uzbekistan has launched construction of what is expected to become the region’s largest airport, Almaty is pursuing a different strategy: expanding capacity while investing in operational efficiency, cargo infrastructure, digitalization and international connectivity.

The latest milestone in that transformation came as Qazaqstan Investment Corporation (QIC), a subsidiary of Baiterek National Investment Holding, completed its exit from the Almaty International Airport project through the sale of the Kazakhstan Infrastructure Fund’s 15% stake to TAV Airports for $133 million. While the transaction marks the end of one investment cycle, it also reflects how the airport has evolved from a modernization project into one of Kazakhstan’s key transport assets.

From investment project to regional gateway

QIC entered the project in 2021 through the Kazakhstan Infrastructure Fund, contributing $30 million in equity financing as part of TAV Airports’ $415 million acquisition of Almaty International Airport.

During the investment period, the airport underwent its largest modernization in decades. A new 53,500-square-meter international passenger terminal, a VIP terminal and an engineering facilities building were commissioned, alongside a modern baggage handling system with four times the capacity of the previous facility.

The results have also been visible in passenger traffic. Annual passenger numbers more than doubled from 5.6 million in 2021 to 11.93 million by the end of 2025, while the city’s tourism services market reached 110.9 billion tenge. In the first half of 2026 alone, the airport served 5.76 million passengers, generating revenues of $257.9 million.

The next bottleneck is no longer the terminal

The current phase of investment illustrates how airport development has shifted beyond terminal construction. Rather than simply expanding passenger halls, Almaty is investing heavily in operational infrastructure that determines how efficiently an airport functions.

One of the flagship projects is the Ground Handling Village, a 7,110-square-meter complex that will consolidate technical, maintenance, warehouse and administrative services into a single operational center. The facility is expected to improve coordination among ground handling teams, reduce aircraft turnaround times and provide modern maintenance facilities for specialized airport equipment.

Equally significant is the construction of a new four-kilometer parallel taxiway, extending to 5.2 kilometers with connecting taxiways. Today, one of Almaty’s runways serves both aircraft movements and taxiing operations, creating operational constraints as traffic grows. Once completed, the dedicated taxiway will separate aircraft movements, shorten taxi times, increase runway availability and improve overall airport capacity.

Winter operations are also being modernized through the construction of Central Asia’s first dedicated aircraft de-icing platform. By moving de-icing operations away from aircraft stands and enabling treatment closer to the runway, the project is expected to reduce delays, improve winter operational reliability and enhance environmental sustainability through a specialized de-icing fluid collection and recycling system.

Together, these investments reflect a broader shift in airport strategy, improving operational performance rather than simply adding passenger capacity.

Cargo is becoming as important as passengers

Passenger growth often dominates headlines, but cargo increasingly defines the competitiveness of international airports. Almaty has begun positioning itself as a logistics gateway alongside its role as Kazakhstan’s largest passenger airport.

In June, Emirates SkyCargo launched its first scheduled freighter service between Dubai and Almaty using Boeing 777F aircraft. The weekly service provides more than 100 tonnes of cargo capacity, enabling direct transportation of electronics, industrial equipment, perishables and consumer goods through Emirates’ global logistics hub in Dubai.

The launch is significant because Almaty became Emirates SkyCargo’s first dedicated cargo destination in Central Asia, strengthening logistics links between the region, the Middle East and international markets.

The airport is also preparing for Cathay Pacific’s direct Hong Kong-Almaty passenger route, scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027 with three weekly Airbus A330 services. Together with new routes operated by LOT Polish Airlines, FlyOne Armenia and Thai AirAsia X, the expansion reflects a deliberate effort to diversify international connectivity across Europe, the Middle East and Asia.

Rather than relying on one or two major markets, Almaty is gradually building a broader network that increases both passenger options and transit opportunities.

Regional competition is intensifying

Almaty’s modernization is unfolding amid a broader race to establish Central Asia’s leading aviation hub.

Uzbekistan recently launched construction of a new international airport in the Tashkent region that is expected to become the largest in Central Asia. Scheduled for completion in 2028, the project will accommodate up to 20 million passengers annually, process 129,000 tonnes of cargo and support more than 40 aircraft movements per hour. The airport is also designed as a multimodal transport hub connected to highways and high-speed rail while operating entirely on renewable energy.

At the same time, Uzbekistan’s existing airports continue to record strong growth. During the first half of 2026, the country’s airports handled 64,831 flights, an increase of 8% year-on-year, while passenger traffic rose 16% to 8.15 million. Cargo volumes increased 33% to more than 51,500 tonnes.

Against this backdrop, Kazakhstan’s strategy appears less focused on building the region’s largest airport and more on maximizing the efficiency and competitiveness of its existing hub.

According to Almaty’s tourism department, the airport handled 2.2 million foreigners during the first five months of 2026, a 10% increase compared with the same period last year. International flights rose by 8.6% to 20,600, while the airport currently maintains direct connections with 53 cities worldwide.

Under the airport’s modernization plan through 2029, backed by investments totaling $362 million, Almaty aims to increase annual passenger capacity to 19 million by 2030.

Aviation is becoming economic policy

Airport development is increasingly aligned with broader national transport and economic strategies. Earlier this year, Kazakhstan strengthened cooperation with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) through a new agreement aimed at enhancing the country’s aviation accident investigation capabilities.

It comes as ICAO former President Salvatore Sciacchitano has said that global air transport is expected to triple by 2050, making investments in infrastructure, safety and sustainability increasingly important.

“Kazakhstan’s liberalization policy means more opportunities for international airlines and passengers, strengthening its position as a regional hub. The country’s investments in air traffic management and airport infrastructure are key to meeting ICAO’s safety and sustainability goals,” he said previously in an interview with the Astana Times.

Outlook: Competition will be measured by connectivity

The coming years will determine whether Almaty can translate infrastructure investment into genuine hub status. Passenger numbers will remain an important benchmark, but they are unlikely to be the only measure of success. More revealing indicators will include cargo growth, transit traffic, aircraft turnaround efficiency and the airport’s ability to attract additional long-haul carriers.

The next stage will be defined less by construction milestones than by the airport’s ability to attract transfer passengers, strengthen its cargo role along Eurasian trade corridors, and integrate more deeply into international aviation networks

If successful, the airport could evolve from Kazakhstan’s largest passenger gateway into one of Central Asia’s principal aviation and logistics hubs, as the modernization of recent years has provided the physical foundation.

World.title: August 23: Kazakhstan’s First Vote Under New Constitution
World.content:
Kazakhstan’s elections to the new Kurultai on Aug. 23 will give practical effect to the provisions of the new Constitution adopted in March. These elections represent an important stage in the implementation of the new constitutional order and the first nationwide vote under the new constitutional framework, making them an early test of the new institutional model based on the concept of Just Kazakhstan and the supreme status of citizens’ rights and freedoms.

A milestone in constitutional reform

The new Constitution, approved with over 73% turnout and more than 87% support, was presented to citizens as a comprehensive recalibration of the political and legal system. It reinforces Kazakhstan’s identity as a democratic, secular, legal and social state and elevates the principles of protecting human life and rights, interethnic and interfaith harmony, and long-term sustainable development to constitutional status. The Kurultai is part of this and not a standalone innovation, it is a central element within the frame of modernisation of the government, increasing accountability and making public policy more predictable.

Kurultai’s institutional role

The establishment of the Kurultai replaces the former bicameral parliamentary structure with a unicameral model of 145 deputies elected through a proportional party-list system for a five‑year term. The overall design of this system is broadly in line with international practice and is designed to professionalize legislative work and help preserve political pluralism, and to foster more programmatic party systems. A smaller Parliament will be able to make decisions more quickly, and will have a smaller administrative structure, and each deputy will be responsible for a large population, making the Kurultai the main forum for national debate.

The Constitution significantly strengthens the role of the Kurultai in the system of checks and balances. It is necessary for its consent to the appointment of the Vice President, the Prime Minister, all judges of the Constitutional Court, all members of the Central Election Commission and the Supreme Audit Chamber, and thus for the new chamber to have a meaningful role in the formation and oversight of key state institutions. Meanwhile, its jurisdiction has been broadened to incorporate a broader range of key public policy areas, thus placing the Kurultai at the center of Kazakhstan’s policymaking process.

Election process and party competition

According to the decree of President Kassym‑Jomart Tokayev, the first elections to the Kurultai will be held on Aug. 23, upon which the Central Election Commission is to be responsible for preparing and conducting the elections, while the government and the regional authorities will be tasked with providing full logistical and financial support. The CEC has decided on a comprehensive calendar: party lists will be nominated and registered in July, campaigning will be carried out in the second half of July up to the day of silence (Aug. 22 ) and voting will be held on Aug. 23. This structured approach is intended to provide clarity for political parties, election administrators and voters.

Seven political parties have been cleared to participate, ranging from agrarian to social-democratic, green to liberal/reformist. The decision of the ruling Amanat party not to contest the elections is a notable feature of the current electoral landscape, though the broader significance of the vote lies in the institutional consolidation of the new constitutional framework. For observers, the campaign and voting will offer a concrete opportunity to assess how the new constitutional framework facilitates political competition, voter engagement, and representation.

Implications for Kazakhstan’s political development

From a professional perspective, the August elections should be seen as a functional stress‑test of the reformed institutions rather than a referendum on their legitimacy, which was already conferred by the March vote. The quality of the electoral process, the effectiveness of the CEC’s administration, and Kurultai’s early legislative and oversight practice will all be key indicators of whether the promised transition to a more accountable, law‑based and people‑centred governance model is being realized in practice.

Equally important is the Kurultai’s interaction with newly established bodies such as the People’s Council of Kazakhstan, which has the right of legislative initiative and is intended to channel broader societal participation into law‑making. If these institutions operate in a complementary manner, they can strengthen public trust by making the political system more open, responsive and predictable, in line with the constitutional emphasis on the Unified People of Kazakhstan and social cohesion.

For Kazakhstan and for external observers, the upcoming elections therefore represent both continuity and change: continuity in the commitment to stability and gradual reform, and change in the architecture of representation and accountability. A balanced assessment will focus less on short‑term electoral arithmetic and more on how the Kurultai contributes, over time, to consolidating a Just Kazakhstan based on law, effective institutions and inclusive political participation.

The author is Dávid Biró, a historian, senior advisor, research and academic network lead of the Ludovika Center for Turkic Studies, Ludovika University of Public Service, Hungary.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Heatwave Drives Electricity Demand Growth in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Abnormally high temperatures have contributed to rising electricity consumption and increased pressure on Kazakhstan’s power system, notably during evening peak hours, according to the Ministry of Energy.

The ministry said the national energy system is operating normally, while additional demand is mainly observed during periods of maximum consumption. Higher temperatures have increased the use of cooling systems and other equipment, adding to electricity demand, reported Kazinform on July 29.

The ministry noted that weather conditions are only one factor behind consumption growth, with rising household and economic activity also contributing to the trend.

Electricity consumption in Kazakhstan has continued to increase in recent years. According to the ministry, consumption reached 57.1 billion kilowatt-hours as of July 1, compared with 48.4 billion kWh on June 1 and 43.7 billion kWh on May 1.

To manage peak demand, Kazakhstan uses electricity imports from neighboring countries when necessary. The ministry emphasized that such supplies are used only to cover temporary local shortages.

Kazakhstan is expanding generation capacity to meet future demand. The government expects the introduction of new capacities to fully cover domestic electricity demand from 2027 and create additional reserves for economic growth.

The impact of extreme heat in Kazakhstan has also extended beyond energy demand, affecting public health and daily life.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.
