Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Palestinians long for peace but doubt Trump's deal with Hamas will hold
World.content:
Palestinians in Gaza have expressed scepticism about Hamas's declaration it will lay down its weapons in a bid to kickstart the stalled peace process, concerned it will not actually change the situation in the war-ravaged strip.

On Friday, local time, US President Donald Trump heralded Hamas's agreement to "completely disarm", after months of backroom diplomacy to convince the militant group to make the concession.

But Hamas insisted its decision is conditional on Israel upholding its side of the deal, withdrawing its forces from large swathes of Gaza and ending its daily strikes on the strip.

Since the ceasefire was announced in October 2025, Palestinian health authorities in Gaza have reported more than 1,200 people killed in Israeli strikes, many of them civilians, including children.

"We welcome any agreement that is genuine and will actually be implemented," Rabih Al-Balawi, 57, told the ABC.

" Over the past three years, we've heard many agreements and proposed solutions, yet the situation on the ground has only continued to deteriorate. "

Rabih said he had been displaced 23 times during the war in Gaza, something even more difficult considering he cannot walk unaided.

"It seems Israel is refusing to reach any agreement until after the elections, waiting to see what happens," he said.

"From what I've seen, believing they will honour any agreement would be naive. These people keep neither promises nor agreements.

"We know Israel's history of expansion, and they never withdraw from occupied areas. It's impossible."

Sanaa Shreir hoped it would be the beginning of an improved humanitarian situation in Gaza. (ABC News)

Sanaa Shreir, 54, said she hoped it would mark the beginning of an improvement to the humanitarian situation in Gaza.

"Disarmament is not an easy issue for us, but given what our people are going through, it may be acceptable," she told the ABC.

"Israel's word doesn't mean much in reality. We can only hope that God makes this happen.

"Maybe that's how Trump sees it. As for us, we just hope they do something for these poor people, for our people who have suffered so much; our community has been devastated in every possible way."

'Weapons are only a pretext'

Hamas, which is considered a terrorist organisation under Australian law, had been involved in lengthy negotiations with mediators Egypt, Qatar and Türkiye.

It has said it will hand over its weapons, to be stored and supervised by the Palestinian technocratic body set up by Mr Trump's Board of Peace, known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).

Israel has long insisted the weapons be removed from Gaza altogether, and to this point it has not even allowed NCAG to enter the strip.

Abu Ramzi Al-Salakhi does not believe Hamas will surrender its weapons. (ABC News)

Hamas has said it will disarm when Israeli forces withdraw from territory in Gaza, while Israel has repeatedly argued it will only pull troops from the strip once the militant group has completed that process, highlighting another sequencing issue.

"Hamas will never surrender its weapon; it would only hand them over to the authority that replaces it," Abu Ramzi Al-Salakhi, 70, told the ABC.

"There is a difference between not using weapons and giving them up.

"If it ever hands over its weapons, it would only be to Palestinians."

Hamas has also demanded an end to all strikes in the territory, while Israel has said over the months since the truce was declared that it would continue to attack threats posed by Hamas fighters and facilities.

Hours after Mr Trump's announcement, local authorities reported another attack.

"The enemy's warplanes kill innocent children, the elderly, everyone," Abu Ramzi said.

"Weapons are only a pretext. The attacks continue over and over again."

Israelis critical of deal

NCAG, which has been conducting its affairs from Cairo, welcomed the Hamas announcement and the Trump declaration.

"This development represents an important milestone for our people in the Gaza Strip," it said in a statement.

"After years of conflict, destruction, and uncertainty, the priority today is to translate this progress into practical steps that have a tangible impact on citizens' daily lives."

Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative for Gaza under the Board of Peace, insisted that while the agreement was important, "what happens next matters even more".

"Implementation and verification have to be real. Withdrawal must move in lock step with decommissioning," he posted on X.

In the absence of a formal response to the announcement by the Netanyahu government, the void was filled by some of the most outspoken members of his coalition cabinet.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who quit the government in protest over the January 2025 ceasefire before rejoining when that truce collapsed weeks later, railed against the announcement and labelled it "not acceptable to Israel".

Itamar Ben-Gvir (centre) has spoken out against the deal. (AP: Ohad Zwigenberg )

"After the October 7 massacre, the blood of every Hamas man is forfeit — and therefore, a commitment to cease the eliminations of the terrorist organisation's murderers is tantamount to consenting for Hamas to regroup toward the next massacre," he posted on X.

"The targeted killings in Gaza must continue, encouraging emigration must happen, Israel must win."

One of Benjamin Netanyahu's political opponents, former Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief Gadi Eisenkot, also criticised the agreement.

"Once again, Israeli citizens are learning about a fateful agreement from foreign publications, and the outrageous gap between Netanyahu's promises and reality is exposed," he posted on X.

"He has capitulated in his political weakness without achieving the war's objectives, instead of ending it from a position of strength.

"The State of Israel must not accept a reality in which Hamas survives, rearms, and waits for the opportunity to carry out the next massacre!"

Mr Eisenkot is surging in the polls ahead of the Israeli election, scheduled for October 27.

World.title: Trawlers sit idle as tiger prawn season gets underway
World.content:
The tiger prawn season officially opens today in northern Australia, but the number of trawlers operating this year has sunk to record lows.

The Northern Prawn Fishery (NPF) was established in 1966 when two boats began fishing for banana prawns near Karumba, but the fishery quickly expanded and by 1970 more than 200 boats operated in the fishery.

This year only 27 trawlers have set sail to catch tiger prawns, which is about half the number of vessels that sailed last year.

Administrators are yet to find a buyer for the Raptis prawn fleet. (ABC News: Tim Little)

Where have the trawlers gone?

Some operators are not fishing this season because of high fuel prices and new restrictions on equipment.

Thirteen trawlers are also sitting idle at Karumba following the collapse of seafood giant A Raptis and Sons earlier this year.

In a mid-July report to creditors, administrators FTI Consulting said no buyers had come forward to take over the business.

"Six non-binding indicative offers were received; however none of these offers were capable of being accepted," the report said.

"Subsequent negotiations with one of these parties has resulted in the sale of two vessels and associated licences [located in South Australia]."

A final report to creditors is now due in September following a 45-day extension, with administrators now seeking to sell assets individually or as a whole.

Loading...

Blow to the industry

Michael O'Brien, the general manager of Darwin-based Australia Bay Seafoods, which is fishing for prawns this year, said the collapse or A Raptis and Sons had wide implications.

"Firstly, Raptis has been an institution to the northern prawn fishery for 50 years and it really is a massive blow to the NPF and to the whole seafood industry in Australia," Mr O'Brien said.

"When you have such a large fishery, it takes a number of boats to cover the area.

"If [the NPF] doesn't produce enough tonnage every year you can lose export markets — they'll go elsewhere."

Michael O'Brien has been involved in the industry for more than 50 years. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Mr O'Brien said surveys of the fishery suggested a strong tiger prawn season, which was good news for consumers.

But with fuel prices rising once again, margins for fishers will be tight.

"We use about 45 to 50 tonnes [of diesel] a month per vessel," he said.

"In our business right now, anywhere between 26 to 29 per cent of our costs is fuel, which is massive.

"So what is the market for buying prawn trawlers when you're paying over $2 per litre for fuel? It must make it very hard for an investor to look at this and see how you make the figures work."

Mr O'Brien said the decline of the NPF's prawn fleet was a sad story.

"When I first started 50 odd years ago, we had 302 boats in the NPF," he said.

"We self-managed government reductions and industry reductions and over the last 20 years got it down to 52 [trawlers].

"But today it's 27 [trawlers] and I think that's a very, very sad story to be told about an industry, which had one of the best-managed fisheries in Australia."

Prawn trawlers once owned by Raptis sitting idle at the wharf in Karumba. (ABC News: Tim Little)

On the hunt for tigers

On Thursday FV Warloch skipper Bill West sailed towards the Gulf of Carpentaria from Darwin.

He said a reduced prawn fleet in the north had been noticeable.

"I did most of the banana prawn season this year on my own, I barely saw another boat," Mr West said.

" I've been doing this for 48 years … when you're catching prawns it's magic. When you're not, it's a very big paddock. "

He said after a bountiful banana prawn season he was hopeful of a big tiger prawn season, but there were no guarantees.

"If I can have a good freezer-load at the end of August I think everyone will be happy," Mr West said.

The tiger prawn season runs from August 1 to November 30.

Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm on Sunday or any time on ABC iview.

World.title: The great powers are no longer calling all the shots
World.content:
For much of the past decade, a lot of what has unfolded in the world has been seen through the idea of the rise of strongmen in global politics.

Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladamir Putin have headed the list, along with Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Türkiye.

And that's not to mention the ones who have come and gone in the meantime: Hungary's Viktor Orban, Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, Rodrigo Duterte in the Philippines.

But so much has been transformed in the past year.

In the United States and Russia, two of the strongmen may still hold unprecedented power within their countries, and seek to exert on the rest of the world, but they do so with rapidly diminishing credibility and effectiveness.

Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladamir Putin have headed the list of strongmen in global politics. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque/File Photo)

Trump's rambling pronouncements — someone described them this week as "fantasy announcements" — barely rate any immediate quiver in world markets, let alone diplomatic circles.

For example, there was cautious early reporting in international media on Friday morning, Australian time, of his announcement on social media of a "HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza".

As is so often the case these days, everyone immediately wanted to know if anybody else had actually agreed to this agreement.

As the New York Times reported: "There was no immediate comment from Hamas or Israel, and it was not clear whether either had signed off on the plan after years of war and a fragile cease-fire."

A new conflation of important factors

It's not just that some of the strongmen don't seem so strong anymore, that they often just seem to be lashing out reasonably ineffectively, or even that the "Great Powers" don't seem to be running things.

It's that there is a new conflation of factors proving to be just as important, if not more so, in driving world events in increasingly disturbing directions.

These include the dividend of years of greater powers' efforts at destabilising other states; the rise of states that have never quite got to be stable in the first place; and of the role of non-state actors.

More recently there has been the rapidly and relentlessly expanding story of how technological change in warfare — and rapidly diminishing stockpiles of defensive weapons — are transforming geopolitical power.

Will Hamas disarm? Experts say 'it's difficult to believe' Middle East analysts are sceptical Hamas will willingly lay down its weapons and that Israel will totally withdraw from Gaza.

Just in this week alone, we have seen the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine spread inexorably: conspicuously dragging in Saudi Arabia as well as conflicts in Iraq, Syria and Yemen continuing to escalate.

But Egypt has now also found itself under attack.

Also, Ukraine directly attacked an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea, a move which linked the Iranian and Ukrainian conflicts. It also reflected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's apparent attempts to highlight Russian support for Iran to the US president days before he went to see Trump in Washington.

Then there are reports — denied by the Chinese — of a major deal to deliver Chinese arms to Iran.

In Europe, NATO jets scrambled this week as a Russian missile entered Polish airspace and crashed.

Ukraine has expressed alarm that North Korea is about to send another 30,000 troops to Russia to support its campaign.

Yet even with all this, the impacts of the major conflicts of the time don't just involve crossfire and manpower.

Trump scuttles nuclear power deal with Saudi Arabia

Russia, one of the world's largest resource economies, is now importing oil from India because of the damage Ukraine has inflicted on its energy infrastructure.

The European Union is struggling with a dilemma about placing sanctions on an aluminium smelter in Ireland owned by Russian interests because European nations also need the aluminium.

There are reports that Ukraine has been buying Chinese drone components from an EU defence loan.

The chaos that Trump's increasingly erratic interventions create was highlighted this week by the announcement of a nuclear power deal with Saudi Arabia — a 30-year legal framework which would let US companies build nuclear infrastructure and export civilian nuclear technology to Saudi Arabia while blocking foreign competitors like China and Russia.

Saudi Arabia must recognise Israel for nuclear deal, says Trump A newly brokered nuclear energy deal between the US and Saudia Arabia has drawn criticism from Israeli officials who say it tempts a nuclear arms race in the Middle East.

Critics pointed out some of the alarming shortcomings of the deal. It would allow Saudi Arabia to develop a full-blown civilian nuclear industry (okay so far) but without international safeguards. Unlike stricter historical precedents like the US deal with the United Arab Emirates, reports indicate this agreement may permit Saudi enrichment on its own soil over time.

As former Director General of the Australian Safeguards and Non-Proliferation Office John Carlson wrote this week: "This deal compromises both the non-proliferation standards that up to now have been applied by the United States, and the contemporary standard for International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards applied under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT)."

And, just saying, it would set up exactly the same ecosystem which the US and Israel find so threatening in Iran when it comes to nuclear power, presumably on the presumption that Saudi will always be a friendly state.

Just to confuse things further, Trump then effectively scuttled the deal by saying Saudi would have to sign up to being friends with Israel under the Abraham Accords if the deal was to proceed. Which Saudi won't do.

In doing so, he only highlighted how insane the whole situation in the Middle East really is.

The irony of Israel's invasions

The Arab world in general is going to remain conflicted about Israel, and possibly only become more so, as Israel escalates its brutality and ambitions in what are still technically Palestinian territories, and against Palestinian people.

That is despite the Gulf states' continuing anxiety about Iran.

The ambiguity of Trump's meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this week showed what a mire both countries are now in, partly because of this conflicted, ambivalent position of so many of Israel's neighbours.

Israel may have felt briefly that it had emerged as the new hegemon in the region. And it continues to redefine the language of international affairs by describing invasions into other territories — now Lebanon and Syria as well as Gaza and the West Bank — as "buffer zones".

Israel supporting nascent governments in the region, rather than destabilising them, at some point must become an issue. (Reuters: Ronen Zvulun)

There is an irony in this, as analyst Gregory Gause pointed out in the latest issue of Foreign Affairs magazine.

"Netanyahu believes that Israel is safer when its neighbours are weak and divided," Gause writes.

"But he misses the fact that Israel's peace treaties with Egypt and Jordan, two consolidated states that can control their borders and prevent the rise of violent non-state actors in their territory, have been the enduring pillars of Israel's security for decades.

"Rather than embrace the prospect of a cooperative Lebanese government willing to work against Hezbollah, Israel renewed its war in Lebanon in 2026.

"In Syria, Israel captured a so-called buffer zone, encouraged Syrian Druze to resist the new government, armed Druze militias, and struck Syrian army positions — including the headquarters of the Ministry of Defence — in the name of protecting the Druze."

Supporting nascent governments in the region, rather than destabilising them, at some point must become an issue.

"Iran's allies, although weakened, still wield significant influence across the Arab world. In Iraq's elections in November 2025, Shiite parties aligned with Iran and the Iraqi militias it backs performed well," Gause writes.

"In February, March, and April of this year, those militias lobbed missiles at US bases in the region. The new Iraqi government under Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, like its predecessors, has filled important positions with many of Iran's local allies."

Which brings us to Iran.

Loading

A more sophisticated assessment of Iran

Two major analysts of Iran, Narges Bajoghli and Vali Nasr, both of Johns Hopkins University, have also written in the latest Foreign Affairs, offering a somewhat more sophisticated assessment of the Iranian leadership and its strategy than we get from Trump's expletive laden assertions of imminent collapse.

The new generation of Iranian leadership, the two men say, "has separated revolution from statecraft".

"At home and abroad, it neither espouses revolutionary grandiosity nor advocates revolutionary activism."

The new leaders, Bajoghli and Nasr write, are "establishment actors: pragmatic, hardened nationalists operating with a clear-eyed assessment of Iran's capabilities and vulnerabilities".

"Unlike their predecessors, they can exercise strategic patience and act decisively. They look at Iran's weaknesses frequently and publicly — something the founding generation was too insecure to do honestly — and they treat them as problems to be solved."

Trump vows to hit Iran 'hard' in expletive ridden warning In a phone interview with Fox News, the US president reportedly said the US would "beat the f****** s***" out of Iran in response to the surprise strikes.

The Islamic Republic had long operated through a chaotic maze of competing power centres, which produced unending internal debate and sclerotic inertia.

But they say this chaos has given way "to organisational discipline and resilience" with a structure involving defence, civilian and economic bureaucracies.

As a result, Bajoghli and Nasr say, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance "are wrong" in their fundamental assessment of Iran".

"Tehran's defiant approach reflects neither ideological rigidity nor factional infighting," they write.

"The country's leaders understand that the United States is seeking to get from talks what it could not achieve in war and that Washington is not interested in a deal but in Iran's surrender."

The only problem is "Iranian leaders already claim they have won the war".

"This self-confidence — rooted in the belief that the war has empowered Iran rather than weakened it — is informing their international outlook."

Abroad, they say this does not mean it will abandon its regional allies, like Hezbollah, Shiite militias in Iraq and the Houthis in Yemen. "But it will manage them with more strategic discipline and less ideological romanticism."

The new Iranian leadership will not sacrifice Iran's interests at the altar of revolutionary solidarity, Bajoghli and Nasr say.

"These alliances will be deployed as part of a coherent regional strategy designed to sustain Iran's strategic depth against sustained US and Israeli pressure."

The most important message in that assessment, of course, is that Iran actually has a coherent regional strategy. Something that cannot necessarily be said for the great powers who might like to think they can still call the shots.

Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

World.title: A week of AUKUS double-speak leaves everyone scratching their heads
World.content:
Americans love a sheep dog breed known as the "Aussie Shepherd". Spend time in the US and you'll meet them everywhere.

A lively fluffy-looking herder claimed to have partly originated from antipodean imports to California in the 19th century.

The name is striking because you don't really see them here.

There's no way to know for sure but I'd wager a few of these popular pets will soon be coming "home".

Specifically among families of the some 1000 US military personnel moving to HMAS Stirling in WA.

So serious were the Americans about getting settled into their AUKUS deployment their officials were busy a year ago negotiating quarantine arrangements for US submariners' dogs.

"US service personnel very much like their pets," Australian Submarine Agency chief Jonathan Mead told ABC's Jane Norman last September.

A US submarine at HMAS Stirling last year. (Royal Australian Navy: ABIS Jayden Fahy)

A level of constructive ambiguity

The question for these mutts — triggered by this week's misty verbal bouillon of bollocks over how enduring America's presence will be — is whether they'll enjoy a lengthy stay frolicking on Perth's southern beaches or merely a temporary posting.

My bet is some could end up enjoying a long and happy retirement here.

That's because we've now been informed that their owners' presence on Australian soil will be "enduring".

The core of this question sits in the shroud of double-speak that afflicts so many things related to defence and AUKUS.

A charitable interpretation is that Industry Minister Pat Conroy's repeated insistence in his interview this week from Washington DC with 730's Sarah Ferguson that the US submarine presence will effectively end in the early 2030s is because he wants to maintain a level of constructive ambiguity.

Henry Kissinger is said to have coined the term which describes when two sides want to disguise the fact they're not on the same page or have differing interpretations of language.

Perhaps they have constituents they need to satisfy or mollify.

Less flatteringly, he misspoke.

Perhaps it was the jet lag.

Either way, he went on to make similar remarks to other media outlets.

Conroy told The Australian that the Submarine Rotational Force-West agreement, which will see up to four US Virginia-class boats operate from HMAS Stirling from next year, would begin "fading away" as Australia began to operate its own nuclear-powered boats.

Conroy added the US was likely to retain a submarine presence in Australia but that would be a decision for future governments.

His remarks left everyone scratching their heads. Even AUKUS diehards.

Opposition defence spokesman James Paterson accused Conroy of issuing the US navy with an eviction notice before they'd even arrived.

Conroy himself took to X where he posted a statement — without any official signature or letterhead — agreeing that having Americans in Stirling will be "enduring". (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

When is a base a base?

By Friday there was much mopping up afoot.

"The Submarine Rotational Force West at HMAS Stirling is intended to be an enduring feature of America's force posture in Australia," Defence Minister Richard Marles told News24 (formerly Sky News).

Conroy himself took to X where he posted a statement — without any official signature or letterhead — agreeing that having Americans in Stirling will be "enduring".

While it was all baffling, we do seem to have had a few things reinforced this week.

For one thing Americans will almost certainly "rotate" a future fleet of nuclear armed submarines through WA facilities in coming decades.

Whether they are "based" there or merely in transit will be a matter of semantics.

The governments wants voters to believe it's not a permanent US base.

As Alice noted in her journey through the Wonderland, "one can't believe impossible things". To which the Queen replied: "I dare say you haven't had much practice."

Former courtier to Australian leaders Mike Pezzullo is more blunt.

"When they bring their families and pets, it's a base," he tells this column.

Former home affairs secretary Mike Pezzullo. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

Having invested in such a capability it defies logic to claim the US then wouldn't continue to take advantage of its strategic military benefits.

Publicly available US war plans support the interpretation that this is anything but temporary.

Indeed the WA facility is so significant that the US navy has re-established and will headquarter its submarine squadron 3, which previously operated out of Pearl Harbor and was decommissioned in 2012.

And the purpose of Stirling? "Keeping those boats fit to fight," said director of submarine programs, Vice Admiral Rob Gaucher.

"Adding an additional forward-positioned submarine squadron in the Indo-Pacific enhances our presence, agility, and responsiveness across a range of operations," said Rear Adm. Chris Cavanaugh, Commander, Submarine Force, US Pacific Fleet, in June.

None of that feels temporary.

Which is what the Stirling locals are anticipating as well.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

Local MP and shadow Home Affairs Minister Andrew Hastie told the ABC nearly a year ago that it was not simply a rotation of US sailors.

"There'll be a permanent presence at HMAS Stirling, and they'll be integrated into our community", he said.

This week's back-and-forth over AUKUS adds to the hubbub in June about whether it was a major setback that Australia's future Virginia Class submarines will be used US boats rather than some fresh off the construction dock.

These communications stumbles have hung lanterns on a deal — which former Labor foreign minister Gareth Evans recently described as "one of the worst defence and foreign policy decisions" in Australia's history that will "profoundly limit" the country's freedom to make its own strategic decision — that will continue to draw criticism.

Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

World.title: Australian band counts missiles as they gear up to play Kyiv's major music festival
World.content:
'Ninth intercepted, tenth, we can't keep up, eleventh, twelfth ... another one."

It's the middle of the night in Kyiv and an Australian band having rushed to their hotel's bomb shelter are counting the number of missiles intercepted.

It's not the first time that night they've headed underground. They spend the rest trying to sleep in there.

The Ukrainian capital is experiencing one of the largest ballistic missile attacks since the start of the war.

Members of band breathe. in a bomb shelter under their hotel in Kyiv. (Supplied: Tall Story Films)

Later that day Sydney band breathe. are scheduled to play their biggest show ever — that's if Russian missile strikes don't force the cancellation of Atlas, a music festival that draws thousands of people to Kyiv each year.

Breathe. is the only international headliner booked to play.

"We've wanted to play a show in Ukraine for many years," breathe.'s Andrew Grant told 7.30.

Andrew Grant, Dylan Wright and Sean Walker are interviewed by local media after arriving by train in Kyiv. (Supplied: Atlas Festival)

The electronic and soul outfit, who have had music featured on Netflix shows You and Elite, and documentary series Couple Therapy, are relatively unknown in Australia.

After the band's creators, Sean Walker and Andrew Grant started uploading their music online seven years ago, millions on the other side of the world listened.

"When we started releasing clips on YouTube, an audience in Ukraine, Moldova and Türkiye started appearing," Grant said.

Their song Are You All Good has over 13 million streams on YouTube.

Breathe. is the only international headliner at the Atlas Festival. (Supplied: Atlas Festival)

"Ukraine is our number one audience on YouTube. It accounts for a fifth of our views on YouTube, which is mind-blowing," Walker told 7.30.

After Russia invaded Ukraine in early 2022, the band started getting messages on social media from their fans now living daily life in a war zone.

"The first was a video that landed in our inbox from someone that was playing piano at night time as drone strikes were happening in the background. It was this unbelievably heartbreaking, surreal moment for both of us," Walker said.

The main stage at the Atlas Festival in Kyiv. (Supplied: Atlas Festival)

Some wrote about family members and friends being killed at war and others themselves fighting on the front line, telling the duo that their music was getting them through it.

"We were getting texts at all hours of the day and night from people that were under attack in bomb shelters," Grant told 7.30.

"When a country is going through a period of fear, they want to turn to safety and maybe they found that in our music somewhere."

A war-time music festival

Breathe. at a press conference during the festival. (Supplied: Atlas Festival)

Atlas Festival's program director, Vlad Yaremchuk, says no one quite understands how the band took off in Ukraine.

"I think there was some stroke of luck there where the algorithm would somehow find their way to Ukrainians," Mr Yaremchuk told 7.30.

"They were just listening to some random playlist, breathe. comes on. It feels like everyone immediately pays attention and are like, "What is this? " And then it very quickly becomes an obsession."

When breathe. were invited to play Ukraine's biggest music festival, they quickly checked if one of their collaborators, Dylan Wright, the 2024 winner of Australian Idol, would go with them to Kyiv.

Atlas Festival's program director Vlad Yaremchuk with the Australian musicians. (Supplied: Atlas Festival)

He said yes.

"There was this moment where Andy and I both looked at each other and we said, 'We're doing this' and from that moment onwards, there was a deep solidarity and a deep conviction to making this happen," Walker told 7.30.

Before Putin's war began the festival drew over half-a-million people over seven days.

It first had to be cancelled, then in 2024 was relaunched as a three-day-event and in 2025 had nearly 100,000 people attending at the Blockbuster Mall, where the underground car park functions as a bomb shelter.

"What it means is that it enables us to evacuate the entire festival in mere minutes into the underground in the case there is an air raid alarm," Mr Yaremchuk said.

Thousands of people at the main stage at the Atlas Festival. (Supplied: Atlas Festival)

The festival has changed in other ways too. It's now a fundraising event for the war effort.

"You will really struggle to spend any money here without a big chunk of it going into the fundraiser, " Mr Yaremchuk said.

The festival has stalls from military brigades showcasing information about the war.

Some are looking for new recruits and run VR simulators with replica weapons to raise interest in supporting the war.

A woman holds a replica anti-armour launcher at the festival. (Supplied: Atlas Festival)

"For some people it becomes a place where they ultimately make that decision that they want to start preparing to enrol into the army and help the effort," Mr Yaremchuk said.

NGOs are raising awareness of how life is changing in the country. One of them at the festival invites people to sit in wheelchairs to experience what life is like with a disability.

"That is a really important topic here," Mr Yaremchuk said.

People are invited to try sitting in wheelchairs at the festival. (Suplied: Atlas Festival)

"Our cities have to become a lot more accessible because of how [many] more people with disabilities there are."

There are also stalls teaching resuscitation, tactical medicine, and how to tie a tourniquet.

"It's a difficult concept to grasp in most other countries because the military is seen as something that is not necessary," Mr Yaremchuk said.

A man holding a replica weapon at the festival. (ABC News: Dave May)

" But here the military is respected. These are the people that are spilling blood for us every single day so that we can keep on living in a free Ukraine. "

Breathe. are donating profits from the tour to the festival's fundraising initiatives.

Those include a children's hospital in Kyiv that was bombed during the war, a music school through humanitarian initiative UAME Music Saves Ukraine and drone defence capability through foundation Come Back Alive.

Beats and bombs

Singer Dylan Wright performs with breathe. at the Atlas Festival in Kyiv. (Supplied: Altas Festival)

After a night of intense bombing in Kyiv, the festival is given the green light and the crowd pours in for the final day.

"Despite how tired you are and how sleepless the night was, especially those who are waiting for breathe. to see them for the first time in their lives, nothing would have stopped them," Mr Yaremchuk said.

Less than an hour before the Australian band hits the stage, air sirens wail.

The act before breathe. only got two songs in as the whole festival was evacuated to the shelter.

Breathe. perform at the Atlas Festival. (Supplied: Atlas Festival)

But this time there's no barrage of ballistic missiles and the band take to the stage as the crowd exits the bomb shelter.

"We walked on stage to an empty shopping mall and by the end it was flooded," Grant said.

Together the crowd sing along to breathe.'s lyrics, having shared one of Kyiv's worst nights since the war began.

The enthusiastic crowd watching breathe. perform at the festival. (Supplied: Altas Festival)

"Are you all good? Are you alright? I'm in your neighbourhood for your darkest times," echoes through the mall.

"Music in Ukraine right now reflects the wartime reality in so many ways. It helps you grieve. It cheers you up. It helps you deal with the separation," Mr Yaremchuk told 7.30 after the set.

Before leaving Kyiv breathe. went to see where the bombs were falling during their stay.

Less than an hour before breathe. took to the stage the whole crowd was evacuated to a bomb shelter. (Supplied: Atlas Festival)

What they saw had a profound impact. Walker wiped away tears and his voice cracked as he described it to 7.30.

"We go back to safe old Australia and they're left here with this," he said.

" It's so f***ing unfair. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: India's gen Z protesters forced a minister to resign. What's next?
World.content:
The "cockroaches" won.

The group that spearheaded nationwide protests, sit-ins and hunger strikes over the last two months, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), has claimed victory following the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

During Prime Minister Narendra Modi's more than 12 years in office, the government has rarely yielded to sustained public pressure.

Following Mr Pradhan's resignation last weekend, movement organisers called off the large-scale protests that rose up across the country.

So what happens next? And is a one-off resignation enough to satisfy India's youth?

For some, the government's concession was only "a small step" in a larger movement.

Model and student Rhiya Ahir said the movement's focus should now be on the new education minister, Pralhad Joshi.

"The next step is making sure he enforces the new education reforms," the 27-year-old told the ABC.

The protests were sparked by anger over the leaking of an exam paper that forced 2 million students to resit the test for entry to medical school. Local media reported that 20 took their own lives.

Ms Ahir, who was the subject of a viral photo of her blocking a police van during a protest in Mumbai, also said the 20 students "must not be forgotten".

Rhiya Ahir says the movement should now focus on Dharmendra Pradhan's replacement and the new reforms. (AP: Rafiq Maqbool)

"How is the government dealing with the students who are no longer with us, and their parents?" she said.

"We must keep questioning this."

Pradhan's replacement does not comfort all

In a letter published on X, Mr Pradhan said he "took responsibility" for the leaking of India's national medical entrance exam in May.

"I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations of the country's youth," the letter said.

For 22-year-old Ravi Vishwakarma, who attended protests in Delhi, Mr Joshi was "not a suitable leader".

Ravi Vishwakarma says Dharmendra Pradhan's replacement is "not a suitable leader". (Supplied: Ravi Vishwakarma)

For Mr Vishwakarma, Mr Joshi's ties to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) — a right-wing Hindu volunteer organisation founded in 1925 — were a source of alarm.

For the group, Indian civilisation is inseparable from Hinduism, while critics say its philosophy is rooted in Hindu supremacy. The RSS is often described as the ideological parent and mentor of Mr Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

"The history of the RSS is totally against Indians," Mr Vishwakarma said.

"They know how to mislead the nation through casteism and religious discrimination," he said.

"If the government really want to improve India's education system, they must choose a worthy leader."

Like many of India's youths, Ravi hopes to see "a transparent investigation and accountability" come out of this.

"We need meaningful reforms that improve safety and prevent similar tragedies from happening again," he said.

Education in India a 'sensitive issue'

In India, almost 40 per cent of graduates aged 15 to 25 and 20 per cent aged 25 to 29 are jobless, according to the latest State of Working India report by Azim Premji University.

It is why education is "a very sensitive issue", said Harsh V Pant, professor of international relations at King's College London.

"A lot of middle-class families sacrifice and spend a lot on their child's education," Professor Pant said.

"They feel education is one of the most important ways for social mobility in India."

Some experts say the government and youth should work together on long-term structural reform. (AP: Rafiq Maqbool)

'It's time to revive' India's democracy

Yashi Verma believes the movement has inspired many in India to "look forward to a complete regime change".

The 25-year-old lawyer and actor in Delhi said India's youth have been frustrated at the current regime for some time now.

"Be it the dwindling economy, unemployment rates or attacks on minorities and marginalised people," she said.

Yashi Verma says a range of issues have contributed to people's frustration with the government. (Supplied: Yashi Verma)

"I think people of the country have finally woken up to the fact that democracy in India has long been dead and it is time to revive it."

International organisations such as the United Nations and Amnesty International have documented human rights concerns in India, including systemic police violence, suppression of free expression and discrimination based on religion, ethnicity and caste, affecting groups including Muslims and Dalits.

The Indian government has consistently rejected these findings.

"Hopefully, the resignation of the education minister is only building momentum for far bigger reforms," Ms Verma said.

For some members of India's diaspora in Australia, who had been following the protests from afar, the minister's resignation came as a shock.

"I didn't expect it to happen," said Mrinaal Datt, a news production editor and podcast host in Melbourne.

"Gen Z is usually looked down upon as a nonchalant generation. So to see them band together and own the 'cockroach' label was impressive."

However, Ms Datt said paper leaks had plagued India for years.

And they happened "because there's a market for it", she said.

"Who are the buyers? Sometimes, it's the very students and their parents who appear for these exams," she said.

Mrinaal Datt says she did not expect India's education minister to resign. (Supplied: Mrinaal Datt)

"It's an uncomfortable conversation, but an important one to have."

Where to from here?

A day after Mr Pradhan resigned, Mr Modi vowed to fast-track the court process to punish those responsible for the leak.

Changes have been proposed to the Public Examinations Act, a law made in 2024 after similar National Eligibility Entrance Test (NEET) exam leaks.

The 2024 law prescribed penalties for a range of violators, including those resorting to unfair means, firms involved in helping conduct the exam and those at the examination authority.

The proposed amendments would increase the minimum prison term for culprits from three years to five years and raise the maximum fine five-fold from 10 million rupees ($149,623) to 50 million rupees ($748,169).

The ban on firms found guilty would double to eight years.

Narendra Modi has vowed to fast-track the court process to punish those responsible. (AP: Rafiq Maqbool)

Following the protests, Mr Modi also announced a "high-powered panel" headed by technology expert Nandan Nilekani to focus on examination reforms, saying the government aims to make the "greatest possible use of technology" to strengthen the system.

Mr Nilekani is an entrepreneur best known for leading the creation of India's digital identity system Aadhaar and co-founding software major Infosys.

Based on the panel's recommendations, steps would be taken "as quickly as possible" to ensure the "credibility and reliability" of examinations, Mr Modi said.

Professor Pant said Mr Pradhan's resignation reflected a pattern seen under Mr Modi and that it showed there was "flexibility" in his government to meet the demands of the youth protesters.

But he said the outcome was a "short-term" solution.

"Whether these issues on India's education system posed by the country's youth are managed over a longer term remains to be seen," he said.

He said the "real challenge" lay in the entire system, "not just one minister".

"It's very likely that challenges in India's education system will continue. But whether the government and the youth can work together on long-term structural reform is the real issue," he said.

World.title: Director Destin Daniel Cretton on making Spider-Man grow up
World.content:
The superhero business isn't what it used to be.

After 2008's Iron Man and the spawn of cinematic universes, it seemed as though nothing could stop the juggernaut of superhero blockbusters.

As we marched into the 2010s, Marvel lore-expanders like Captain America: Civil War and Black Panther consistently made billions. Avengers: Endgame remains the second highest-grossing movie of all time, pulling in an eye-watering $US2.799 billion dollar box office when it was released in 2019.

Despite constantly fighting to get out of Marvel's cinematic shadow, DC's gloomier fare like The Dark Knight Rises and Joker gained their billion badge; even critically trashed editions like 2018's Aquaman splashed over the billion-dollar threshold.

Avengers: Endgame ends Marvel's decade reshaping Hollywood All it took was five years for the Marvel Cinematic Universe to change the way blockbusters were made. And rom-coms, comedies and dramas are feeling the heat.

But then at the turn of the decade, the world stopped for COVID. Even when cinemas were able to open their doors again, safe-bet sequels such as Black Panther: Wakanda Forever didn't live up to its predecessors, and adventures into more prestige output like Eternals and The Marvels crashed spectacularly. Star-stuffed vehicles like Fantastic Four and Thunderbolts (or The New Avengers, to give it the marketing-approved name) didn't quite reach intended impact.

Only two superhero movies have grossed over $US1 billion worldwide in the 2020s; 2023's R-rated Deadpool & Wolverine and 2021's Spider-Man: No Way Home.

So, no pressure for Destin Daniel Cretton, director of No Way Home follow up, Spider-Man: Brand New Day. The filmmaker isn't going in blind though; he was plucked by Marvel Studios in 2019 to direct Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings before sliding into TV with Wonder Man, a series he directs and co-created, which lead to an Emmy nomination for its lead Yahya Abdul-Mateen II.

Already attached to an as-so-far untitled Shang-Chi sequel, the superhero genre might have changed since it re-wrote the box office rule book but Cretton is just getting started.

Spiderman: Brand New Day director Destin Daniel Cretton (second from right) with his cast, writers Chris McKenna and Erik Sommors and producer Amy Pascal. (Getty: Tim P. Whitby)

Brand New Day is such a highly anticipated project. When you're in the 11th hour, moments before opening what are the thoughts rushing through your head?

I just can't wait for people to see it.

I cannot wait to be in the theatre and see all of the decisions that we made and see reactions to these incredible performances for the first time. It's the completion of a long cycle, to something on screen that feels so personal to me, is really one of the biggest emotional highs of my life.

And it does feel — I don't know — it feels very intimate and it feels like it gives me hope.

What is your earliest memory of Spider-Man?

I grew up on Maui, so I wasn't exposed too much to really any kind of pop culture. My parents didn't really allow us to watch too much TV, so I spent most of my time outside with my five siblings playing in the pineapple fields and in the mud puddles near our house.

But somehow Spider-Man made it into my life through just a couple of comics that I was able to see at my friend's house.

My mum has a picture of me and my older brother when I was about six years old, and I'm wearing a Spider-Man tank top and my older brother's wearing a Hulk tank top and we're just in our backyard in Haiku, Maui.

I just find it fascinating that that character somehow made its way across the Pacific Ocean to this tiny island in the middle of nowhere. And that was still the character that I wanted to pretend to be. So it's crazy to be sitting in this chair right now.

Mark Ruffalo returns as Bruce Banner, aka The Hulk, in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)

You've been helming these superhero projects for a while, but you have a background in indie drama. I loved I Am Not a Hipster, by the way. What is something that you bring from those independent days that helps you on these massive studio productions?

I love that you mentioned I Am Not a Hipster. The same director of photography, Brett Pawlak, who did Hipster, is also on Spider-Man.

Doing small indies is like, that is what I psychologically want to do, that's where I want my brain to always be. It's a place where creatively you take risks, you don't think about outcomes, you don't think about millions of people watching every decision that you make. There's a purity to that form; there's like a childlike freedom to the creative process when you're making movies at that level.

That's what I strive for, at least my DP and I would often reference that movie as something to strive to be with our decision making.

Destin Daniel Cretton with his long-time collaborator Brett Pawlak (left), with actor Adam Shapiro promoting their 2009 film Short Term 12. (Getty: Charley Gallay)

You're also a prolific screenwriter on a lot of the projects you direct. What was the experience directing something that you hadn't written this time?

Well, the writers' room in movies like this is still very collaborative.

I was in the writers' room with our writers for months in prep as we were getting ready to shoot. It was an amazing experience with Chris [McKenna] and Erik [Sommors], they're incredible writers and they're very collaborative. We kind of just come up with scenes and then they go off and write it.

Loading...

So in the end, it just feels like the movie is very much ours. It's a very team effort. And then once we got into production, our other screenwriter, Justin, came on board and he helped us all the way through production to the end.

It was a real joy to work with, with these, all of these incredible writers.

One of the more heartbreaking aspects of the movie is MJ not remembering Peter at all. What is it like directing Tom Holland and Zendaya as strangers when they have such an established connection on and off screen?

I mean, they are incredible actors, as I'm sure you know. So it's, once you're in a scene, you're just directing actors who know what they're doing. But it was kind of fun to see Jacob and Zendaya ignoring Tom on set while we were shooting.

And you know, I think there were times where it did kind of hurt his feelings, not in a real way, but it's not fun to watch your friends getting close when you have to be the outsider.

MJ (Zendaya) doesn't remember Peter Parker or their relationship in Brand New Day. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)

It felt like in previous films, a teenage Peter was grappling with responsibility but now he is this young adult, he's facing consequences. Why is it important for audiences to see Spider-Man mature?

Well, I think it'd be just a natural progression of the story. The audience is ready to see Peter and MJ enter the next stage in their life. It makes sense as we've left that last movie with a very big cliffhanger, and now we're four years later. So, there's a very clear reset button and it felt nice to start this next movie with some more mature subject matter. Some emotions that are connected to what many of us go through in our twenties when we leave university.

Spider-Man in Brand New Day develops organic webbing in a throwback to Sam Raimi's early 2000s trilogy. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)

You no longer have the shelter of a set schedule, that a school allows you, you're not under your parents' roof anymore. It's like, life just slams you in the face and it's hard. And sometimes it's lonely. You're saying goodbye to friends that you saw every single day, and some of them move on with their lives. So all of these emotions I think are incredibly relatable. I think for me, exploring them through the lens of Peter Parker was a very fulfilling experience.

Final question, why does the world still need superhero movies right now?

I feel like the world needs this movie right now because what Peter Parker is going through, I think, is something that many people can relate to at this moment.

Review: Spider-Man Brand New Day Tom Holland returns as a now-anonymous Peter Parker in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

I think it's very easy to feel the confusion of being surrounded by thousands and thousands of people, of thousands of comments and likes and people looking at your photos or your videos and Peter Parker is living in the middle of a city surrounded by millions of people, and he still feels entirely alone.

I think it's very easy right now to have many relationships but it's more difficult to have deep relationships and to have deep connections with other people.

I think the experience of sitting in a theatre and watching this movie with your friends or your loved ones or a group of strangers, I think this movie has the ability to bring people together. This experience of going through this movie is exhilarating, funny, fun, but also healing. I find it to be a journey that makes me want to connect with my loved ones or just the stranger sitting beside me.

I hope that other people get to have that experience as well.

Some quotes have been lightly edited for clarity and brevity.

World.title: Chinese AI shakes up global markets
World.content:
When China's DeepSeek sent shock waves through the technology world early last year, it raised a confronting question for America's tech giants, could China build cutting-edge artificial intelligence for a fraction of the cost?

More than a year on DeepSeek is no longer the only strong challenger.

In recent weeks, Chinese AI developers Z.ai (formerly known as Zhipu AI) and Moonshot AI have released new models that have made a splash on the global tech sector.

Moonshot AI's release of Kimi K3 in particular, shook Wall Street, triggered accusations from Washington that the startup was using proprietary US technology to develop its models and even won praise from competitor OpenAI's president.

Moonshot AI’s release of Kimi K3 has made a splash on the global tech sector. (AP Photo)

Markets are rattled

Despite a strong finish to the month, key AI bellwether indexes have been volatile.

The Nasdaq 100 briefly entered correction territory earlier in the week, while this year's world beating South Korean Kospi fell as much as 38 per cent in July before recovering some of its losses.

Many analysts say the recent sell-off in tech has been largely fuelled by concerns about whether the hundreds of billions of dollars of spending on AI by the technology giants will generate adequate returns.

The Korean Kospi fell as much as 38 per cent in July. (AP Photo: Ahn Young-joon)

One key reason analysts fear those eye-watering investments may not be recouped is growing competition from cheaper Chinese owned rivals.

"The broad thinking was the US was about six to nine months ahead of Chinese competitors but after developments recently, we now know that Chinese AI, Chinese infrastructure, are as good as some of the US frontier models, and that is providing another shake-up for Wall Street and those markets which are associated with Wall Street, such as in South Korea and Japan," said IG Market analyst Tony Sycamore.

"The pullback is being most acutely felt in South Korea, but if we were to see the US tech market continue to accelerate lower, that would certainly flow through to Australians via the returns which their super funds are earning," he said.

Australian businesses react to the shift

For some Australian businesses, particularly startups and companies building AI into their products and supply chains, the fierce international competition is changing the economics of AI.

Jacky Koh, co-founder and co-CEO of Sydney-based startup Relevance AI, has had a front-row seat to this shift.

His company helps businesses (like Canva, KPMG and Autodesk) build AI agents, systems that can essentially carry out tasks on their own, rather than simply respond like a chatbot.

Jacky Koh said his Sydney based company is increasingly directing more work towards models it can download and operate itself. (ABC News: Dan Irvine )

The models powering those agents broadly fall into two camps.

Open, or, more specifically, open-weight models are free to download and most of the leading open models now come from Chinese developers.

Self-hosting allows businesses to avoid paying a developer each time the model is used, although they must still cover the computing power required to run it.

Return of competing superpowers When it comes to AI, Australia is a spectator at a UFC cage fight between the United States and China, except the spectators are inside the cage with the combatants.

Leading proprietary models, mostly developed by American companies, remain controlled by their developers and are far more expensive to use.

Until recently, Mr Koh said those agents were overwhelmingly powered by closed source models from US companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.

Open models are free to download and most now come from Chinese developers.

But his firm is now increasingly directing more work towards models it can download and operate itself, including Chinese-developed 'open' models GLM and Deepseek.

" Before the start of this year, I would say honestly, about five, if not 7.5 per cent of traffic were mainly in open weight models. "As of right now, we're closer to 20, if not 25 per cent. "

The economics are hard to ignore

A major driver is cost.

As businesses move beyond asking chatbot questions and deploying AI agents that carry out multiple steps autonomously, the number of tokens they can consume can rise dramatically.

Tokens are the currency of the AI economy — every question AI reads and answers uses them — and businesses pay for that usage.

Deepak John Joseph said inquiries about Chinese AI models have surged from clients in recent months, with cost a major consideration. (ABC News: Dan Irvine )

Deepak John Joseph, who runs a product engineering business, Pupa Clic Technologies, says some businesses are coming to him because those bills have ballooned.

"We have customers explicitly asking, for example, we currently consume $20,000 worth of tokens per day, and how do we drastically reduce this as our volumes are hitting through the roof and we need to really bring this down." he said.

" We are looking at almost 80 per cent of savings in using hosted models in compared to the cloud hosted variants. "

For Australian businesses, the emerging picture appears to be firms increasingly mixing models, reserving the most powerful, expensive systems for difficult jobs and routing simpler work to cheaper alternatives.

Will Liang, from Sydney-based AI advisory firm Amplify AI, calls the approach "model routing".

Will Liang from Amplify AI Group said Australian business are mixing models reserving the most powerful, expensive systems for difficult jobs and routing simpler work to cheaper alternatives. (ABC News: Dan Irvine )

"You use the top tier large language model to figure out what are the list of tasks you need to do to complete this objective, and then route different tasks to different models.

"Some of the simpler tasks to more a cheaper model, as example."

Concerns about Chinese AI

There have been concerns about bias in Chinese-developed models, particularly around politically sensitive subjects.

"It won't, for example, tell you very much about Tiananmen Square or tell you things maybe that are unfavourable to the Chinese regime," said UNSW AI Institute chief scientist Toby Walsh.

However, Mr Liang says for most Australian businesses, a bigger barrier to adopting Chinese AI is the lack of trust and uncertainty around regulation.

Testing AI chatbots' harm potential An investigation into how AI chatbots respond to violent requests produces "deeply disturbing" results, as OpenAI denies ChatGPT encourages crime.

"We do get a lot of pushback (to using Chinese-developed AI), especially in healthcare as well as on the finance-based domains," confirmed Mr Joseph.

To increase security, Trivium China partner in technology, Kendra Schaefer says firms should ensure that Chinese developed models are accessed through "trusted domestic cloud providers, or installed on premises under their own control".

While open weight models mean they can be downloaded locally, she also cautioned it does not equate to freedom from security risk.

"Like any locally installed software, a locally installed model is a vector for compromise.

"Every time you download software onto your computer you accept the risk that it contains a malicious backdoor," she warned.

She says it is not a China specific issue but rather an issue around cybersecurity risk.

World.title: Dan Gorringe was a battling ruckman. He’s now a social media star and might even become an AFL rights holder
World.content:
Gorringe is edgy, but even the AFL wants him.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you’re a football fan under the age of 35, chances are Dan Gorringe is everywhere when you pick up your phone. Log on to Instagram, he’ll be there, over-celebrating a Carlton win or mourning a loss. You’ll find his mildly more serious football views on his Dan Does Footy YouTube channel. On TikTok, you’ll get his almost instant hot takes, delivered in his typically edgy style. Dan Does Footy podcast host and social media identity Daniel Gorringe has become a key player in the AFL’s targeting of the youth market. Chris Hopkins He’s labelled goalkicking great Matthew Lloyd a “dirty rat”, called prominent broadcaster Gerard Whateley a “muppet”, and told arguably the greatest player of all time Leigh Matthews to “f--- up”. He has had commercial partnerships with corporate bookies, sports drinks and alcohol brands. It will come as a surprise, then, that Gorringe the footballer was the polar opposite in personality. “He was as straight as six o’clock,” his first senior coach Guy McKenna said. Former Carlton captain and one of Gorringe’s closest friends Sam Docherty, who was unwittingly embroiled in his stoush with Whateley, said his former teammate was rarely the centre of attention in the Blues locker room.



“He was fairly quiet, [but] still very funny,” Docherty said. “If you listen to him speak, he’s probably socially anxious and awkward through footy because he didn’t know where he stood or what he was doing. He always had that funny side to him. “He joked around with a small group of mates as opposed to the whole locker room. Most people who played with him would have thought he was fairly reserved and didn’t speak very much.” Dan Gorringe takes on North Melbourne’s Todd Goldstein in a ruck contest in 2016. Getty Images In many ways, Gorringe is the most unlikely of football personalities: polarising, unfiltered and contemptuous of traditional media. But even the AFL wants him. Traditionally, it has taken a long and distinguished on-field career for a retired player to make it in the media. Though a No.10 pick in 2010, his 26 games for Gold Coast and Carlton fall well short of the mark. As a player, his most memorable moment came in retirement when he clattered into comedian Dave Hughes in a legends charity match. But the world of social media does not follow the same rules, and there are few in Australian sport better at playing this game than Gorringe, who has a team of more than 10 full-timers and additional casual and part-time staff behind the scenes managing content and his commercial partnerships. His success is no accident.



The former ruckman has a greater digital presence than some clubs. His 378,000 followers on Instagram is well over double that of Gold Coast, the club that drafted him. His 43,200 subscribers on YouTube is close to 50 per cent higher than another of his former teams, Carlton, and his TikTok following of 298,000 is more than the Blues and Suns combined. His average of more than 300,000 views and 20,000-plus engagements per content item across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube makes him “one of Australia’s highest-performing independent sports creator brands”, Nathan Powell, the chief product and strategy officer at AI-powered creator technology platform Fabulate, said. “Dan has managed to build something that’s much harder than simply accumulating followers,” Powell said. AFL CEO Andrew Dillon with influencer Dan Gorringe, announcing the league’s first official watchalong. AFL “He’s built a highly concentrated Australian sporting audience that consistently chooses to engage with his content.
