The audience is also predominantly male and heavily concentrated in the 18-to-34 demographic, which is one of the most valuable audiences for sporting organisations and advertisers. “That tells me people aren’t just following Dan because they know who he is – they’re following him because they genuinely value his perspective on sport and the content he creates.” No wonder the AFL has Gorringe on its books as part of what its customer and commercial boss Bec Haagsma says is a “rapid transformation and evolution of our fan engagement and fan experience strategy”. They see Gorringe as pivotal to targeting the younger market – those under the age of 34.



In collaboration with the league’s broadcast partners, Gorringe appeared on The Ultimate Footy Watchalong for the Fremantle v Sydney and North Melbourne v Melbourne games, streamed live on the AFL’s YouTube channel, Kayo and 7plus. “Watchalongs”, where fans stream themselves watching a game live and connect online in real time, are a new concept in Australia and, if experience overseas is any indication, here to stay. “It goes back to the idea that media is changing, and social media is a massive part of the media industry,” Michael Neill, the head of Fox Footy, said. “It won’t get any smaller. We’d be foolish if we didn’t look at these new ideas and different ways to broadcast. “The immediacy of his posts and how he gets his opinion out there really quick, it’s out there and it’s different. “It comes from an ex-player’s perspective as well, and from someone who’s very smart when it comes to communication and how to get his message out there.” For Seven, it gives the network another way to reach the younger market.



“Working with creators who love the game allows us to connect with audiences in authentic new ways,” Seven’s head of sport digital Kirsty Bradmore said. “We are continually exploring more ways to innovate our broadcast offering for viewers across Australia.” This collaboration drew 250,000 live viewers across the league’s YouTube channel, Kayo, Foxtel and 7plus to watch while Gorringe and co-hosts – Seven reporter Xander McGuire and Collingwood AFLW captain and Kayo personality Ruby Schleicher – casually discussed the game, as opposed to the serious analysis on the main coverage. Socceroos goalkeeper Patrick Beach, a GWS fan, featured at half-time. ‘People aren’t just following Dan because they know who he is – they’re following him because they genuinely value his perspective on sport and the content he creates.’ Nathan Powell of creator technology platform Fabulate “Dan has been with us for a year now doing some hardcore engagement stuff,” Haagsma said. “He’s part of that strategy. For us, looking at how we attract, retain and engage with our avid fans is a different proposition to our younger fans. “We knew we needed to engage a different strategy. We can’t put highlights on TikTok and go, ‘That will bring the kids in’. Dan has got a voice that we know speaks in a different way, and just resonates. He’s authentic in his point of view, and he loves the game.” Gorringe’s channel markets itself as “unfiltered and unqualified”. The wider football community saw this side in March after he aired a voice memo left by Docherty of a candid and expletive-laden analysis of his former club’s failings in their thumping by Sydney on the opening night of the season. Gorringe did not check with Docherty if the message was to be aired, as is the practice in mainstream media, drawing condemnation from Whateley – who slammed him for “reprehensible behaviour”.

World.title: Knock on wood, but I think I’ve wasted enough time on silly superstitions
World.content:
August 1, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We were sitting outside in the sun, on the broad steps of Sydney’s new fish market, when a bird flew overhead and launched a massive poo on the young woman sitting in front of us. The “dropping” was enormously accurate and voluminous, covering all of her left hand, part of her left arm and much of her dress. Keen to make her feel better, I told her: “They say it brings good luck.” What’s so bad about a black cat? Getty Images Her boyfriend turned with a smile. “In that case,” he says, “she’s in for a lot of good luck. Heaps of it.” At which point he began helping with the laborious clean-up. What are the origins of these superstitions? Who was the first person to see someone cop a flying splodge of bird poo, and then say: “They say it brings good luck”?



I understand the principle: something unfortunate has happened, so you want to make the person feel better. But why bird poo? We don’t offer this consolation after other misfortunes. If someone smacks their head into a low-lying branch, we don’t say: “Lucky dog! You better buy a lottery ticket.” If you get mugged, the thief pushing you to the ground and stealing your phone, the next person along doesn’t help you to your feet with the cheery observation: “Well, there’s nothing like a violent mugging to bring a bit of good luck.” Most superstitions make no sense. Why does a rabbit foot bring great fortune? It certainly didn’t work for the rabbit from which it was removed. And what’s so bad about a black cat? You wouldn’t dream of judging a person according to the colour of their skin, but apparently cats are fair game. It’s true my generation didn’t have YouTube or Netflix, but frankly we were flat-out keeping the devil at bay. When I was growing up, we lived in a world of superstitions. We were told not to step on the cracks in the pavement, to avoid the number 13, and to never open an umbrella when indoors. Saying something positive about oneself or hopeful about the future was generally frowned upon. But if you insisted – “hopefully I’ll pass my exams”, “no way will I crash my bike” – you had to immediately say “knock on wood” and then find some wood on which to knock. Since most 1970s houses were constructed from a mix of fibro, brown linoleum and orange Laminex, this was often hard to achieve.



Also, every time someone sneezed you had to say “bless you”, which apparently stopped the devil from using that moment of inattention to enter their soul. If you spilt salt, you also had to throw some over your left shoulder (using your right arm) which had the excellent effect of blinding the devil as he hovered at your shoulder. It’s true my generation didn’t have YouTube or Netflix, but frankly we were flat-out keeping the devil at bay. Special occasions such as birthdays were marked by a dinner of roast chicken, the climax of which involved two people grasping the “wish bone” and tearing it in two, good fortune going to the person who ended up with the larger bit of bone. The chicken, already having been throttled, plucked and baked, might have wondered about the purpose of this final indignity, yet it was not possible to eat a chicken while leaving its furcula alone. At Christmas, meanwhile, a silver sixpence would be baked into the Christmas pudding, ready to bring good luck to whoever found it. Or bad luck if you were a seven-year-old and ended up with it stuck in your windpipe, a leading cause of Christmas hospitalisations. The same coin, should it be located in the pudding or returned later by the surgeon, could then be offered as payment for a kitchen knife should you wish to give a knife as a present. It was bad luck to give knives as gifts – it would “cut” the friendship – so the gift had to be turned into a purchase. We were also told we could get rid of warts by “washing our hands in moonlight”, or rubbing them with a piece of meat which you’d then bury in the backyard. If you’ve ever found an old chop bone in your backyard, it was buried there by some warty kid.



You may think this was a charmingly enchanted world, but it did add a lot of fuss to the simplest of tasks, as we were constantly forced to leap over cracks, throw salt over our shoulders, and search for wood to knock upon. In hay fever season, you’d bless more people than the local priest. Related Article Opinion

Health I’m just a creature of habit. Sometimes that creature is a gorilla Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist Did any of the superstitions make sense? Perhaps a couple. I still avoid walking beneath a ladder, based on the practical consideration that a bucket of paint might be up there somewhere, ready to fall on my head. I also believe that it’s bad luck to put shoes on a table – the bad luck being the transmission of some nasty bug, picked up off the floor of a Sydney bus. As for those low-flying birds at the Sydney Fish Market, I’m betting they did bring good luck. That young woman’s boyfriend was so solicitous, tenderly dabbing her with napkins. It was probably the confirmation for which she’d been hoping: this one was a keeper. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: An ‘informal’ will and the missing jewellery: What will happen to Virginia Giuffre’s $30 million estate?
World.content:
Virginia Giuffre was trying to reclaim control. In early January 2025, she was allegedly assaulted by her husband, Robbie Giuffre, during a family holiday in Dunsborough, Western Australia. Robbie then secured a family violence restraining order against Virginia, which banned the prominent Epstein accuser from contacting her two youngest children for six months. It also meant she was not allowed to go to the family’s beachfront home in Perth, which is where her belongings – including important documents, her memoir manuscript, jewellery and mementos – were kept. So Virginia decided to take back some control and spoil herself.



Virginia’s carer, Cheryl Myers, estimates the mother of three spent about $100,000 at luxury jeweller Linneys, and a local pearl retailer, on jewellery for her mother, and diamond rings and necklaces for herself. She had the money to splurge. As Good Weekend senior writer and Walkley Award-winner Melissa Fyfe and WAtoday journalist Carla Hildebrandt reveal in The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald’s four-part investigative podcast, Virginia, the payments Virginia received from various confidential settlements with prominent people – such as the man formerly known as Prince Andrew – came to the equivalent of $US25 million ($35.6 million).



What’s remarkable about this shopping spree is not the amount of money Virginia spent. Rather, as Fyfe and Hildebrandt reveal in episode four of Virginia – out today – it’s that, more than a year on from Virginia’s death, no one seems to know where the jewellery is. Related Article Visual story

Domestic violence ‘Mommy pls call’: The secret ‘scrapbook’ of Virginia Giuffre “Everybody wants to know about the jewellery,” says Myers. “A couple of days after Virginia had passed, one of Virginia’s friends called me, and asked me, ‘Where was the jewellery?’ And I was like, ‘I’ve got no idea’. “She said, ‘Well, we’ve been to the house, me and Rob, and we’ve looked everywhere for the jewellery, and we can’t find any’. And I said, ‘Well, I don’t know’.” But the jewellery is only one part of the puzzle. Virginia also had a chunk of money in cryptocurrency, and now no one knows what happened to that investment.



Virginia Giuffre is pictured here outside a Manhattan court after Jeffrey Epstein’s death in 2019. She received the equivalent of $US25 million in confidential payments after multiple legal battles over the years. AP Following Virginia’s suicide in April 2025, the rift between her family in the United States, including her two brothers, and Robbie worsened. They are now embroiled in a legal battle over Virginia’s estate, which is estimated to be worth up to $30 million, including the compensation payments, assets, investment properties and book royalties. Virginia, whose divorce from Robbie had not been finalised before her death, died without a valid will. She was supposed to sign it on April 26, 2025 – the day after she died – and had marked this date on the magnetic whiteboard on her fridge. Myers and Virginia’s Perth lawyer, Karrie Louden, say Virginia had an “informal will” expressed to Louden and also emailed to her accountant in February 2025.



“I don’t want Robbie blowing my children’s money on himself.” Virginia Giuffre’s diary notes, written before her death This is backed by Virginia’s brothers and their wives. The “informal will” stipulates a small amount of money going to Virginia’s family and friends, including Myers and her brothers, but the bulk to her children and a small amount to Robbie. They say she wanted the money held in trust until the kids turned 25. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life According to court filings, Virginia’s sons Christian and Noah – backed by their father – are arguing their mother lacked “testamentary capacity” when the informal will was created. If Christian and Noah win, Robbie stands to inherit just over a third of what’s left after the divorce settlement, with the remainder divided between the three children: Christian, Noah, and their daughter.



That would make Robbie the main beneficiary, and most likely the administrator of Virginia’s worldwide estate. “What a terrible, tragic story that everything that she fought for against monsters of sexual assault on the most powerful level, every single dollar is going to go back into the hands of her final abuser, and that’s the last chapter,” says Sky Roberts. “Can we imagine that that’s the way the story ends? Because I can’t, and I can’t live with that.” Listen to the fourth episode of Virginia – where hosts Fyfe and Hildebrandt reveal Virginia’s arrest weeks before her death, the real story behind the bus crash that prompted Virginia to tell the world she had days to live, the complicated truth behind her posthumous memoir, and how Virginia’s suicide is part of a wider, systemic problem that is impacting other Australian women – in the player above, wherever you get your podcasts, or click here.



A statement from Robbie Giuffre’s lawyers says the following: “What appears to be an orchestrated attempt by persons to gain financially from Virginia’s death by making unsubstantiated allegations, when they should have been aware of Virginia’s medical conditions, is simply disgraceful. “In the late Virginia Giuffre’s book published and titled Nobody’s Girl, Virginia praised and thanked Robert for his support of her throughout their marriage and in particular, her struggle to be heard.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: Carroll’s long run: Can the boy from Airport West outrun Andrews’ ghost?
World.content:
Retiring Sydenham MP Natalie Hutchins makes no attempt to disguise the unsentimental calculation behind the move.

That internal alarm explains why the Labor caucus executed its late-term change of leader, dumping Jacinta Allan after nearly three years in office to install her deputy, Ben Carroll.

“In some ways, Ben’s two biggest rivals are not on the ballot paper: Dan Andrews is not on the ballot paper, and Pauline Hanson isn’t on the ballot paper, but that’s what people are voting on.”

Shorten, a long-term powerbroker and former federal leader, argues the hostility confronting state Labor reflects a post-COVID frustration with all political parties, but especially Labor.

“Labor was heading off a cliff,” Shorten says. “In 1992, Joan Kirner got 27 seats and [Jeff] Kennett got 61. It [the 2026 election] was going to be worse than that.”

Translated to the looming November election, the result would be a ruin deeper than that inflicted on Joan Kirner’s Labor government in 1992.

Bill Shorten spent much of his political life doing numbers. And the polling numbers coming out of Victoria’s Trades Hall a fortnight ago were scary.

Faced with $190 billion in state debt, ongoing revelations surrounding the $109 billion Big Build, and an electorate itching for change after 12 years of Labor rule, caucus concluded Allan could never separate herself from the era that created those problems.

Hutchins says Carroll has a strong sense of social justice and an understanding of the issues in Melbourne’s west, which she hopes will improve the party’s prospects.

“A lot of people, particularly in the outer west and newer suburbs, are pretty rattled about community safety,” Hutchins says. “And it’s not just the youth crime; it’s also the organised crime, the drug dealing, and also family violence that is all connected.”

Voters in the established estates of Taylors Lakes and Hillside cited crime, government inaction on CFMEU corruption, bad roads, and a sense that Melbourne’s east receives lavish infrastructure while the west misses out. For the first time, a disturbing number told her they intended to vote for One Nation.

Her outer-western electorate shares a boundary with Carroll’s seat of Niddrie. During four weeks of door-knocking, Hutchins encountered anger unprecedented in her political career.

“Labor is in real danger in its seats in the west, and it’s time to have a premier willing to take on the hard issues affecting our residents,” she said.

For three years, he served as Allan’s deputy, and for nine years before that, he sat around the cabinet table under Andrews, rising through government while two premiers came to define modern Victoria.

It’s easy to see why the 51-year-old Carroll was eager to press this point.

How hard? Don’t take our word for it. Read Carroll’s handwritten notes, captured during his first press conference as premier. “Not Daniel Andrews” was scrawled at the top of his talking points.

On his first afternoon as premier, Carroll stood at a media podium inside Parliament House and delivered a declaration explicitly designed to draw that line.

Shorten sees Carroll as Labor’s only remaining path to a shifted conversation. “This state election was looming as a referendum on the question: ‘Are you dirty with the state of politics in Victoria?’ His promotion to leader provides a bit of a circuit-breaker to that.”

The question confronting the ALP is whether the boy from Airport West has the time, the authority, and the independence from his two far better-known predecessors to drag his party back from the brink.

Carroll inherits a state carrying enormous debt and a government battered by two years of revelations surrounding the Big Build. The teachers he was responsible for until a few days ago are threatening to strike again.

But it will take more than pragmatism to solve the problems on his desk.

Where Andrews centralised power with ruthless discipline, and Allan sought to weather scandal through endurance, Carroll belongs to a tradition of Labor pragmatism. His persona is suburban: a Catholic, straight-laced family man with a lifetime love of the Kangaroos who got a taste for marathon running in middle age.

Carroll is a more anonymous political figure than the leaders he follows.

Now, just four months before the state election, Carroll confronts the defining challenge of his political career: can a long-serving Labor insider, groomed by party hard heads, persuade a sceptical electorate that his elevation represents genuine change rather than a cosmetic reshuffle?

Carroll said his parents had “instilled in me the importance of family and the value of hard work”. As soon as he reached the legal working age of 14 years and nine months, he walked into Airport West Kmart looking for part-time work. “I soon found myself working on the cash registers as a checkout chick.”

Opportunity, he told parliament, brought his parents, Greg and Kay Carroll, to Airport West, where they built the family home in 1974 and established a small electrical business. His mother Kay migrated from Texas and worked at Glenroy West Primary School. His father ran the family business until it collapsed during the recession of the early 1990s.

Carroll’s roots in his electorate run deep. Raised in Airport West as the eldest of three children, he entered parliament in 2012. In his inaugural speech, he framed his story around the idea of opportunity, tracing his family’s journey from Irish labourer Michael Carroll from Tipperary, who arrived in Victoria in 1840, to his election more than 170 years later.

Carroll lives in tree-lined Aberfeldie with wife Fiona Rothville – a lawyer who serves as director of Workplace Integrity at Deloitte – and their young daughter. Rothville’s father is a director of Nilsen, a major electrical contractor that has worked on state infrastructure projects; Carroll declares it in his register of interest.

He remained at the store for eight years while completing an arts degree with honours at La Trobe University in 2000. He joined the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association, later saying it gave him “a good understanding of the importance of unions in helping working people”. At times, he recalled, the union helped pay for his university textbooks.

On Wednesday morning, less than 24 hours after taking the top job, Carroll leaned into that retail origin story for his first public press conference as premier. Standing inside Kmart on Bourke Street in Melbourne’s CBD, he announced legislation for Workplace Protection Orders, giving courts powers to ban violent or abusive customers from retail, hospitality, and public transport workplaces for up to 12 months.

During his years behind a Kmart register, Carroll recalled being intimidated and threatened on the job, describing those checkout shifts as “crucible years”.

From the year 2000, Carroll advised premier Steve Bracks, then planning minister Justin Madden. After a stint as a trainee lawyer at the Victorian Government Solicitor’s Office, he moved to Canberra in 2011 to advise Right-faction powerbroker Stephen Conroy on the National Broadband Network.

Emma Dawson, executive director of Labor Party think tank the Chifley Research Centre, worked alongside Carroll in Conroy’s office, where he managed caucus relations.

Emma Dawson says her former colleague Carroll is “a very studious, serious person”. Luis Enrique Ascui

She remembers an adviser distinct from typical Canberra political figures: “He’s a very studious, serious person.” Dawson recalls him parsing complex legislation before briefing MPs – a habit of constant note-taking highlighted by several people during the compilation of this story. “Ben is not afraid to ask questions and to listen to people. He takes notes – copious notes.”

Dawson says Carroll values evidence over factional orthodoxy, pointing to his decision as education minister to mandate synthetic phonics despite union pushback. “He’s interested in the evidence behind what works,” she says.

A son of the west rises

When former attorney-general Rob Hulls resigned from Niddrie in 2012, Carroll won the byelection, aged 36.

Standing in Parliament after his victory, Carroll described representing Niddrie as his “greatest honour” because he would be serving “the community I was raised in, the people I am one of”.

Sebastian Agricola is a lawyer who has worked for more than 30 years in St Albans, just outside of Carroll’s electorate. The two met when they faced off as candidates for preselection in Niddrie.

Agricola recalls a younger man with similarly strong ties to the north-western suburbs, who engaged in the hand-to-hand combat of Labor preselection in a respectful and refreshingly down to earth way.

“He was competitive, in the sense of you have to be for that sort of a contest. But he played it straight down the line. He was fair, he never criticised me,” Agricola says. “People can let those preselections become very personal and vitriolic. Ben never did that.”

Agricola, veteran president of the St Albans Business Association, has remained plugged into community and political circles in Melbourne’s west, and says Carroll has been an approachable figure locally, who never gave in to cynicism.

Sebastian Agricola, who competed with Carroll for Labor preselection, says the premier is no cynic. Luis Enrique Ascui

“If people just accept that what you see is actually genuine, I think there’s a good chance that he’ll have a significant impact,” he says of the newly minted premier.

Carroll never hid his ambition. “I was always very keen to rise,” he told reporters at his first press conference after being made deputy premier.

That ambition fuelled years of quiet tension with Andrews who, after Labor’s 2022 election victory, installed Jacinta Allan as deputy, leaving Carroll in the corridor for an hour to receive his portfolio – a spot known as “Dan’s freezer”.

In 2023 when Andrews tried to hand-pick his successors – Allan as premier, treasurer Tim Pallas as deputy – Carroll threatened a membership ballot, which would have left Victoria without a permanent premier for a month. It triggered what colleagues described as a “nuclear meltdown” from Andrews. But Carroll was made deputy premier.

The political scar never healed. Later, Carroll was the only sitting Labor MP to publicly criticise Andrews after the former premier posed in a photograph in Beijing among a group of foreign officials and leaders that included Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong-un.

Shorten contrasts Carroll with his predecessors, pointing to his local focus and willingness to fight cabinet over the Airport Rail Link.

“He’s never been a schemer. He’s never tried to be a factional mini state warlord. He’s very different from someone like Dan Andrews. But he’s capable of being a very good state leader.”

Shorten says both he and Carroll advocated for an Airport Rail Link, putting Carroll at odds with colleagues focused on the Suburban Rail Loop.

“That made him not popular with the SRL zealots in the cabinet. He didn’t get the memo that he shouldn’t speak up about it,” says Shorten, who is now the University of Canberra vice-chancellor and who says he is no longer active in the Labor Party.

Former Labor leader Bill Shorten, now the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Canberra. Alex Ellinghausen

Carroll has held 14 separate ministerial portfolios. Danny Pearson, the retiring Labor MP for Essendon, says Carroll’s rise is the result of years of toil and ambition.

“To be the leader of a major political party, you’ve got to really want it, you’ve got to have ability and you’ve got to work hard,” he says. “You can’t be some sort of part-time dilettante who thinks, you know, swanning around in the members’ bar is the pathway to power.”

Former Andrews government minister Philip Dalidakis, a longtime friend who lured Carroll from a short career in law back into politics in Stephen Conroy’s office, describes him as “extraordinarily earnest” in his approach to both public policy and politics.

“He doesn’t yell, he doesn’t scream ‘Look at me!’, he just quietly goes about his policy work.”

Dalidakis sees Carroll’s style setting up a contest of substance against Liberal leader Jess Wilson, while signalling an end to the “command and control” cabinet model of Andrews and Allan.

“He doesn’t use policy to wield power for power’s sake, and I think that’s what we probably want in our leader. I think that’s probably why Jess Wilson has made a really good start in the last six months because she’s focused on good policy.”

Carroll needs to listen, he says, both to voters and to his cabinet colleagues. “The premier has said that he’s going to return to a proper cabinet consultative process … that can only be a good thing for Victoria.”

Carroll’s difficult task now is to speak to the big-spending legacy of the Andrews era without repudiating the government that elevated him.

His first major announcement was a state royal commission into corruption and organised crime infiltration across the Big Build, reversing the position Allan defended for two years.

Carroll promised sweeping terms of reference, a special prosecutor operating alongside the inquiry, and retrospective “follow-the-money” powers for IBAC.

The move illustrated how sharply he intends to distinguish himself from his predecessors.

Tim Read, the Greens MP who chairs parliament’s Integrity and Oversight Committee that monitors and reviews the performance of IBAC, says he’s reserving final judgment until the premier delivers deeper anti-corruption measures. “Without other powers, including removing the requirement that corrupt conduct [for IBAC] constitute a criminal offence, any new powers will be limited,” he says.

Carroll has moved quickly to distance himself from existing cabinet policy. He has put the SRL under review; one of his first phone calls as premier was to Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush; and he has previously publicly rejected the government’s push to phase out household gas connections.

Can Carroll outrun the past?

Yet, the greatest obstacle confronting Carroll is not policy. It is credibility among voters.

Carroll is attempting to convince the electorate that someone who has spent years at the centre of power can embody a fresh start.

David Hayward, RMIT emeritus professor and an expert analyst of Victorian politics, says it was evident from his first speech as leader that Carroll is channelling his former boss Steve Bracks.

“I thought he handled it really well by coming out and using a Bracks-like phrasing of integrity, economy, and community safety as the leitmotif of his new government, and immediately saying, ‘I am not my predecessors’,” Hayward says.

Bracks pulled off a surprise heist when he defeated Kennett in 1999. Carroll will need to produce an even bigger upset if he is to deliver Labor a fourth term in government, unseen in Victorian politics since Henry Bolte and Rupert Hamer led the Liberals to nine straight election wins between 1955 and 1979.

To do so, Labor must treat the day that Carroll rolled Allan as day one of the election campaign, Hayward says.

“I think he had to distance himself from the malaise that had come to settle upon the government. It’s not like the Allan leadership was full of ideas and policy innovations. It really appeared to be very flat-footed.”

Anxious though he may be to separate himself from Andrews and Allan, Carroll cannot shrug off the state’s record debt.

Hayward says most voters were once unfazed about debt while it could be justified as delivering infrastructure assets, but that changed when the debt and the Big Build were linked with corruption, which was uncovered by a series of reports in The Age.

“Everything suddenly switched … this suddenly raised questions about the spend, about the infrastructure and [Allan] was never really able to respond.”

Carroll’s move to call a royal commission and establish a special prosecutor alongside it gives Labor one last chance to change the script.

“That’s another point about the change of leader. With somebody appearing to be so different to the previous premier, it gives a new energy,” Hayward says.

Time is working against him. Carroll has 119 days before Victorians go to the polls on the final Saturday in November.

He must also contend with the fatigue that follows 12 years of Labor rule, while confronting a surging One Nation vote, now polling at 22 per cent across Victoria and threatening Labor in outer-suburban seats.

By establishing a royal commission into the Big Build on his first day as premier, Carroll sought to isolate the scandal and cast it as part of Allan’s legacy rather than his own.

Whether voters accept that distinction – or regard Carroll as an equal participant in more than a decade of Labor government – could shape the outcome of November’s election.

Fourteen years after promising parliament he would “strive to work every day with that sort of passion and dedication”, Ben Carroll occupies the office he spent his political life pursuing.

For the marathon runner from Airport West, the final sprint has begun.

World.title: The strange rule that denied Australia a chance to race for a medal
World.content:
SportCyclingCommonwealth Games The strange rule that denied Australia a chance to race for a medal Billie Eder Updated August 1, 2026 — 5:25am ,first published 2:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Australia’s cycling team is unhappy but unable to appeal a decision by race officials to disqualify a rider from a bronze medal race over the taping of her shoulders, even though she had them taped when she won gold a day earlier. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden, who was part of the women’s team that won gold in the team pursuit, was disqualified on Friday from the women’s 4000m individual pursuit for wearing strapping tape under her race suit. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden celebrates victory after the women’s 4000m team pursuit finals. Getty Images The 21-year-old cyclist finished fourth fastest in individual qualifying to book herself a spot in the bronze medal race against Scotland’s Erin Boothman, before officials from world cycling’s governing body, the UCI, disqualified her for a breach of equipment and uniform rules. Those officials deemed that the tape, on Wilson-Haffenden’s shoulders, caused a “morphological change” – a change to the physical shape, outer appearance or internal structure of the body – which is against racing rules.



The official rule says, “clothing and other items or accessories worn by a rider may not modify the morphology of the rider”. It is unclear how and why officials picked up on the taping on Friday and not Thursday, and whether the check of the two Australian athletes was random. The UCI has been contacted for comment and clarification. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden during the individual pursuit. Quinn Rooney The same officials ruled that another Australian, Sophie Edwards, would also be disqualified for having “excessive” padding in her helmet. Both Wilson-Haffenden and Edwards had the same taping and helmet, respectively, when they raced the previous day. No clothing or equipment issues were raised after officials completed inspections on Thursday.



Executive general manager of performance at Aus Cycling, Jesse Korf, said the Australian team was frustrated by the decision to disqualify Wilson-Haffenden. He described the decision as subjective and said Wilson-Haffenden received taping to her shoulders after having discomfort and mobility issues. Australia’s gold medal winning women’s pursuit team. Getty Images “On inspection after the race, the UCI [Union Cycliste Internationale] concluded that the taping of the shoulder constituted, according to them in the rule book, a morphological change, but they weren’t able to articulate what that exactly was because it’s a grey area. You cannot measure what a morphological change is,” Korf said. “They made that conclusion, we looked into it and, being that it’s non-measurable and subjective, unfortunately that conclusion is final, which we’re most certainly not happy with and Felicity is upset, of course.”



Korf said the team was also disappointed in the decision to disqualify Edwards, but she had not qualified for a medal race. The Australian team does not believe there is a risk that the team’s gold medal will be stripped or under review, given both riders passed inspections on the day. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden celebrates victory in the women’s team pursuit. Getty Images “We heard nothing after inspections yesterday,” Korf said. “After races, riders get inspected, there’s always checks, and there was no challenge, no nothing yesterday, so that’s in the clear. “The challenges [today] are from what was faced in the individual pursuits and the conclusions of the commissaires.”



Related Article Commonwealth Games Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist Korf said Australia would seek more clarification on the rules moving forward. “Well, we’ll definitely try to learn more around how the assessment is done so that we can learn and mitigate,” Korf said. New Zealand’s Bryony Boothman has now been promoted to the bronze medal race. Glasgow 2026 has also been contacted for comment.



Before her disqualification, Wilson-Haffenden had said she was looking forward to the bronze medal race despite appearing quite distressed and unwell after qualifying. She needed extra recovery time, was shaky, and needed assistance when leaving the track. “No doubt I’ll be riding tonight. I mean, a 4000m effort takes a lot out of you, and I needed a little longer to recover, but I’ll be all good,” she said. It was only her second individual 4000m pursuit, and said her post-race condition was a result of giving it her all. “I enjoy suffering, so I quite enjoy this race,” she said.



“Of course, it’s not a nice experience at the finish, but yeah, I hope tonight will be nicer.” Georgia Baker celebrates during the medal ceremony of the women’s 10km scratch race final. AP Photo/Manish Swarup The double-disqualification was a dampener on what was a hugely successful day for Australian cycling. Georgia Baker won gold in the women’s 10km scratch race to equal Anna Meares, Matthew Glaetzer and Bradley McGee as Australia’s most-successful cyclist at the Commonwealth Games with five gold – a title she has the chance to claim for herself with the points race and elimination race still to come for her. Minutes later, Australia swept the podium in the men’s 4000m individual pursuit, as Oliver Bleddyn won gold, beating Conor Leahy for the first time in his career and setting a new national and Games record, while James Moriarty won bronze.

World.title: Banks are quietly gutting credit card perks. Here’s what you stand to lose
World.content:
MoneySavingLoyalty programs Opinion Banks are quietly gutting credit card perks. Here’s what you stand to lose Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor August 1, 2026 — 5:01am

August 1, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It is a time-honoured strategy for points hackers like me to use credit cards, in an earn-then-churn rewards play. No, you shouldn’t have a credit card if you can’t trust yourself to clear your credit card balance in full, say because you have a spending weakness. Incur interest and you’ve forgone your advantage. Small businesses are passing on far higher surcharges than needed and are rewarded with Qantas Frequent Flyer points for their trouble. Simon Letch But, for me, credit card reward points have long been a big part of how I fly me and my kids internationally for just fees and taxes – we are headed to Vancouver again next year for just $600. But what I feared – and forecast – is coming true: banks are quietly slashing consumer perks – even before the October 1 surcharge ban hits. The deals for new customer have been pared back in multiple cases, as expected: reduced bulk sign-up points with a higher initial spend to qualify.



ANZ on its Frequent Flyer Black Card, for example, culled its bulk up-front points on July 22 from 130,000 to 80,000 Qantas points. At the same time, the minimum spend requirement increased from $5000 in the first three months to $6000, while the $200 cashback offer was removed. On its Frequent Flyer Platinum Card, on the same date, the sign-up bonus went from 75,000 to 40,000 Qantas points. The minimum spend requirement also increased from $2500 in the first three months to $3500 in the first four months, and the accompanying $100 credit was removed. You are just going to need to wait, optimise the other ways to get points, and plan your holidays a little more carefully. But you can expect similar moves all over the market. And already the trend is towards an increased timeframe to get bonus points. Instead of qualifying after, say, three months in, they are most likely to be delivered in two tranches with the second portion after the annual fee is due 12 months or even 18 months later – card companies can no longer afford to have points players who are going to ditch and switch cards in less than a year. And it will be a whole new points-accrual landscape, probably even for existing cardholders, from October 1.



Qantas itself, on its credit card page, states: “Fees, charges and earn rates (if applicable) are subject to change from 1 October 2026. If we make changes, these will be communicated in accordance with our terms and conditions.“ Editor's pick Opinion

Credit cards My sneaky $66 fee shows what credit card perks really cost us Victoria Devine Money columnist Of the existing customer clawbacks known so far, datahouse Canstar has trawled the fine print for me to reveal where the issuers are compensating for lost revenue. Please note this is not to pick on the providers below but what they are doing will likely become the norm, so it’s important to know. To date, NAB is making the most significant changes on October 1, to a bunch of cards. A few cards, curiously, get renamed too. Take the off-sale NAB Qantas Plus Card, which will be renamed to the NAB Qantas Rewards Premium Card. Common cost-saving moves look likely to include … Lower earn rates: The NAB Qantas Rewards Premium Card earn rate will be reduced from 1 Qantas Point per $1.50 spent to 1 point per $2 on the first $3000 of monthly spend, and from 1 point per $3 to 1 point per $4 on the next $3000.



That’s a huge reduction and reflected across most of its products, to some degree. (Note the international spend bonus of 1 bonus point per $2 remains unchanged.) And caps are creeping in too, on products where they were previously absent. Points caps: For NAB, on its NAB Rewards Card, formerly the NAB Rewards Platinum, the earn structure will change from an uncapped 1 point per $1 to 1.25 points per $1 on the first $5000 of monthly spend and 0.5 points per $1 thereafter. On the NAB Qantas Rewards Signature, the monthly points cap will also be reduced from $20,000 to $15,000 in eligible spend. Higher interest: Possibly even more concerning, NAB is also typically upping interest rates with purchase and cash advance rates moving to the likes of 22.49 per cent and 22.99 per cent respectively. Upped annual fees: NAB has also announced a potential hike in annual fees on its NAB Rewards Travel Card (formerly NAB Rewards Signature). The monthly $35 fee will be replaced with a $395 annual fee, but the monthly fee waiver will be removed.



NAB has previously announced it is overhauling its white-label rewards portfolio, including MyCard, BOQ and Virgin Money credit cards, with changes taking effect from October 1. The flavour of changes is similar to the above with an increased number of points required to redeem rewards, by up to 62 per cent. From October 1, charging an explicit fee when customers use a credit card will be banned. iStock As I said, I don’t mean to pick on NAB – it’s just one of the first to disclose its product repricing. And Westpac has made a different margin-saving move … Insurance decreased: On Westpac’s Altitude credit cards, complimentary travel insurance will be limited to International Medical Travel Insurance, Domestic Travel Insurance and Rental Vehicle Excess Insurance in Australia, with several existing protections removed. Complimentary International Medical Travel Insurance including trip cancellation, travel delay and luggage cover will no longer be covered. There will be a higher excess for international travel claims and the maximum covered trip length will be just one month for many cards.



A vital word of warning too: cardholders will now need to activate their complimentary international medical travel insurance before leaving Australia to be eligible for cover. Editor's pick Exclusive

Credit cards Surcharge ban could end popular free travel insurance perk Other complimentary protections removed: Gone from Westpac’s complimentary insurance package are also Extended Warranty, Purchase Protection and Overseas Transit Accident Insurance. So why is all this happening? What is the actual surcharge change? From October 1, charging an explicit fee when customers use a credit card will be banned. But the fees that fly between the terminal-operating bank and the payment-providing banks to facilitate the transaction will also be reduced. What’s called the interchange fee will be cut 63 per cent from 0.8 per cent to 0.3 per cent. And that’s part of what card providers have been using to pay airlines for points.

World.title: Why your bank might be overcharging you interest – and how to check
World.content:
MoneySavingHome loans Opinion Why your bank might be overcharging you interest – and how to check Bec Wilson Money contributor August 1, 2026 — 5:01am

August 1, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Have you got an offset account, and if so, have you ever checked it’s working properly to reduce the interest paid on your home loan? Sounds like something most people would assume the bank knows how to get right, right? Well, according to a report by ASIC that was published this week, it’s now something we should all be worrying about, and checking on promptly. Banks are bad at catching their own mistakes, with 77 per cent of the failures banks eventually reported going undetected until ASIC forced the data from them. Ryan Stuart The Australian Securities and Investments Commission has reviewed the practices of eight banks, looking at more than 200,000 individual home loans to check whether the offset accounts in place were delivering the savings that were promised, and the commission has been unimpressed by the mess. Its report shows that, in the period from September 2023 to August 2025, banks paid out compensation of more than $55 million to customers for cases where offset accounts were not offsetting correctly – and that was chiefly only to people who discovered a problem and asked about it.



Fifty-five million dollars in compensation is what banks have so far admitted to getting wrong – but ASIC says the real number could be a lot bigger. Several banks couldn’t even reliably tell them who had asked for an offset account in the first place, let alone who had lost money on one that hadn’t been set up or linked correctly, or even set up at all. An offset account is a transaction account linked to an eligible home loan that is designed to reduce the amount outstanding on the loan used to calculate interest. Offset accounts, when set up correctly and used well, can significantly decrease your interest costs over a lifetime. Even after a mortgage could be paid down outright, many Australians approaching retirement choose to keep their money in an offset account – rather than closing the loan down entirely – so they can have access to credit in their later years that might otherwise be difficult to get or even be inaccessible. According to the report, in March this year Australians held $349.1 billion in offset accounts, a number that grew by an enormous 28 per cent over the past two years.



Yet, with this growth, there is clearly a job to be done in properly enabling these accounts and checking that they are doing what they’re supposed to do – because many are not. I sat down this week with the new chair of ASIC, Sarah Court, to unpack the problems with offset accounts on the Prime Time podcast. She broke the failures down by type. ‘A number of the banks really struggled to identify when offset accounts had been requested in the first place.’ Sarah Court, chair of ASIC “Of the significant failures we found, 55 per cent were cases where the bank had opened the offset account but not linked it to the home loan. In another 22 per cent or so, the offset account wasn’t opened in the first place. And in some other circumstances, the account was eventually linked, but not in the timeframe the customer was expecting.” The written report ASIC published this week, called “Offsets, out of mind”, goes further on the cause. It found that 86 per cent of failures came down to plain manual error, such as a staff member misreading an instruction, entering the wrong account number or missing a step when a loan was refinanced.



It also found that banks are bad at catching their own mistakes: 77 per cent of the failures that banks eventually reported went undetected until ASIC forced the data out of them. One bank had a report specifically built to catch broken offset links that had sat unreviewed for almost five years. Editor's pick Home loans Home owners warned to check offset accounts after $55 million interest issue “We asked the banks: how can you guarantee that these accounts are all being linked?” Court says. “We were disappointed, I think it’s fair to say, with some of the responses we got. A number of the banks really struggled to identify when offset accounts had been requested in the first place.” The report singles out that offset accounts are frequently going wrong when a customer is refinancing and coming off a fixed rate. These are the moments when accounts most often come unstuck because many banks automatically delink an offset account when a loan changes and expect the customer to separately ask for it to be relinked. The most challenging reality of this problem is that it’s hard for people to see it and know that it’s not working. Most people set up their loan repayment amounts based on their minimum payment requirements. These are usually set by the loan amount, terms and interest rate, not by how much they have to pay when the offset balance is taken in.



So the amount leaving your account each month doesn’t usually change when an offset account fails – making the failure almost impossible to notice. There’s no red flag on your statement, and no notification in your inbox. You have to go looking for whether your home loan and offset are in place and working together to know. “We were disappointed,” said Sarah Court, chair of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. Edwina Pickles And going looking isn’t as easy as it should be. Half of the banks ASIC reviewed don’t even show their customers, in their app, how much interest their offset account has saved them. That information shows up only in a statement. “Sometimes it can be really hard for customers to even check whether their offset account has been linked,” Court says. “You have to do a bit of detective work. We’re very reliant on the banks doing the right thing behind the scenes.”



Part of that comes down to the way in which many banks are run. Home loan teams and everyday transaction account teams often run on completely separate systems, with completely separate goals, KPIs and reporting. So, linking the two parts of the same bank can be a manual process, handled by people, with nothing automated to catch errors and issues. Yet while clunky systems might explain how the mistakes happen, they don’t explain what happened next. The report found that some banks investigated and compensated customers only after receiving complaints, with one bank telling ASIC it has no process to check routinely for errors “unless there is an associated customer complaint”. I asked Court directly whether it’s fair that consumers have to fight for something they already filled out the forms for. “I would be hoping there’d be very few, if any, scenarios where a customer is told their account has not been linked without the bank very promptly dealing with remediation,” she says. “We’re not seeing resistance to paying compensation. Where a bank has failed to deliver on its promise to a customer, it is completely incumbent on the bank to promptly remedy that.” ASIC named all eight banks reviewed – AMP, ANZ, CBA, Credit Union Australia, HSBC, ING, Macquarie and Westpac – but every case study in the report is anonymous, and Court would not attach specific failures to specific banks when I asked.



“I think it’s fair to say some of them are performing better than others,” she says. “Having said that, if I look at the $55 million that’s been remediated, that is spread across a wide number of banks. So it is clear that across the board, all banks have some challenges.” Editor's pick Opinion

Home loans Check your offset account: Are the banks returning to bastardry? Elizabeth Knight Business columnist So, should you worry? Court says it’s wise to be vigilant, which is regulator-speak for “don’t panic, but don’t assume you’re fine either”. And if that’s the case – how do you check? First, open your online banking app and look at your offset account and your home loan side by side. Check if the offset account is linked to that loan. Second, check it’s linked to the right loan, particularly if you’ve refinanced, switched products or come off a fixed rate at any point. Third, pull up a recent statement and see whether the interest you’ve been charged looks like it’s calculated on your loan balances minus your offset balances, not your full loan balance alone.



If anything makes you feel concerned, call your bank. Ask them to confirm – in writing, by email or secure message – that the account is linked, has stayed linked, and is reducing your interest the way it’s supposed to. If the bank can’t or won’t give you a straight answer, and you’re worried that there’s an unsolved issue, you can report it directly to ASIC through its website to escalate things. Bec Wilson is author of the bestseller How to Have an Epic Retirement and the newly released Prime Time: 27 Lessons for the New Midlife. She writes a weekly newsletter at epicretirement.net and hosts the Prime Time podcast. World.title: If you wanted to create the ultimate ski resort, this place would be the template
World.content:
InspirationSki holidays If you wanted to create the ultimate ski resort, this place would be the template Jim Darby August 1, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When it comes to rating snow resorts, so much of it is subjective. By and large, skiers and snowboarders relate in a tribal way to one or two destinations, sticking with them from their early days and gathering, over the seasons, an intimate understanding of the way they work. A big mountain with ski-in/ski-out village and 750cm average annual snowfall. Big White Ski Resort Suppose you’re a traveller though, looking to explore some new terrain, what do you look for? One thing that immediately springs to mind is how much snowmaking there is. If there is major snowmaking infrastructure, that isn’t necessarily a negative, it’ll guarantee coverage. But if you come across a popular destination with little or no snowmaking, then that’s telling you a lot about the quality and reliability of its snow cover. Somewhere like Canada’s Big White, for example. Indeed, if you were setting out to build your fantasy snow resort, you could do worse than use Big White as a template. The highest peak in British Columbia’s Okanagan Highlands, the resort has an average annual snow fall of 750 centimetres, making for an operating season nudging five months.



You’d want your fantasy resort to be close to an airport – for Big White, Kelowna is 55-minutes down the road. You’d want it to have a village with some scale but still some character and heart, where most of the accommodation was ski-in/ski-out. 



It was in a perilous state financially and the story goes that the patriarch, Desmond Schumann, bought it for one Canadian dollar. He also had to honour about $C4.5 million in debt that came with it, but what he got was the lease on the existing snowfield and vast areas beyond and the ability to develop the real estate in the village. So it was “see you later” Hotham and “how’s it going?” Canada. The resort chief executive is Schumann’s grandson, Peter Plimmer, a keen skier but also a keen mountain biker, with an aim to expand that side of the business, which is booming in some parts of Canada. But back to our fantasy snowfield – what matters as much as anything is the quality of the terrain, the runs you’ll be using. The groomed terrain here is seemingly endless, miles and miles of smooth runs, sometimes steep, sometimes with some big rolling bumps to better let you work the shape of your skis (or board). They’re like big, long, beautiful fairways. Fresh tracks at Big White. My guide, Gavin Crawford – another Mount Hotham veteran who now calls Big White home – shows me the mountain, and it takes most of the day to cover it. His tip on the groomed runs? “Ski Sun Run early, the groomer drivers use it to head home and make their final pass on skier’s left of the run.”



Much of the terrain (54 per cent to be exact) is of the cruisy intermediate kind, but there are also steeps up high for more of a challenge, a terrain park for the young and restless and some long beginner runs. And then there are the trees to ski through and the snow ghosts – trees in their frozen winter state – to ski around, all of this with views into the vast mountain ranges into the distance. And if you need a hand to find your way here, mountain hosts lead 90-minute complimentary mountain tours departing from the village centre daily at 10.15am. Apart from the village centre, there are base areas for day visitors who might be staying in Kelowna, for example. Big White also has an extensive trail network for cross country skiers and “the biggest tube park around” (that’s tobogganing on big tyre inner tubes). Quite the complete experience.



THE DETAILS Related Article Ski holidays The Aussie former ski instructor now running North America’s No.1 resort STAY + SKI

Big White’s POWDer Card, available in January, offers flexible three‑ to five‑day lift pass options, while season passes are the best value for guests planning to ski more frequently (they sell “a couple of thousand” of these annually to Australians). For a package including lift passes, equipment hire, accommodation and resort transfers, go through Big White Direct Bookings. See bigwhite.com FLY

Air New Zealand (airnewzealand.com.au) flies daily to Vancouver where there are onward connecting flights to Kelowna (about an hour in the air). Big White is a 55-minute drive from Kelowna Airport; there are frequent shuttle connections in winter, hire cars are also available. Go through Big White Direct Bookings for shuttles. The writer flew to Canada as a guest of Air New Zealand and visited Big White as a guest of Destination British Columbia (supernaturalbc.com) and Big White.

World.title: Dan Gorringe was a battling ruckman. He’s now a social media star and might even become an AFL rights holder
World.content:
Gorringe is edgy, but even the AFL wants him.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you’re a football fan under the age of 35, chances are Dan Gorringe is everywhere when you pick up your phone. Log on to Instagram, he’ll be there, over-celebrating a Carlton win or mourning a loss. You’ll find his mildly more serious football views on his Dan Does Footy YouTube channel. On TikTok, you’ll get his almost instant hot takes, delivered in his typically edgy style. Dan Does Footy podcast host and social media identity Daniel Gorringe has become a key player in the AFL’s targeting of the youth market. Chris Hopkins He’s labelled goalkicking great Matthew Lloyd a “dirty rat”, called prominent broadcaster Gerard Whateley a “muppet”, and told arguably the greatest player of all time Leigh Matthews to “f--- up”. He has had commercial partnerships with corporate bookies, sports drinks and alcohol brands. It will come as a surprise, then, that Gorringe the footballer was the polar opposite in personality. “He was as straight as six o’clock,” his first senior coach Guy McKenna said. Former Carlton captain and one of Gorringe’s closest friends Sam Docherty, who was unwittingly embroiled in his stoush with Whateley, said his former teammate was rarely the centre of attention in the Blues locker room.



“He was fairly quiet, [but] still very funny,” Docherty said. “If you listen to him speak, he’s probably socially anxious and awkward through footy because he didn’t know where he stood or what he was doing. He always had that funny side to him. “He joked around with a small group of mates as opposed to the whole locker room. Most people who played with him would have thought he was fairly reserved and didn’t speak very much.” Dan Gorringe takes on North Melbourne’s Todd Goldstein in a ruck contest in 2016. Getty Images In many ways, Gorringe is the most unlikely of football personalities: polarising, unfiltered and contemptuous of traditional media. But even the AFL wants him. Traditionally, it has taken a long and distinguished on-field career for a retired player to make it in the media. Though a No.10 pick in 2010, his 26 games for Gold Coast and Carlton fall well short of the mark. As a player, his most memorable moment came in retirement when he clattered into comedian Dave Hughes in a legends charity match. But the world of social media does not follow the same rules, and there are few in Australian sport better at playing this game than Gorringe, who has a team of more than 10 full-timers and additional casual and part-time staff behind the scenes managing content and his commercial partnerships. His success is no accident.



The former ruckman has a greater digital presence than some clubs. His 378,000 followers on Instagram is well over double that of Gold Coast, the club that drafted him. His 43,200 subscribers on YouTube is close to 50 per cent higher than another of his former teams, Carlton, and his TikTok following of 298,000 is more than the Blues and Suns combined. His average of more than 300,000 views and 20,000-plus engagements per content item across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube makes him “one of Australia’s highest-performing independent sports creator brands”, Nathan Powell, the chief product and strategy officer at AI-powered creator technology platform Fabulate, said. “Dan has managed to build something that’s much harder than simply accumulating followers,” Powell said. AFL CEO Andrew Dillon with influencer Dan Gorringe, announcing the league’s first official watchalong. AFL “He’s built a highly concentrated Australian sporting audience that consistently chooses to engage with his content. The audience is also predominantly male and heavily concentrated in the 18-to-34 demographic, which is one of the most valuable audiences for sporting organisations and advertisers. “That tells me people aren’t just following Dan because they know who he is – they’re following him because they genuinely value his perspective on sport and the content he creates.” No wonder the AFL has Gorringe on its books as part of what its customer and commercial boss Bec Haagsma says is a “rapid transformation and evolution of our fan engagement and fan experience strategy”. They see Gorringe as pivotal to targeting the younger market – those under the age of 34.



In collaboration with the league’s broadcast partners, Gorringe appeared on The Ultimate Footy Watchalong for the Fremantle v Sydney and North Melbourne v Melbourne games, streamed live on the AFL’s YouTube channel, Kayo and 7plus. “Watchalongs”, where fans stream themselves watching a game live and connect online in real time, are a new concept in Australia and, if experience overseas is any indication, here to stay. “It goes back to the idea that media is changing, and social media is a massive part of the media industry,” Michael Neill, the head of Fox Footy, said. “It won’t get any smaller. We’d be foolish if we didn’t look at these new ideas and different ways to broadcast. “The immediacy of his posts and how he gets his opinion out there really quick, it’s out there and it’s different. “It comes from an ex-player’s perspective as well, and from someone who’s very smart when it comes to communication and how to get his message out there.” For Seven, it gives the network another way to reach the younger market.



“Working with creators who love the game allows us to connect with audiences in authentic new ways,” Seven’s head of sport digital Kirsty Bradmore said. “We are continually exploring more ways to innovate our broadcast offering for viewers across Australia.” This collaboration drew 250,000 live viewers across the league’s YouTube channel, Kayo, Foxtel and 7plus to watch while Gorringe and co-hosts – Seven reporter Xander McGuire and Collingwood AFLW captain and Kayo personality Ruby Schleicher – casually discussed the game, as opposed to the serious analysis on the main coverage. Socceroos goalkeeper Patrick Beach, a GWS fan, featured at half-time. ‘People aren’t just following Dan because they know who he is – they’re following him because they genuinely value his perspective on sport and the content he creates.’ Nathan Powell of creator technology platform Fabulate “Dan has been with us for a year now doing some hardcore engagement stuff,” Haagsma said. “He’s part of that strategy. For us, looking at how we attract, retain and engage with our avid fans is a different proposition to our younger fans. “We knew we needed to engage a different strategy. We can’t put highlights on TikTok and go, ‘That will bring the kids in’. Dan has got a voice that we know speaks in a different way, and just resonates. He’s authentic in his point of view, and he loves the game.” Gorringe’s channel markets itself as “unfiltered and unqualified”. The wider football community saw this side in March after he aired a voice memo left by Docherty of a candid and expletive-laden analysis of his former club’s failings in their thumping by Sydney on the opening night of the season. Gorringe did not check with Docherty if the message was to be aired, as is the practice in mainstream media, drawing condemnation from Whateley – who slammed him for “reprehensible behaviour”.

World.title: Knock on wood, but I think I’ve wasted enough time on silly superstitions
World.content:
August 1, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We were sitting outside in the sun, on the broad steps of Sydney’s new fish market, when a bird flew overhead and launched a massive poo on the young woman sitting in front of us. The “dropping” was enormously accurate and voluminous, covering all of her left hand, part of her left arm and much of her dress. Keen to make her feel better, I told her: “They say it brings good luck.” What’s so bad about a black cat? Getty Images Her boyfriend turned with a smile. “In that case,” he says, “she’s in for a lot of good luck. Heaps of it.” At which point he began helping with the laborious clean-up. What are the origins of these superstitions? Who was the first person to see someone cop a flying splodge of bird poo, and then say: “They say it brings good luck”?



I understand the principle: something unfortunate has happened, so you want to make the person feel better. But why bird poo? We don’t offer this consolation after other misfortunes. If someone smacks their head into a low-lying branch, we don’t say: “Lucky dog! You better buy a lottery ticket.” If you get mugged, the thief pushing you to the ground and stealing your phone, the next person along doesn’t help you to your feet with the cheery observation: “Well, there’s nothing like a violent mugging to bring a bit of good luck.” Most superstitions make no sense. Why does a rabbit foot bring great fortune? It certainly didn’t work for the rabbit from which it was removed. And what’s so bad about a black cat? You wouldn’t dream of judging a person according to the colour of their skin, but apparently cats are fair game. It’s true my generation didn’t have YouTube or Netflix, but frankly we were flat-out keeping the devil at bay. When I was growing up, we lived in a world of superstitions. We were told not to step on the cracks in the pavement, to avoid the number 13, and to never open an umbrella when indoors. Saying something positive about oneself or hopeful about the future was generally frowned upon. But if you insisted – “hopefully I’ll pass my exams”, “no way will I crash my bike” – you had to immediately say “knock on wood” and then find some wood on which to knock. Since most 1970s houses were constructed from a mix of fibro, brown linoleum and orange Laminex, this was often hard to achieve.



Also, every time someone sneezed you had to say “bless you”, which apparently stopped the devil from using that moment of inattention to enter their soul. If you spilt salt, you also had to throw some over your left shoulder (using your right arm) which had the excellent effect of blinding the devil as he hovered at your shoulder. It’s true my generation didn’t have YouTube or Netflix, but frankly we were flat-out keeping the devil at bay. Special occasions such as birthdays were marked by a dinner of roast chicken, the climax of which involved two people grasping the “wish bone” and tearing it in two, good fortune going to the person who ended up with the larger bit of bone. The chicken, already having been throttled, plucked and baked, might have wondered about the purpose of this final indignity, yet it was not possible to eat a chicken while leaving its furcula alone. At Christmas, meanwhile, a silver sixpence would be baked into the Christmas pudding, ready to bring good luck to whoever found it. Or bad luck if you were a seven-year-old and ended up with it stuck in your windpipe, a leading cause of Christmas hospitalisations. The same coin, should it be located in the pudding or returned later by the surgeon, could then be offered as payment for a kitchen knife should you wish to give a knife as a present. It was bad luck to give knives as gifts – it would “cut” the friendship – so the gift had to be turned into a purchase. We were also told we could get rid of warts by “washing our hands in moonlight”, or rubbing them with a piece of meat which you’d then bury in the backyard. If you’ve ever found an old chop bone in your backyard, it was buried there by some warty kid.



You may think this was a charmingly enchanted world, but it did add a lot of fuss to the simplest of tasks, as we were constantly forced to leap over cracks, throw salt over our shoulders, and search for wood to knock upon. In hay fever season, you’d bless more people than the local priest. Related Article Opinion

Health I’m just a creature of habit. Sometimes that creature is a gorilla Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist Did any of the superstitions make sense? Perhaps a couple. I still avoid walking beneath a ladder, based on the practical consideration that a bucket of paint might be up there somewhere, ready to fall on my head. I also believe that it’s bad luck to put shoes on a table – the bad luck being the transmission of some nasty bug, picked up off the floor of a Sydney bus. As for those low-flying birds at the Sydney Fish Market, I’m betting they did bring good luck. That young woman’s boyfriend was so solicitous, tenderly dabbing her with napkins. It was probably the confirmation for which she’d been hoping: this one was a keeper. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: An ‘informal’ will and the missing jewellery: What will happen to Virginia Giuffre’s $30 million estate?
World.content:
Virginia Giuffre was trying to reclaim control. In early January 2025, she was allegedly assaulted by her husband, Robbie Giuffre, during a family holiday in Dunsborough, Western Australia. Robbie then secured a family violence restraining order against Virginia, which banned the prominent Epstein accuser from contacting her two youngest children for six months. It also meant she was not allowed to go to the family’s beachfront home in Perth, which is where her belongings – including important documents, her memoir manuscript, jewellery and mementos – were kept. So Virginia decided to take back some control and spoil herself.



Virginia’s carer, Cheryl Myers, estimates the mother of three spent about $100,000 at luxury jeweller Linneys, and a local pearl retailer, on jewellery for her mother, and diamond rings and necklaces for herself. She had the money to splurge. As Good Weekend senior writer and Walkley Award-winner Melissa Fyfe and WAtoday journalist Carla Hildebrandt reveal in The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald’s four-part investigative podcast, Virginia, the payments Virginia received from various confidential settlements with prominent people – such as the man formerly known as Prince Andrew – came to the equivalent of $US25 million ($35.6 million).



What’s remarkable about this shopping spree is not the amount of money Virginia spent. Rather, as Fyfe and Hildebrandt reveal in episode four of Virginia – out today – it’s that, more than a year on from Virginia’s death, no one seems to know where the jewellery is. Related Article Visual story

Domestic violence ‘Mommy pls call’: The secret ‘scrapbook’ of Virginia Giuffre “Everybody wants to know about the jewellery,” says Myers. “A couple of days after Virginia had passed, one of Virginia’s friends called me, and asked me, ‘Where was the jewellery?’ And I was like, ‘I’ve got no idea’. “She said, ‘Well, we’ve been to the house, me and Rob, and we’ve looked everywhere for the jewellery, and we can’t find any’. And I said, ‘Well, I don’t know’.” But the jewellery is only one part of the puzzle. Virginia also had a chunk of money in cryptocurrency, and now no one knows what happened to that investment.



Virginia Giuffre is pictured here outside a Manhattan court after Jeffrey Epstein’s death in 2019. She received the equivalent of $US25 million in confidential payments after multiple legal battles over the years. AP Following Virginia’s suicide in April 2025, the rift between her family in the United States, including her two brothers, and Robbie worsened. They are now embroiled in a legal battle over Virginia’s estate, which is estimated to be worth up to $30 million, including the compensation payments, assets, investment properties and book royalties. Virginia, whose divorce from Robbie had not been finalised before her death, died without a valid will. She was supposed to sign it on April 26, 2025 – the day after she died – and had marked this date on the magnetic whiteboard on her fridge. Myers and Virginia’s Perth lawyer, Karrie Louden, say Virginia had an “informal will” expressed to Louden and also emailed to her accountant in February 2025.



“I don’t want Robbie blowing my children’s money on himself.” Virginia Giuffre’s diary notes, written before her death This is backed by Virginia’s brothers and their wives. The “informal will” stipulates a small amount of money going to Virginia’s family and friends, including Myers and her brothers, but the bulk to her children and a small amount to Robbie. They say she wanted the money held in trust until the kids turned 25. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life According to court filings, Virginia’s sons Christian and Noah – backed by their father – are arguing their mother lacked “testamentary capacity” when the informal will was created. If Christian and Noah win, Robbie stands to inherit just over a third of what’s left after the divorce settlement, with the remainder divided between the three children: Christian, Noah, and their daughter.



That would make Robbie the main beneficiary, and most likely the administrator of Virginia’s worldwide estate. “What a terrible, tragic story that everything that she fought for against monsters of sexual assault on the most powerful level, every single dollar is going to go back into the hands of her final abuser, and that’s the last chapter,” says Sky Roberts. “Can we imagine that that’s the way the story ends? Because I can’t, and I can’t live with that.” Listen to the fourth episode of Virginia – where hosts Fyfe and Hildebrandt reveal Virginia’s arrest weeks before her death, the real story behind the bus crash that prompted Virginia to tell the world she had days to live, the complicated truth behind her posthumous memoir, and how Virginia’s suicide is part of a wider, systemic problem that is impacting other Australian women – in the player above, wherever you get your podcasts, or click here.



A statement from Robbie Giuffre’s lawyers says the following: “What appears to be an orchestrated attempt by persons to gain financially from Virginia’s death by making unsubstantiated allegations, when they should have been aware of Virginia’s medical conditions, is simply disgraceful. “In the late Virginia Giuffre’s book published and titled Nobody’s Girl, Virginia praised and thanked Robert for his support of her throughout their marriage and in particular, her struggle to be heard.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636.
